HERBERT A. HUEBNER
GRAND MASTER OCTOBER 16, 1970- 0cTOBER 15 1 1971

Herbert A. (Herb) Huebner is known as a "Mason's Mason." Bear witness
this with his election as Chairman of the Conference of Grand Masters of
;ortb.America in February, 1971, convened in Washington, D.C.. Throughout
Jail Grand Lodge activities he tempered justice with mercy and compassion.
M the 104th Grand Master of this jurisdiction his reputation for sound
]eadership is renowned. Herb's legal background served him well. He demands
the facts seeks counsel and then makes his determinations. Always his
tbollgbts ~re for the benefit of the Craft and the image of Freemasonry. Herb
is a man befitting the Rank; serious, dedicated, able to move to what ever
tevel he is called. Recall his custom of circulating among his Brethren to
Issue warm words of friendship and greetings to those known and unknoW11
to him. Others will recall his stem, yet scholarly admonitions, decisions and
actions which reflect his burning desire to create unity, growth and respect

for Masonry.
Our Grand Master was born in Washington, D. C. in 1902 and moved to
• Fresno in 1906 with his family. There he attended public schools and in
1920 came to Southern California and attended the University of Southern
California. After completing his undergraduate work and only two years of
Jaw school he took the California Bar Examination, passed it and commenced
bis cllstinguished career in patent law in 1926. In 1936 he became a member
also of the New York Bar.
Professionally, he served industry as a corporate patent counsel in New
York for seven years and later, upon returning to California, became founder
and present senior partner of his patent law firm in Los Angeles and Fresno.

In 1925 he married a native daughter, Lorna Pierce, the daughter of a
distinguished Los Angeles physician and surgeon. A son Harlan, a daughterin-law Joan, three granddaughters Jo-Ellen, Lori and Libby and a brother Jim
complete his immediate family. Harlan as a young man was active in
DeMolay, in due time became a Past Master of Wilshire Lodge No. 445, and
bas been serving Grand Lodge as Chairman of the Code Commission and Code
Revision Committee.

HERBERT A. HUEBNER

Herb's Masonic life commenced in 1938 when he was raised in Wilshire
Lodge No. 445. While serving as Master of that Lodge in 1944 he was active
u a member of the Grievances Committee of Grand Lodge. He has served on
the History Committee and Chairman of the Charters and Public Schools
Committees. Intervening he was Grand Orator in 1954. It was during that
)'Mr after a constitution ceremony he was inspired to compose the poem

Expansion Council. He has been a member of the Los Angeles Rotary Club
for more than 25 years. In religious faith he is a Presbyterian.
His charm, friendly smile, warm greetings and affection for Masons
"withersoever dispursed," and his ability to lead yet not dictate, make him
truly a Grand Master.

form and length this presentation should take. This was not, I remind you,

I found it almost a pattern that my very worthy and reverend brethren

I believe I have, during my Chaplaincy, informed the Grand Master re.
peatedly of my pleasure in working with him and with his officers - but - I
have done it in another way. I have informed him that he used a superlative
degree of wisdom when he appointed me as the Grand Chaplain. I have also
mentioned to him and to the appointed and to the elected brethren how
fortunate they were to have me as their Chaplain. This appointment was
one of the best of the Grand Masters selections.
.To change the. mood just a bit, I have traveled with many groups, delegations and committees and without reservation I can report that these, your
officers, have been superior. The roster of the attendance of Grand Lodge
officers at Grand Lodge functions has been remarkable. There were lighthearted times of fellowship, all within the bounds of propriety, but always
the serious responsibilities of Grand Lodge assignments were carried out in
the dignified manner which these tasks demand. These duties, well performed
brought honor and dignity to the Grand Lodge. I wish to voice publicly m~
respect and fraternal love for each of my Grand Lodge brethren and my admiration for the manner in which they carried out the responsibilities of
their respective offices.
Many temptations present themselves as one contemplates the opportunities which are afforded a Chaplain on an occasion such as this. Here is a
splendi.d, a captive audience of well informed Master Masons. What an opportumty to promote a pet theme or scheme!
Naturally I had a full year in which to prepare this message. Quite
naturally I waited. until October came, and then a little longer, before writing
a word of that which I am to say today. Oh yes, the thought of what I might
say has haunted me for months. Sometimes I had some brilliant ideas even
in the middle of the night, but I refrained from making hurried notes. Afways,
I thought, some real inspiration will come! Finally, in all seriousness I faced
the fact that the time was almost now and I had better get to work:
Many years ago, in another State, I was given a monitor. At that time
quite by habit, I turned to an explanation of the Grand Chaplain's duties'.
Naturally, I never expected to find myself in such position. Now, so many
years later, I recalled what a profound impression this reading had made
on me. In keeping with my philosophy, that there is no such thing as
chance or of luck, that nothing ever "just happens" but that everything is
for a purpose, I found my old monitor. Now, almost forty-two years have
passed since I received it and time and again in my packing and moving I
d~ided ~o. discard it, but, here it was. Then all thoughts of bringing something bnlliant and popular left my mind. I felt that I had truly found the
key to that which I am to say today. Let me share this with you. It is taken
from the Installation Ceremony in another jurisdiction. The installation of
the Grand Chaplain reads: "Reverend and Worshipful Brother that book
which is the chart and textbook of your sacred calling, is also th~ great light
of Masonry, and forever sheds its benign rays upon every lawful assembly

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

7

free and Accepted Masons. Teach us from its life-giving precepts; inter-

Cllle for us with the Divine Majesty which it so fully reveals and unfolds to

and warm us with the lessons of infinite wisdom and truth, and you will
: . faithfully performed your sacred functions and fulfilled your important
trUll· It is fitting that an emblem of that sacred volume should be the jewel
of your office - - - ." What a splendid explanation of a Chaplain's duties!
DuriJJg the year I instinctively endeavored to live by this teaching; how
JDuch better had I read the words so much earlier in my Masonic Chaplaincy.
But that is past and there is still this my message. Suffice, I found the theme
uiJ' the inspiration for which I had been seeking.
In p.ieparation for a message to "warm us with lessons of infinite wisdom
and truth" I turned to a rereading of the Old Testament prophets. Masons
would do well to turn to this source for readings that will educate, inform
and edify with thoughts Masonic.
In Isaiah 6: 1-8 I found again a very beautiful story, simply told. These
events took place 2 700 years ago. This is my interpretation of the meaning
of the story: It tells of a young man who had placed his trust in a young
lting. He, and some of his young friends were certain that their future, honors
and assignments, depended on the King. Suddenly the King died. Greatly
saddened the young men sought and found, through a remarkable religious
emperience, much more than an earthly King could ever have provided.
Answering His call to service they realized their own unworthiness, were
cJeam;ed of their sins and iniquities, and prepared to serve "The Lord of
Hosts." With that as a background let me now recite the account as you will
find it recorded in your Bible, the Book of Isaiah, Chapter VI- Verse 1-8:
"In the year that King Uzziah died I also saw the Lord sitting upon a
throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple. Above it stood
the Seraphims: each one had six wings; with twain he covered his face, with
twain he covered his feet, and with twain he did fly. And one cried unto
another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord of hosts: the whole earth is
filled.with his glory. And the posts of the door moved at the voice of him
that cried, and the house was filled with smoke. Then said I, Woe is me!
for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips and dwell in the midst
of a people of unclean lips: for mine eyes have seen the King, The Lord of
Hosts. Then flew one of the seraphims unto me, having a live coal in his
hand, which he had taken with tongs from the altar: And he laid it upon my
mouth and said, Lo, this hath touched thy lips: and thine iniquity is taken
away, and thy sin is purged. Also I heard the voice of the Lord saying,
Whom shall I send and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me."
So, in this account, so movingly told, we seem to hear, vicariously, a call
to service, and after a preparation, a correct answer: "Send me!" And so,
void of the drama, of course, calls of "Whom shall I send!" or "Who will
take this as&gnment?" or "Here is a job which should be done!" has come
to many of us. Just because it lacks the drama does not make the assignment

8

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

less important when it comes to us for community service, church or synagogue, or lodge-connected opportunity. "Whom shall I send" seems to echo
in each lodge, in every community. Certainly our work would prosper even
more if, instead of our usual, "I'm too busy," we might hear someone say,
"Here I am, I'll do it." Then our youth work and our lodge work and our
community activities and our church and synagogue would take on new
life and prosper. Our youth organizations are waiting for such an affirmative
reply I
Having heard such a call, those who are sincere, may well examine themselves and say, "What really does the Lord require of me?" Again I turn to
the Old Testament and in Micah 6:8 I find an answer, clear and unmistakable:
"The Lord hath shown thee 0 man," says Micah, "what is good. And what
does the Lord require of thee but to do justly, to love mercy and to walk
humbly with they God." Hear it again:
1. To do justly - which means, be upright and honest.
2. To love mercy - which means, deal mildly even when severity might
be justified and expected.
3. Walk humbly with thy God - which means, free yourself from pride
and vanity, be unassuming.
So we are progressing: A call - and an experience - and an answer then another question, "What is required of me?" and again a divine reply.
Remarkable isn't it, that when we truly seek we find. Too many of us ask
questions feeling that there is no answer to these our questions, and since
we do not listen for an answer we are satisfied that there is no answer.
Answers are available for our most sincere questions: "Search and ye shall
find," is more than a very nice platitude for the prophet Jeremiah says:
"And ye shall seek me and find me, when ye shall search for me with all
your heart.,,
So, again we progress. We heard a call - experienced a cleansing received an explanatory answer to the question "What is required of me,"
and now move to the more intimate question; "How can I serve?" Many,
many years ago I served in the army in a Field Artillery battery. The battery
to which I was assigned was horse drawn. We traveled about twenty-five
miles each day. Picturesque, as I envision it now over this wide span of years.
I thrilled, and still do at the variety of bugle or trumpet calls. Then, of
course, we were guided and directed by bugle calls. There was an officers
call, a mess call, a charge, a retreat, reveille, taps and dozens of others.
The bugler had better be a man of temporate life and disposition for if his
call was not true and clear and certain he could well lead our battery to
disaster. There was no time to try and interpret a bugle or trumpet call. The
response had to be immediate, an instinctive reaction was necessary, the call
had to be certain. The scripture passage to which I now refer was written
by a soldier, a captain, a centurion and he writes, in 1 Corinthians 14:8
"For if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

9

battle." Now, how does this scripture passage apply to us? During the
~ few years I have been greatly disturbed by the lack of faith and of
~ which our older generation has had in a younger generation.

JllaDY have appeared to have fallen victims to a great whispering campaign

which set out to degrade our youth, and that indiscriminately. That our

,-th needs direction is certain, that it merits our ridicule is questionable.

1'Jle trouble appears to lie in the fact that, like in so many other circumstances
1"I Jump them all into one grouping. Our young people do not deserve such
..,mcation. It would be as right to call all Masons unworthy of respect
blc&1JSe of the actions of a very few. Actually, our statistics would indicate

that a mere 2% of our youth has been getting the head-line treatment and
.tortunately many are branding all of our youth with the brand that a
mere 2% deserve. I am also interested in an 18% of our young people
wbo are even now making a decision whether to choose the high-road or the
low. It is for this 18% and for the 80% who are good, clean and honorable
that I plead. I direct my pleas to you through this scripture passage: "If
die trumpet give an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself for the battle."
Which means to me, that if we as adults can not speak with a certain voice,
how can we expect our youth to follow the high-road to honest, right living.
If we cannot solve the major lessons of life, how can we expect our young
people to find the way? If we continue to damn everything that was the
dnam of our founding fathers how can we expect our youth to kneel at
our altars. It takes adults to mislead youth. Therefore, with all the strength
I can muster I beg of you do not let our young people down I We, in our
generation also had wild, wild dreams and unworthy ambitions. But if in your
case, as in mine there was a steadying influence of an adult, these wild
desires were properly classified and distinquished and life went on without
too much turmoil. It is this guidance which our young people are seeking, it
is this guidance which is lacking, it is this guidance which you can supply.
If the trumpet, if you as a God-fearing adult, do not speak out positively and
clearly on the issues we face and help to supply the answers our honest
seeking youth is requesting, then we are not speaking with a certain voice.
Can you imagine the effect on our youth if we here were dedicated to an
endeavor to understand their wishes, if we would foster and sponsor DeMolay
and our other youth groups - and I mean really sponsor them? If then it is
so difficult for us to distinquish between that which is right and that which
is wrong, how then are our young people to make their decisions? In stating
these things I give credit to the thousands of parents who have maintained
their ~mmunication with their children and grandchildren and to the many
~ have, after a break, reestablished such communication. If the trumpet,
If you, do not speak with a positive, and certain voices, our young people
will look elsewhere for their answers. Needless to say, there are many comIU.Dding and very positive voices which are ready and willing to lead our
10Uth down the low road to ruin. Please do not give up in this fight for the

10

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

moral life of our young people. They are good, they are honest, and the great
majority of them are trying to solve their problems. Do not brand them all
as "no good." Do not sell them short. They are more honest in their dealings
than my generation was!
So we take another step! We have heard a call - experienced a cleansing,
received an answer - had a suggestion to the question, "How can I serve?"
I return again to our Holy writings and find in the Book of Esther 4: 14
these words: "- - and who knoweth whether thou art come into the kingdom
for such a time as this?" Another translation reads: "Who knows whether
thou wast born for such a time as this." "Such a time as this" may mean
many things for many people. I will not grant that these are the world's worst
times. I will not grant that we have become so degraded that we can not find
our way out of this seeming jungle. If I read history correctly I must conclude
that this world has advanced out of darker ages into this present light. If this
were not true many of our efforts are already damned. As Masons we believe
that we are traveling from darkness to light. It would be a denial of all we
hold true if we were not. Who knows but that you were brought into this
world of Masonry for just such a time as this. A time when we must stand
together, that our search for truth, that our quest for light and that our hope
for a marvelous future might be realized.
I have only one more Scripture passage, but most important to us as
Masons. It is found in Hebrew 13: 1 and it reads: "Let brotherly love continue" just that, just as brief as that. "Let brotherly love continue!"
Now you may feel that I have regaled you with Bible passages. Usually
your clergyman uses only one Bible passage for his sermon. That it usual. But
you are not usual, and I am not usual and I think we can handle the Bible
passages I have quoted. Therefore in review, I have tried to explain to you
why I search Scripture for this mornings devotional service. I have tried to
explain the Bible passages:
1. "Here am I send me I "
2. "What does the Lord God require of thee?"
3. "For if the trumpet give an uncertain sound - - - ."
4. "Who knows but that thou wast born for such a time as this?"
5. "Let brotherly love continue."
Now, it is my sincere hope and my earnest prayer that I, in my own
peculiar way, may have obeyed that old mandate of a Grand Chaplain's
duties: "Reverend and Worshipful Brother, that book which is the chart and
textbook of your sacred calling, is also the great light of Masonry, and forever
sheds its benign rays upon every lawful assembly of Free and Accepted
Masons. Teach us from its life-giving precepts; intercede for us with the
Divine Majesty which it so fully unfolds and reveals to us; and warm us
with the lessons of infinite wisdom and truth, and you will have faithfully
performed your sacred functions and fulfilled your important trust."

George Cornwell, The untimely death of the Grand Bible Bearer, George
W. Cornwell, on June 28th, came as a great shock to all who knew this fine
Mason and gentleman.
He was born September 18, 1904 in Louisville, Mississippi. Most of his
adult life was spent in the vicinity of Fort Bragg and Arcata in the heart of
the redwoods where he became a Master Mason in Arcata Lodge No. 106
an June 27, 1949. He served his lodge as Master in 1957 and for the following
thirteen years as officer's coach until his appointment as Grand Bible Bearer
by Grand Master Huebner. He also was active in the Scottish Rite Bodies
and the Shrine. He was engaged in the lumber business for many years in
J.i'ort Bragg and Arcata and at the time of his retirement was storekeeper
for the Georgia Pacific Company.
His funeral was held in Arcata on June 30th and he was laid to his earthly
rest in Fort Bragg on July 1st. He is survived by his widow Pearl and a host
of friends.
Gerald Sanford Levin-Funeral services were held in this Memorial Temp)e on June 8th last for Brother Gerald Sanford Levin under the auspices of
Plcific Lodge No. 136 of San Francisco. Brother Levin was not only eminent
ia his chosen profession as an attorney, he also served his Lodge and this
Grand Lodge with distinction and devotion, in many capacities and on many

committees, and at the time of his passing was a member of the Jurisprudence

Brother Levin was a native of Danville, Illinois, where he was born
January 19, 1907, moving to San Francisco with his family as a boy in 1910.
A graduate of University of California, Berkeley, and Harvard Law School.
As a young attorney he joined the San Francisco Law firm of Pillsbury,
Madison and Sutro in 1931 where he served as a noted civil lawyer. Appointed
to the Municipal Court bench in 1956 and to the Superior Court bench in
1962 where he served until he was appointed to the United States District
Court by President Nixon in June, 1969.
He served Pacific Lodge as its Master in 1945. From 1953 to the time of
his passing he remained active in Grand Lodge serving in the trial procedures,
mutual aid, masonic information, history and jurisprudence committees, and
as Grand Orator in 1960. A past Venerable Master (1953-54) of the San
Francisco Bodies of the Scottish Rite, he attained the highest honor within
the Supreme Council's power when he was coroneted a 33°, Honorary Inspector General in 1963. Brother Levin was also active in Islam Temple of
the Shrine.
The lives of such men are an inspiration to all and the good deeds that
he wrought will long be remembered by his hosts of friends. He is survived
by his wife, Frances, two step brothers, Madison and Donald Marcus and
stepsister, Marilyn Baxter.

Robert E. Burns-Our Supreme Grand Master saw fit to call to his wellearned heavenly home on Saturday, February 13th, Brother Dr. R. E. Burns,
Past Grand Chaplain of the Grand Lodge of California, and at the time of his
passing, President of the University of the Pacific at Stockton, at the age
of 61. A graduate of the then, College of the Pacific, in 1931, he served that
institution in many capacities from that time until his election as president
at the age of 37. The nineteenth president in the school's history, he was
also its first alumnus to attain that distinction and the youngest college president in the state. Under Dr. Bum's administration, the state's oldest chartered college, ( 1851), attained university status. Dr. Burns instituted the
"cluster college" system in 1962 with the opening of Raymond College on
the Stockton campus. Other additions followed; the 67 year old School of
Dentistry, College of Physicians and Surgeons in San Francisco, and Elbert
Covell College as a North American Center for Spanish speaking students.
In addition he instituted Callison College as a school for non-western studies.
In addition, several years ago, the University of the Pacific consented to Dr.
Burns' election as President of the Presbyterian Medical Center in San
Francisco. Subsequently it was changed to the Pacific Medical Center. Under
Dr. Burns' leadership it experienced. a great growth, adding a wing to include
its own University of the Pacific School of Dentistry.

EULOGY
.ALP°RED F. BRESLAUER
By Eugene S. Hopp
,Destiny's child was born in Redding, California, on a bright Wedne

sday

morning, the 26th of August, 1898. His future promise manifested itself at an

ALFR ED F. BRES LAUE R
Grand Maste r - 1960
Born
August 26, 1898
Redding, California

Died
Janua ry 27, 1971
Menlo Park, Califo rnia

early age. He stood near the top of his class at the Pacific Heights
Grammar
School and later at Lowell High School, both in San Francisco.
It was a keen sense of the importance of the individual human being,
and
a regard for duty, obligation and responsibility, which led young Alfred to the
study of law at the University of California and Boalt Hall School
of Law.
In 1922 he was admitte d to the Bar.
A recognition of the need of the world for an underst anding of the brother
hood of man as a fundamental principle of life, inevitably brough t Alfred
Breslauer to receive the degrees of Freemasonry in Starr King Lodge
No. 344
in 1923. He served as Master of that Lodge in 1930.
In consideration of his leadership, his knowledge and understanding of
our ritual, his dedication to the Master Mason, he was appointed Inspect or
of the 43d Masonic Distric t in 1931 and performed most ably in that capacit
y
for seventeen years. Brothe r Al then served on numerous Grand Lodge
Committees, always giving of his time and energies withou t stint. Those of us
who
had the privilege of serving with him as Trustee of the Masonic Homes,
a
Board he ultimat ely headed as its Preside nt, will never forget his devotio
n to
the children and the aged, his skill and never-failing good humor as presidin
g
Clfticer, and his personal commitment to the practice of fundamental Masonic
\'irtues.
In 1960, Brothe r Alfred Fisher Breslauer was elected Grand Master
of
Masons in California and so typically, prompt ly proclaimed the Year
of the
Master Mason with the quote: "It is the high calling of every Mason
to keep

18

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

alive in the hearts of men the love of freedom and the willingness to fight
and die for it if necessary. It will be seen, therefore that the source of power
in Masonry is in the individual Mason. Furthermore, if Masonic power is
to be used to promote the welfare and happiness of the community and to
safeguard the freedom of the people, the individual Mason must exercise it
whenever and wherever it is needed."
It was to help the Lodge in the pursuit of these goals that our dearly
beloved brother first wrote The Master's Handbook in 1941. It was a small
volume that soon came to be the guide for generations of Masonic Lodge
Officers, and still provides today, invaluable assistance in the planning of
Lodge work.
Brother Alfred Breslauer worked in Freemasonry wherever his ability
and service was sought. He was elected Wise Master of the Rose Croix and
later Venerable Master of the Lodge of Perfection in the San Francisco Bodies
of the Scottish Rite, where he also was honored with the 33 °.
Patriotism and service to country being among the charges of an Entered
Apprentice Mason, our brother served as a private in World War I and a
Captain in World War II, on which lat~r occasio? he was in ~e Uni~ed
States Army Specialist Reserve charged with prepanng the Selective Service
Act and Regulations.
In serving his fellow-man, our brother authored the California Small Loan
Act and then was called upon to advise State agencies in administering the
Act. He labored in many civic organizations, including the Commonwealth
Club, the Public Education Society and the Administrative Committee of the
State Bar of California.
Tragedy beyond the patience of Job stalked our Brother's life but throughout he mustered that fortitude which we recall as that noble and steady
purpose of the mind whereby we are enabled to undergo any pain, peril or
danger, when prudentially deemed expedient.
In 1931 Alfred Breslauer married Marion Joseph and they were blessed
with two fi~e children, Kathryn and Alfred J. But Marion was struck down
by a devastating illness.
In 1948 a kind fate brought Al and Margaret Slate to the altar and their
happiness was blessed with a son, B~ce.. But agai~ our M. W. brother was
to see his wife struck down by devastating illness.
Yet amidst these and other personal tragedies our Brother continued to
erect that magnificent house not made wih hands - a life of great moral
values. Just as the Ancient Hebrews knew and wrote of the value of moral
education so did M. W. Alfred Breslauer serve for thirty years as teacher
and Superintendent of Sherith Israel Religious School. Countless young people went forth from that Synagogue school with a better sense of the importance and moral worth of truth, justice, brotherhood and charity. They
learned these lessons not only from his words of instruction but even more
from the example of his life.

In closing his message to this Grand Lodge in 1961, our M. W. Alfred
Breslauer quoted from the great scientist Michael Faraday, and I should
like to paraphrase that quotation: All I can say to you at the end of this
life (and we must all come to an end at one time or another) is to express
the wish that each of you may, in your generation, be fit to compare to his
candlelight; that you may, like him, shine as a light to those about you; that
in all your acts you may justify the beauty of his taper, by making your deeds
honorable and effectual in the discharge of your duty to your fellow-man.

EULOGY
ELBERT

~

I

w. DAVIS

By Donald G. Campbell
When death took our friend and teacher, Elbert W. (Bill) Davis, it removed pillars from the structure of Masonry well nigh impossible to replace.
The Pillar of Strength in his case was Character. Plain spoken and forthright, Bill imparted a sense of integrity to every activity in which he engaged.
Truth, that divine attribute, was the foundation upon which this Pillar stood,
without dissimulation or deceit in any form. We are surrounded by those
who bend the truth. Bill never would because it was not in his character
so to do.
The Pillar of Wisdom was there for everyone to lean upon. Grand Masters
who knew him learned early to depend upon Bill for advice in situations confronting the Grand Lodge and its constituent Lodges, for Wisdom comes from
experience and a wealth of experience had come to Bill over the years. Almost
no situation could arise which had not in the past been dealt with and Bill,
in his capacious memory, could use the lessons there learned to the advantage
of the occasion.
The Pillar of Beauty was truly there in his love of Masonry and his
respect for its ritual and the lessons contained therein. He was a purist
because he was convinced that time had brought down to us a heritage which
was too precious to sully by easy substitution and sloppy execution. As Grand
Lecturer, he imparted to his Assistants the same sense of respect which was
so much a part of him and the Beauty of Masonry shone as a reflection of
this man.
Bill was born in Houston, Texas November 30, 1894 and spent his boyhood there but came to California in time to attend and graduate in law from
the University of California with the Class of 1916. All of his time was not
spent on his law books for within a year after graduation, on April 12, 1917,
he married Marie Kingman. Their marriage carried to Bill's death, a period
of more than fifty-four years, and produced two sons, Willard Kenneth and
Keith Kingman Davis, and a daughter, Gertrude Ellen Nelson. The children,
grandchildren and great grandchildren form a loving circle to sustain Marie
in her years of memory.

20

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Bill actively engaged in his large law practice to the day of his death.
Senior partner in the firm of Hoffman, Davis and Moon, he daily commuted
to his San Francisco office. Upon the withdrawal of P.G.M. Laurence E.
Dayton from the post, Bill assumed, at considerable sacrifice, the post of
attorney to the Board of Trustees of Masonic Homes. His service here, as in
all facets of his Masonic activity, was marked with quiet efficiency and solid
good judgment.
Raised in Francis K.Shattuck Lodge No. 571February24, 1925, Bill chose
the York Rite and was, during his lifetime, a member of Berkeley Chapter
and Berkeley Commandery. His true love was always Blue Lodge Masonry,
however, and joining the appointive line as Marshal in 1934, he served as
Worshipful Master in 1940. Before this, his talents became known and in
1939 Bill was appointed to the Grievance Committee and upon relinquishing
the Master's Chair, he became Inspector of the 33rd Masonic District in
January of 1941, Assistant Grand Lecturer in October, 1949 and, upon the
death of Walter Von Konsky, Grand Lecturer in November of 1952. Reelected through the years, Bill served until December 31, 1959, at which time
and with his blessing, friendship and generous help, the torch was passed to
his successor. Since that time, he has been an invaluable member of the Committee on Jurisprudence, adding the quiet strength and balance of his knowledge to that important Committee.
How to close a tribute to a man like this? Perhaps to say that the final day
was like many others since 192 5 when he first could attend Lodge. In the afternoon, he was in the Grand Lodge office in an ordered review of Homes' matters. That night he attended Lodge, came home to Marie and slept away into
the transition from life to the greater life in that house not made with hands
eternal in the heavens. We have had our lives enriched by the privilege of
knowing this man who was a true Pillar of Masonry.

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE
My Brethren, on October 16, 1970 you confided to me the implements
of speculative Masonry, entrusting me with the care of the Craft in California and Hawaii for a term which concludes on Friday next.
The duties and responsibilities have been challenging, the fraternal support heartening, the friendships created stimulating, and the realization of
having served you to the best of my ability, deficient as it may have been,
has contributed a fullness to my life which could not otherwise have been
achieved. Please accept my profound thanks for the confidence expressed
and the opportunity bestowed.
GENERAL CONDITION OF MASONRY

The general condition of Masonry within the jurisdiction is sound.
Harmony has prevailed within the Grand Lodge official structure and, subject
to a few exceptions, within the Lodges themselves. The exceptions simply
reaffirm the truism that in a membership of more than 233,000 the human
element will sometimes erupt in a fashion not countenanced by the teachings
of Masonry. Where that has occurred I have endeavored to bring about a
better Masonic relationship, and failing that have taken such corrective
steps as my judgment dictated.
The office of Grand Master requires the discharge of executive duties and
the performance of ceremonies together with the pursuit of fraternal
relations.
In the first phase, it has been my policy to delegate responsibilities to
the Committees and Boards which rightfully should assume them, and to
intervene only when I deemed it essential for the welfare of the Craft or
the proper administration of Grand Lodge and its related entities, and the
constituent Lodges. I have found this practice to be effective and productive..
Most Committees and Boards have diligently and intelligently rendered the
required services, some with especially commendable enterprise and devotion.
The counsel, cooperation and support of all the elective Grand Officers
has proved invaluable. The entire appointive line of Grand Officers has demonstrated a loyalty and enthusiasm quite unsurpassed. Residing in areas well
dispersed throughout our Jurisdiction, they have effectively brought the
entire Jurisdiction into closer unity.
In stating that the general condition is sound I do not overlook the
scattered situations where Lodges have suffered depleted membership, financial debility, inharmonious relationship among some of the members, and
lack of officer material. These occur through changing conditions and other
factors, and for the most part are dealt with by mergers, consultation and
admonishment. They are not sufficiently serious to discuss at length except
for those which are treated individually later in this message.

THE RELATION OF MAsoNRY To THE
WoRLo AoouT Us
The Grand Masters' Messages in the years gone by, for a century and
more have decried the state of immorality, the decadence of religion and
cultu~e and diminishing economic stability in our Nation and in the World.
Concu~ently they have declared that Freemasonry has contributed character to our social structure, inspiration to our religious and cultural efforts,
and strength to our economy.
I offer the following observations as prevailing in the month of October
in the year 1971.
During the last five decades we have achieved a life expectancy increased
by fifty percent, we have reduced epidemics to a shadow, we have progressed
in science from elementary in automobiles and aircraft to interplanetary travel
and ground transportation on the moon itself. We can see on a screen and hear
by electronic vibrations people and events on the other side of the world. We
have afforded our youth educational opportunities beyond comparison.
The adult population, however, has failed in some respects. We have
not found a way to end war; we have not offered a solution for racial discrimination · we have not been able to reduce crime nor even to stem it. We
have not b~n able to repress numbers of revolutionary youth, aided and
abetted by traiterous adults, from criminally destroying public school facilities and other property, viciously assaulting our fire department personnel,

29

and villifying and murdering our law enforcement agents. We have not
llllJUlled the tide of resort to the use of drugs. We have witnessed an ap-

palling attrition of patriotism, and loss of respect for our courts of law.

The whole fabric of a relatively minute fractional proportion of the population of this Nation is gangrenous.
We may be grateful that it is a small proportion. But as cancer unchecked
will a,dvance death, growth of these malignant units in our society will toll
tbe death knell of our America unless they are checked and destroyed.
I suggest no compromise. I propose no dialogue with the so-called dissenters who are in reality criminals and anarchists. Our "Home of the Free"
can remain so only by the exercise of control. The pendulum has swung too
far toward judicial leniency, public inaction, and a shedding of individual
.-ponsibili ty.
This overall condition provides the stage of life where Masonry is needed.
)fasonry possesses the man power, augmented by affiliated organi7.ations, to
exert a beneficial influence throughout our society. The potential, however,
js far from being realized. The teachings of Masonry lie dormant in too
many of our members. I would encourage, yes plead, that every man who
bas knelt at a Masonic alter rise daily with a consciousness of tasks confronting him and those about him, and by precept and by example strive for
that true Brotherhood of Man under the Fatherhood of God which we
cherish so fervently. Then, and only then, may the millions and more millions
of our young people gaze upon a vista portraying a world of the future in
which Glory to God and on Earth peace, goodwill to men will be meaningful.

CLANDES TINE MASONRY

I have received letters during the year asking why we do not invite
Negroes of good character into our membership.
Such letters are answered by referring to our inflexible rule that we invite
no one, and to the C.M.C. provision which expressly requires that no man be
denied membership on ac~ount of color. Moreover, I have been informed
that most Negroes who wish to become "Masons " prefer the Lodges where
their own color dominates.
A "non-Ma son" Black reporter for the Fresno Bee asked me for an intervi~w on this su~ject. I gave him detailed answers along the foregoing lines.
His column, which appeared in print under the heading "MASONS BLUR
COLOR LINE" was a fair statement. In the same articl~ he pointedly commented on the exclusion of Blacks by another fraternal order.
Also I have been urged to study the possibility of an understanding with
Black "Gr~d Lodges" whereby· mutual acknowledgement is granted. In one
case I received, as Chairman of the Conference of Grand Masters of North
America, a direct request for recognition "in amity" of a designated "Grand
Lodge".
Such, of course, would be repugnan t to the fundamental American doctrine
tha~ _there can be only one regular Grand Lodge in a given geographical or
political boundary. Moreover, I am informed that there are so many localized
non-organized "Grand Lodges" that even if it were possible to recognize them
in some manner, a state of confusion would manifest itself.
I am aware of the problem for which I have no solution. With the issue
?f r'.1°al ~is~mination and its elimination looming large in the public eye,
it will be mevitable that the subject will require further attention .

CONTINUATION oF SPECIAL CoMMITTEE To PREPARE
SINGLE lIARD BACK VoLUME OF GRAND LoooE HISTORY

It has long been my desire to see a history of Masonry in California and
Hawaii centered around the Grand Lodge, in a single volume of perhaps 400
pages, more or less, written in popular reading style, well illustrated. The
Whitsell four volume work published in 1950 is exceedingly useful for reference, but it does not invite attention by the casual reader, and also much of
interest bas occurred since its publication.
The new history in booklet form referred to above, provides an excellent
outline for the more extended work suggested. Moreover, in the writing of
the booklet, a large amount of material has already been assembled which
can be used.
Probably much more than a year will be required to accomplish the purpose. It has been estimated that the project may require four years or more.
It would be quite significant to have such a book appear in conjunction with
any observance by the Grand Lodge of California of the 200th Anniversary
of the signing of the Declaration of Independence - in 1976.
Therefore, I recommend that Grand Lodge approve the preparation of a
single volume, in popular reading style, revolving around the Grand Lodge,
to be available in time for any Masonic observance of the 200th Anniversary
of the Signing of the Declaration of Independence; and to that objective:
succeeding Grand Masters continue the appointment of a Speci&l Committee
for such purpose; this policy to continue until the task is completed or is discontinued by action of Grand Lodge at an Annual Communication.

To the Masters of the Constituent Lodges:
AUGUST

DEAR BRETHREN:

In this era of the so-called "Generation Gap," more than ever we need
to solidify our relationships with the young men who will, in such a very
short time, be entrusted with our welfare and well-being. We have a definite
~nsibility to encourage and implement their interest and activities in
those areas which will produce the m<>&t desirous results. The Grand Lodge
of California is vitally interested in the development and growth of DeMolay.
You already know of the great concern the Masons of California have for
the future of our public schools, and the young people of DeMolay make
up a substantial percentage of the students in our schools. The precepts
taught in the Order of DeMolay further advance our objectives in our schools;
Jberefore, we in the Fraternity should take great pride in encouraging our
young men to become members of the Order and assist them as they progress.
Since 1952 the Grand Lodge of California has permitted Lodges to
sponsor DeMolay Chapters. Many Lodges presently are sponsoring a Chapter

and are actively promoting DeMolay. However, there are many DeMolay
Chapters suffering from insufficient interest by our Masonic family.
In order to make DeMolay more meaningful to all members of Grand
Lodge and the Masons of California, earlier this year, I appointed a DeMolay
Liaison Board to encourage greater cooperation between the three DeMolay
jurisdictions functioning in California and Hawaii, to .bring about closer c~
operation between our Grand Lodge and the Intemat1onal Supreme Council
of DeMolay in Kansas City and to bring about greater interest and involvement by the Masons of California in DeMolay and its activities. The meetings of the Board have been productive and encouraging.
Being convinced that it is imperative that we act to create more interest
and Masonic involvement in DeMolay, I direct you, as Master of your
Lodge to appoint at least one member of your Lodge to act as a liaison between' your Lodge and the nearest DeMolay Chapter in your area. Your
appointee should be a man who can communicate well with young people
and relate to them and, if possible, should be a former member of DeMolay.
He, or they, should attend at least one meeting of the Chap~r each month,
as well as Advisory Council meetings, if invited by the Councl. He, or they,
should report the activities of the Chapter, to his Lodge at each stated mee~­
ing, thereby generating an interest among our brethren. Our future 10
Masonry, as well as in the Nation, may well lie in these young men.
The appointment should be made prior to the September Sta~ Meeting
of your Lodge. This directive should be read at each Stated Meeting, and the
appointment be announced and recorded in the minutes of the Meeting.
Should you need assistance in implementing this directive, the names of
the DeMolay Liaison Board to which I referred are listed in the 1971 Grand
Lodge Roster. Please feel free to call the one on your area.
Cordially and fraternally,

HAwAnAN VISITATION

The traditional visitation of the Grand Master to the Lodges in Hawaii
was a time of joyous fraternal relationship. At my request the Grand Marshal,
DeWald Baum accompanied Mrs. Huebner and me, and rendered yeoman
services in attending to details of the trip.
From our welcome at the Honolulu Airport laden with exotically scented
ftower leis, to a white tie reception, a lavish luau with entertainment, ~
devotional service on Sunday and a gathering with the youth groups in the
evening, it was a constantly moving panorama.

We cruised Pearl Harbor by courtesy of the Admiral's Barge placing
a wreath at the Arizona Memorial, and offering some words of appreciation
for the sacrifices of the men there entombed.
On Kaui, Maui and Hawaii we enjoyed the hospitality of the Masons
and their wives at informal dinners and on automobile tours.
It is a land and people beautiful to behold.
PROPOSED GRAND LoDGE OF HAWAII
At the 1970 Annual Communicaton, Grand Master MacPhee reported

ID bis Annual Message the results of a survey conducted by written ballot
among the Lodges in Hawaii concerning the possibility of forming a Grand
~

Lodge of Hawaii. Of the ballots cast, a large majority of the members voting "indicated they were not in favor of a new Grand Lodge of Hawaii.

Seven of the ten Hawaiian Lodges voted heavily against a new Grand Lodge.

Three of the ten Lodges voted in favor of such a Grand Lodge." (1970
Proc. p. 40).
During the current Masonic year the subject of a proposed Grand Lodge of
Hawaii has been activated by the adoption of resolutions in six of the
Hawaiian Lodges providing for the election of a commission to meet with similar
commissions of other Lodges and empowered, authorized and directed conjointly with the other commsissions to form a Grand Lodge of Hawaii.
Each resolution has been adopted by a majority vote of those members present at a Stated Meeting. No assent has been solicited or obtained from those
members who were unable to or for any reason, did not attend even if it be a
llUDllDOned meeting.
These actions cannot go unnoticed, especially because there is a marked
division of opinion on the subject among the brethren residents of Hawaii.
On the Grand Master's visitation to Hawaii, in July last, numerous Masonic
groups, as well as individual brethren, sought and were accorded conferences
with the Grand Master on the topic.
It is recognized that three Chartered Lodges in a State where no Grand
Lodge has been established have the right to meet in convention and organize a
Grand Lodge for such state. (C.M.C. Sec. 16(r).)
Historically there is no record of any problem involving the determination
of each Lodge to enter into the compact with the other Lodges. The method
of reaching such determination conceivably could be a factor in arriving
at a conclusion whether the new Grand Lodge was regularly established.
The situation in Hawaii presents some other complications for which
there appear to be no fully responsive precedents, and which would discourage exercise of the "three Lodge" rule.
Hawaiian Masonry has been closely allied to California Masonry since
1852, and all ten Lodges in Hawaii were chartered by the Grand Lodge of Calibnia, and continue their existence as constituent Lodges within the jurisdiction of California. There are no Lodges in Hawaii chartered by other Grand
Jurisdictions.

Under these conditions, your Grand Master is of the opi?ion tha~. he, and
upon proper presentation, Grand Lodge, owe to our Lodg~s m Hawau and to
the Masons who are their members, a policy statement m the nature of an
advisory declaration, with guidelines delineating procedures w~ich would J?rovide a basis for cooperation and support by our Grand Lodge m the orgaruzational program of our Brethren in Hawaii, and formal recognition of the Grand
Lodge of Hawaii when that eventuality is attained.
This approach is offered in the interest of harmony and the general welfare
of the Craft.
The position of your Grand Master, the Deputy Grand Master and the
Senior and Junior Grand Wardens is that if a majority of the Lodges in Hawaii,
by fair and equitable procedures, resulting in concurrence by a majority of the
members of these Lodges, unite in the movement for a Grand Lodge of Hawaii,
they should be accorded due cooperation and support, and that the remaining
Lodges, in the interest of harmony and the welfare of the Craft, should accede
to the will of the majority.
Suggested procedures will next be discussed.
In the first place, there is no express provision in the Uniform Code of
By-Laws adopted for and by Lodges, or in the California Masonic Code, prescribing action to be taken by a constituent Lodge looking to its participation
in forming a new Grand Lodge. It should not be transacted as routine business.
Nor is a summoned meeting the full answer, because it is well known that by
reason of residence elsewhere or absence in service many members of Hawaiian
Lodges cannot attend.
A procedural analogy is found in the provisions for the consolidation of two
or more Lodges, for in such case at least one of the Lodges receives a new
Charter or an endorsement on its original Charter.
The applicable law is found in Sec. 375 C.M.C. (Supp.). Briefly, it provides
that two or more Lodges contemplating consolidation, should adopt at a stated
meeting, a resolution that a consolidation is expedient, and that committees be
appointed to meet and arrange terms.
Notice in writing of the adoption of such resolution is given forthwith to
all members of the Lodge. The signature of at least three-fourths of the members of each Lodge shall be obtained to a paper or papers substantially in this
form: "In pursuance of certain action of .....• Lodge ••.••. and ...••.
Lodge No...•... , tending to the consolidation of said Lodges into one Lodge,
under the name and number of ...... Lodge No..•.... , we, the undersigned,
members of ...... Lodge No....... , do hereby express our assent to and our
desire for such proposed consolidation."
At a stated meeting not earlier than the third stated meeting after adoption
of the first Resolution, the Master of each Lodge shall canvass the consents of
members of his Lodge, and if he finds the required number of consents have
been properly signed, he shall declare the consolidation to be approved by said
Lodge.

If the Grand Master shall find it impracticable for a Lodge to secure the
requisite written consents, he may approve the consolidation upon the written
consent of not less than a majority of the members of each Lodge.
That general procedure, modified to adapt it to the Haw.~iian situation,
would appear to be entirely feasible, fair and equitable. The wntten consent of
a majority should be accepted.
This should be done by obtaining the signature of at least a majority of the
members of eachLodge on a paper or paper substantially in ~s form:."Subj~ct
to similar action of at least five other regular Lodges located m Hawan, tending
to the formation of a Grand Lodge of Hawaii, we, the undersigned, members
of ...... Lodge No ......• , do hereby express our assent to and our desire for

such proposed Grand Lodge.

Some portions of the foregoing memorandum possibly mig~t be cons~ed
to be legislative in character, but there appears t? be n.o purpose m perpetu~ting
in the California Masonic Code provisions dealing with a non-recurring Situation. Moreover, these guidelines are not offered as mandatory, but as a statement of policy upon which cooperation can be predicated.
Your Grand Master has upon occasion outlined in general the thoughts
expressed in the foregoing statement, and has suggested that Hawaiian Lodges
defer action pending a statement of guidelines and possible action at the Ann~~

I would remind the latter group of Brethren that the Grand Master's responsibility extends to all members of our jurisdiction, which includes those who may
not as well as those who do desire the immediate formation of a Grand Lodge

TO THE LODGES IN THE STATE OF HAWAII AND TO THE

It is reported to me that six Lodges in Hawaii, all in the 382nd
and 384th Masonic Districts, have by ballot at Stated Meetings
voted to form a Grand Lodge of Hawaii and each has elected commissioners with authority and power to join with the others in the
creation of such Grand Lodge;
That the total vote in favor was approximately 246, with 109 in
opposition, the yes vote representing approximately 7% of the total
membership of the ten Lodges in Hawaii;
That in no case has a majority of the membership of a Lodge
assented by written ballot or otherwise to this purpose;
......
That my advisory guidelines have been ignored or rejected by
the officers and members of the six Lodges which are the proponents;
That a meeting of the commissioners has been called for October 9, 1971, and another for October 23, 1971.
The other four Lodges in the 385th Masonic District have refrained from comparable action.
All Lodges, their officers and members are reminded that they
are chartered by and owe their allegiance to the Grand Lodge of
California, and that such Grand Lodge maintains jurisdiction over
all. In the present posture of the situation a Lodge has the choice
of (1) continuing in that relationship; or (2) surrendering its char-

It is clear from developments that any Grand Lodge action adopting in
principle the initially recommended guidelines merely as advisory for the
Lodges in Hawaii would probably be insufficient. Therefore in order to
preclude a possible confusion in the Masonic structure in Hawaii a further
declaration of principles more positive in character is also recommended as
follows:
I. The Lodges in Hawaii are constituent Lodges of the Grand Lodge of
California and owe their allegiance to such Grand Lodge unless and until
they request and obtain permission to sever that allegiance in order to become
constituent Lodges of a Grand Lodge of Hawaii. No such request has been
received from any Lodge in Hawaii.
II. Those Lodges are informed that the Grand Lodge of California does
not look with favor upon the creation of a Grand Lodge of Hawaii by a small
tninority of the members of the Hawaiian Lodges. This would not be considered as a representative action, and the Grand Lodge of California does
not propose to recognize any such Grand Lodge as regularly formed.
III. The Grand Lodge of California, on the record now at hand, does not .
regard the Commissioners presently elected for the purpose of meeting to
form a Grand Lodge of Hawaii as possessing the requisite authority to accomplish such purpose.

DEDICATION OF MASONIC HALLS

For some unexplained reason, there is a notation in the Book of Ceremonies
that the dedication of Masonic Halls is a tiled ceremony. I have found no
legislation nor action by Grand Lodge imposing this restriction.
The Ceremony is one which illustrates certain principles of Masonry without revealing any of its secrets. The entire Ceremony is printed. It is a sequel
to the Cornerstone Ceremony which is open to the public.
I inquired of the Grand Lecturer if there was any reason why the public
should not witness the Ceremony, and his reply was that there was no reason
to bar the public.
It was my opinion that the image of Masonry would be enhanced by
making this Dedication Ceremony open to non-Masons. Also relevant are the
facts that the wives and families of Masons frequently contribute services and
gifts in the erection and furnishing of a Temple, and consequently bold a personal interest in it. The Order of Eastern Star and the Youth Organizations
frequently bold their meetings in the Temple.
After Grand Lodge is opened, it can be called off for the purpose of dedication the same as calling off for a cornerstone laying, and the public may then
be invited into the Lodge Room.
Upon consultation with the Deputy Grand Master, the Senior and Junior
Grand Wardens, and with the Ritual Committee, I found them to be in unanimous accord with the proposal. I therefore declared that the Ceremony of Dedication may be open to the public.
We have followed this practice on most occasions since the decision was
announced. Without exception, the reaction of both Masons and non-Masons
has been very favorable, and attendance has been excellent.
This practice involves no change in the Ritual. Since no legislation is required, I recommend the adoption by Grand Lodge of this procedure as a
matter of policy.
The Assistant Grand Lecturers have all concurred with the Grand Lecturer
in the expediency of the proposed changes.
Your Grand Master, upon being fully informed of th~ proposal, :ind upon
ultation with the Deputy Grand Master and the Senior and Jumor Grand
~=dens finding them to be unanimously in accord, has app~oved the changes
recommended by the Ritual Committee, to become effective on Thursday,
October 14, 1971.

The ceremony of presenting veteran buttons to brethren wh~se me!°bership spans half a century is not readily adaptable nor fully meaningful m the

MORTGAGE BURNING CEREMONY

It is gratifying to note that retirement of mortgages on Masonic Temples
has occasioned increasingly frequent requests for the performance by the
Grand Master and Grand Officers of Mortgage Burning Ceremonies. Such
is an occasion of joy and thanksgiving.
Prior to this year we have not had an official ceremony for this purpose,
and until recently the Grand Officers have assembled at the Temple involved
and performed an impromptu ceremony.
Seeing the need and desirability of a uniform presentation for the intended purpose, the Grand Lecturer, Very Worshipful H. Douglas Lemons,
prepared a ceremony which is appropriate and meaningful. ~r~t and
appreciation for the basic text which the Grand Lecturer utilized and
modified is extended to Ralph H. Head, P .M. and former Grand Orator who
authored the ceremony performed in burning the mortgage on the California
Masonic Memorial Temple. The ceremony prepared by the Grand Lecturer
has the full approval of the Assistant Grand Lecturers. It has the approval
and the commendation of your Grand Master.
There being no prohibition to prevent, we have used it on several occasions with sincere approbation by the brethren whose Temple has been freed
of incumbrance.
A copy of this ceremony is printed below.

task of adopting this addition to our ceremonial observances.
I recommend that the Mortgage Burning Ceremony, as set forth in the

MORTGAGE BURNING CEREMONY
This ceremony is open to all Masons, their families, friends and other
interested persons.
The Lodge should be open in the Masters Degree and called from
labor to refreshment for the purpose of conducting the Mortgage Burning
Ceremony.
The Lodge room is prepared by placing a small table midway between
the altar and the east upon which should be placed a burning crucible in
the center, three small vials of burning fluid, one on north side of table,
one on south side and the other on the west side. A candle in a candlestick
holder should be placed on the east side of table.
The officers of the Lodge are seated in the first row of seats on the
northeast of the Lodge in rank, the Master nearest the east. They wear the
jewels and aprons of their stations.
If the Grand Master fills all the stations and places, the Grand Officers
form outside the Lodge room and enter in the same manner as they enter
for a Grand Lodge opening; regalia is worn. The Master of the Lodge will
raise those present by three raps of the gavel as the Grand Officers enter
the Lodge room, then retire to his position in the northeast.
When all the Grand Officers are in their stations, the Grand Master will
ask all present to join him in the Pledge of Allegiance to the Flag, after
which he will seat the lodge.

Grand Master: From the beginning of time men have been builders. The
earliest man first lived in natural caves but eventually he built
his own dwelling of stones, of hide, of twigs, and branches.
Through the centuries man became more adept and experienced.
His buildings grew in height and stability and eventually in
beauty. As man became more civilized and began to reason, he
realized that there were forces and phenomena beyond his
comprehension and understanding.
It became his nature to fear that which he could not understand
and finally fear turned into a form of worship by which the
forces he experienced but did not understand would be appeased
and pleased. Sacrifices of food and other importa nt worldly
possessions were offered - first on altars in the open and then
enclosed in temples.
And so it is that over thousands of years man has constructed
temples and cathedrals, palaces and public buildings, and these
have taken major space in the history of art. Even from the
dawn of history the art of building has so consistently touched
and mingled with human life in the home - in the shop - in
the temple - that it has often become the best history and
commentary of the times.
Tonight, your Grand Master, together with the Grand Lodge
Officers, the Master, Wardens, Brethren and friends of •..•.•
• .. . . • . . . • • • • • . . Lodge No..... . , have met for the purpose
of celebrating the completion of a resolve which originated
..... years ago.
In ...... , the leaders of this lodge had a vision of a Masonic
Temple of great beauty - erected to God and dedicated to the
true purpose of Freemasonry.
That dream began to take form and substance in a site - in
sketches and then in working designs - in steel and concrete
- in stone and glass - in fine wood - and in skilled workmanship. Contributions made by the Brethre n of this Lodge
were converted into brick and mortar, and Lodge funds were
put to use as this structur e rose from the soil of the land.
Finally, certain lending institutions, as a great example of faith
in the promise and integrity of the members of this Lodge,
completed the financing of this Temple with the dollars of their
investors.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
CALIFORNIA MASONIC CODE

As it became apparent that the new California Masonic Code could not be
ready for use during the year, I directed the Grand Secretary to obtain an
interim supply of the present Code. This was decided after learning that the
type had been saved and the cost would be relatively nominal.
The Code Revision Committee has completed a proposed new Code in
draft form. For various reasons, its final review by the appropriate Committees
and Grand Officers has not been feasible. The Grand Secretary's office is now
in the process of duplicating sufficient copies for such purpose.
Informal discussions have developed the consensus that the desired review
will best be done by a conference of the elective Grand Officers and representatives of the Committees involved, with the Code Revision Committee of
sufficient duration to carefully scan the entire work, and, page by page app;ove
it for publication.
'
I therefore recommend:
1. That the Code Revision Committee be continued for the ensuing year.
2. That an emergent Resolution for action at the Annual Communication
be pre54:nted by the Committee on Jurisprudence in substance, following the
Resolution presented by Leo E. Anderson, as revised by the Committee on Jurisprudence, appearing in the Proceedings for 1970, pages 325-326, and adopted
by 5/6vote.
BLOOD BANK

At the 1970 Annual Communication, Grand Master MacPhee, in his Annual
Message, treated the subject of a blood bank for our entire Grand Jurisdiction,
and tendered the "recommendation that when the incoming Grand Master considered the proper organization is completed he be authorized to declare the
'Grand Jurisdictional Masonic Blood Bank for California and Hawaii' functioning and that the Lodges be advised of all necessary details." This recommendation was adopted. ( 1970 Proc. p. 59).
With attentive regard to this subject, your present Grand Master, as a
stop-gap measure, authorized the Boards of Relief which had been operating
Blood Bank to continue doing so in order that there be no cessation of this
imperative activity.
The question of administrative details was carefully explored, and advice
sought and obtained. Various complications appeared and upon consideration
of these and other factors, your Grand Master has been unable to consider that
the proper organization has been completed.
The final disposition of this matter also may be affected by the action to be
taken at the present Annual Communication with respect to the 1970 Resolution No. 32 relating to Boards of Relief and their authorized activities. A simple majority voted for amended Resolution No. 32 and an applicable paragraph of Resolution No. 33. Failing a 5/6 vote, the matter was held over until
the 1971 Annual Communication. (1970 Proc. pp. 316-322).

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

53

Whether Boards of Relief are continued, under whatever name, and the
operation of blood banks will be construed to be "proper Masonic activities"
(1970 Proc. p. 317) appears to present a possible conflict with the directive to
be exercised in the discretion of the Grand Master concerning a declaration that
a Grand Jurisdictional Blood Bank is functioning.
In my opinion this requires clarification. There should not be concurrently
in effect, Boards of Relief Blood Banks, and a Grand Jurisdictional Blood
Bank.
I recommend that the Committee on Jurisprudence and on Policy and
General Purposes interpret what appears to this Grand Master to be an inconsistency as set forth above or at least an uncertainty, and that a directive to
the incoming Grand Master be given upon consideration of such a report.
LEADERSHIP TRAINING FOR OFFICERS
AND MEMBERS

In his Message at the 1970 Annual Communication, Grand Master
MacPhee discussed this subject and reported that he had requested the Committee on Masonic Information and Responsibility to develop a program
which officers of our constituent Lodges might be invited to attend. He
further urged the Assistant Grand Lecturers and Inspectors to recommend
the course to the officers of the constituent Lodges.
At the date of that Message, no course had been selected and approved
for the program.
During the current year the Committee on Masonic Information and
Responsibility has submitted to me informational material on several such
courses.
For various reasons I have not approved the use of any of them. Those
offered by professional training organizations are expensive and time-consuming. Moreover, classes would have to be repeated in various geographical
areas, or an inordinate travel expense be incurred for the Lodge officers to
meet in a single location.
Further in my opinion, pending a clear demarcation of duties and responsibilities as between the Committee on Masonic Information and Responsibility on the one hand and the Ritual Committee and Inspectoral Corps
on the other, to eliminate all question of duplication, the implementation of
leadership training should be held in abeyance.
It is probable that we have in our own membership men qualified and
willing to offer instruction in leadership as a Masonic contribution. In order
to secure good attendance there should be a compromise between a full
fledged "corporation executive" training course and haphazard nonstandardized lectures.
It is my opinion that a search should be made for qualified brethren who
possess, or will prepare a leadership training program, and make it available
at a nominal cost, or possibly as a Masonic labor.

I leave this subject in the hands of the incoming Grand Master for such
assignment as in his discretion he deems appropriate.

The information upon which I acted, supported by documentary proof,
may be summarized as follows:
The Master whom I suspended, as an authorized cosigner of checks
drawn on DeMolay bank accounts, signed checks beginning in 1957 and
continuing through the years to a date as late as October 2, 1967, payable
to an individual (since deceased) who was then Executive Officer of DeMolay,
Southern Jurisdiction of California. The proceeds of these checks from time
to time were used by said individual for the purchase of automobiles and
other personal purposes, and the brother whom I suspended was aware that
said individual was using this money for his personal benefit. I have seen
the cancelled checks, the total of which amounted to many thousands of
dollars.
Additionally, the brother whom I suspended was in posession of a box
of cash derived from various DeMolay sources amounting to approximately
$31,000. When first interrogated about this subject he denied knowledge of
this money, but subsequently did produce it. Further, this brother co-signed
a check drawn upon a DeMolay bank account in the sum of $2,000 purporting to be a "loan" to a third person. The "loan" has not been repaid, and the
whereabouts of the third person is unknown.
The foregoing are some of the reasons for my action. At the suspended
Master's request for a conference, I met with him and his attorney, at the
office and in the presence of Past Grand Master Leo E. Anderson. During
our discussion, I showed the suspended Master and his attorney photo prints
of the cancelled checks. He admitted he bad signed them, and also admitted
that be knew the proceeds had been used by the then Executive Officer of
DeMolay for the purchase of automobiles and other personal purposes. I
asked him why he did this and his reply in substance was that he wanted
to help the Executive Officer rehabilitate himself financially.
Thereafter, charges were preferred against the suspended Master and a
trial was held. I was astounded when I learned that a majority of the Trial
Commissioners had voted for acquittal.
The Grand Lodge of California proclaims its interest in DeMolay and
authorizes sponsorship of that Order. The members of DeMolay are encouraged to look upon Masons as honorable and trustworthy men. If they
cannot, our objective has suffered immeasurably.
Information relative to the suspended Master's dereliction has reached
members of DeMolay, and is known to DeMolay executives.
Your Grand Master is of the opinion that any Master Mason who knowingly participates in the diversion of funds belonging to the Order of
DeMolay or any of its entities for the personal use of any person, commits
a breach of trust and is guilty of a Masonic offense.
I therefore refer this matter to the Committees on Jurisprudence, Policy
and General Purposes, and Grievances for its review and recommendation
to Grand Lodge.

ARREST OF CHARTER

On May 5, 1971 I arrested the Charter of Mojave Lodge No. 783. The
Lodge was advised of this action by James E. Bacon, Inspector of the S04th
Masonic District, in accordance with my direction.
Circumstances dictating this measure were as follows: In February of this
year the Junior Warden moved away from California leaving the office vacant.
In April the Master resigned. No steps were taken to fill these offices. The Inspector found no member of the Lodge, except possibly Past Masters, qualified
to properly conduct the affairs of the Lodge. He reported an attitude of disharmony and apathy among the Past Masters, Officers and members, as well as
a past history of a belligerent, non-cooperative attitude evidenced by lack of
proper attendance at District Schools of Instruction.
The Secretary of the Lodge, Ray E. Moore, P.M., wrote an explanatory
letter to the members of the Lodge under date of May 10, 1971, urging cooperation of all the members. He is to be commended for that.
In response to a letter of inquiry which he wrote to me, I replied under
date of June 17, 1971, a pertinent paragraph of which I next quote: "I am
hopeful that officers will be found and qualified, and that they will be fully
cooperative in all matters, including attendance at the Inspector's Schools of
Instruction. I admire your statement that 'We in Mojave are proud of our
Lodge and our Masonry.' I hope that sentiment will pervade throughout the
membership. If it does, the Lodge should be able to place itself in condition
for restoration."
I am currently advised that good progress has been made in the desired
direction, and that interested members have been working toward qualification
as officers.
The Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division 5, George W. Perkins, informs
me they are not yet sufficiently proficient to be qualified, but he is hopeful
that they can be prior to the normal date for the next annual election of
officers.
I therefore recommend that the Charter of Mojave Lodge No. 783 remain
in arrest until the Grand Master who succeeds me is satisfied that a line of
officers are qualified for certification, and that thereupon the Charter be
restored to the Lodge.
