SusPENSION OF MAsTER -

MACCABEE LoooE No. 823

On August 11, 1971 I suspended the Master of Maccabee Lodge No.
823. The information on which I acted, provided reasons as follows:
Failure to demonstrate the proficiency in the ritualistic work required
of the Master of the Lodge; neglect or refusal to conduct meetings in
accordance with the prescribed agenda; arrogance and discourtesy toward
some of the brethren.
Various qualified brethren offered their assistance to him, and this was
not productive of improvement. His conduct brought disharmony in the
Lodge. He was requested to resign, and at one time he agreed to resign
if three Past Masters of his own choosing combined in such a request. He
was so requested, but, asserting that his own terms were not met, he declined
to carry out the agreement.
The disharmony in the Lodge due to his commissions, omissions, and
deficiencies prevailed for a number of months. Correction did not occur, and
nothing has been presented to support a belief that his reinstatement would
benefit the Lodge. Therefore, I recommend that the suspension be made
permanent.
EXPENSES OF BOAlIDS OF RELIEF
At its 1970 Annual Communication this Grand Lodge adopted a recommendation presented to it by the Committee on Retirement Plan
requiring that each of the component entities (of this Grand Lodge), members of the Masonic Homes of California Retirement Plan, be required to
assume their full responsibility under the Plan by being obligated to pay its
fair share of employer's premium required for participating employees of
the several component entities. By this action, this Grand Lodge determined
that Boards of Relief would be required to assume their share of the employer's premium for the retirement plan for their employees included in
the plan. (1970 Proc. pp. 226-228).
In making this recommendation to the Grand Lodge the Committee on
Retirement Plan set forth the following reasons:
a. "Each of these entities (of the Grand Lodge, including Boards of
Relief) operate on their own budgets."
b. "It seems unfair to require non-member Lodges of said Boards of
Relief to indirectly support Boards of Relief activities without obtaining
benefits from the same."
In reviewing the expenses of the Grand Lodge I find that the Grand
Lodge is paying the Medical Insurance and Workmen's Compensation premiums for employees of Boards of Relief. These costs are paid for from the
per capita tax levied on all Lodges whether or not they are member Lodges
of Boards of Relief.

ENDOWMENT BOARD EXPENSES CosT OF CoLLEcnoN OF HoMES ENDOWMENT FuNn
This Homes Endowment Board is charged with the responsibility of publicizing, promoting, and encouraging contributions to the Endowment Fund.
Income from the latter is applied toward maintenance and operation of the
Masonic Homes. The Board necessarily incurs substantial expense in printing
and mailing literature, correspondence, meetings and travel.
The proper source of funds required for the activities of this Homes
Endowment Board has been the subject of shifting and uncertain policy. Experience has shown that although the amounts spent annually are substantial,
the results have been highly satisfactory.
Annual budgets for the Board have ranged from $6,800.00 in 1950 to
$19,000.00 in 1970. Total contributions received in the 1970-71 period
amounted to approximately $936,000.00, the highest in our history. Actual
expenditures ($15,873.00 spent for 1970-71) were less than 2% of collections.
However, the $19,000 budget is a substantial item as related to the Grand
Lodge budget, and there have been differences of opinion as to whether this
item should be included in the per capita, paid from the income of the Homes
'
or recovered from the contributions as an expense of collection.
Legislation enacted in 1932 provided that no part of the Endowment Fund
either principal or interest, shall ever be used for any purpose other than th~
maintenance and operation of the Masonic Homes of California· also that
actual expenses incurred by members of the Board in the perf~rmance of
their duties be allowed and paid from the General Funds of the Grand Lodge
(1932 Proceedings, page 344). During that year an appropriation of $5,000.00
for the Endowment Board was included in the budget adopted by Grand
lodge (1932 Proceedings, page 354).
In 1947, Grand Master Moore rendered a decision in compliance with a
ltglllation of the United States Treasury Department, that the Grand Lodge
of California - not the Masonic Homes of California - is the owner of the
Masonic Homes Endowment Fund. In reaching that decision, Brother Moore
set forth a studied historical review of the subject ( 194 7 Proceedings, pages

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

31-34). Grand Lodge approved his decision (1947 Proceedings, page 258).
This policy decision was reversed in 1953, in part because of questions
arising under the Inheritance Tax Laws. Legislation was adopted declaring
the legal title of the Endowment Fund to be vested in the Masonic Homes of
California, a corporation (Resolutions 1953 Proceedings, pages 26-27);
Report of Policy Committee (page 258); Report of Jurisprudence Committee
and adoption of legislation (page 294). That is the way ownership stands
today.
In my opinion the aforementioned transfer of ownership had the effect
of reopening the question as to the source of funds for expenses of the Endowment Board.
C.M.C. Section 247 provides that no part of the principal of the Endowment Fund shall ever be expended for any purpose, and the income therefrom shall be used only for the maintenance and operation of the Masonic
Homes.
Up to 1957 Grand Lodge sustained the cost of the Board's operations
without reimbursement.
In 1957 the Report of the Finance Committee, under the chairmanship
of the late Frank Harwell, Jr., P.G.M., introduced the proposition that because
the Masonic Homes corporation was sole beneficiary of the Fund it appeared
logical that the expenses of the Endowment Board should be defrayed by the
Homes.
In accordance with this policy, the Finance Committee in 1957 included
in budgeted appropriations the sum of $12,000.00 for expenses of the Endowment Board and an equal amount in estimated income as refund from the
Masonic Homes for this purpose. As thus presented the budget was adopted by
Grand Lodge ( 1957 Proceedings, page5 358-366).
This practice continued through 1968.
At the 1968 Annual Communication an appropriation of $12,500.00 was
included in the budget, offset by the same amount to be reimbursed by the
Masonic Homes ( 1968 Proceedings, pages 293-294).
However, the Finance Committee under the chairmanship of Guy B. Mize,
P.G.M., in its 1968 Report, concurred in a recommendation by the Endowment Board that in future years the expenses should be borne by the Grand
Lodge (1968 Proceedings, pages 291-292). This concurrence did not constitute legislation by Grand Lodge. The recommendation of the Endowment
Board was carried out in 1969, the Finance Committee omitting the reimbursement from the Homes (1969 Proceedings, page 316).
Nevertheless, the Finance Committee was not satisfied that this practice
was sound, and in 1970, although it omitted the reimbursement, it commented
in its Report, presented by John A. Sickenberger, Chairman (1970 Proceedings pages 331-332) as follows:
"Our review of the Report of the Trustees of the Masonic Homes
again prompts high praise and commendation to the Trustees and staff

for the efficient operation of our two Homes. We are happy to concur
in their recommendation that the present $1 per capita be continued.
At our 1968 Communication, as requested by the Homes Board of
Trustees, the Committee on Finance concurred in a recommendation
that the expenses of the Endowment Board and the usual expense
of bus transportation and lunches for the annual Wednesday trip to
Union City become a Grand Lodge expense and therefore included
in the per capita tax. Prior to that time, these items of expense had
been borne by the Homes through reimbursement to Grand Lodge.
Your Committee on Finance is definitely of the opinion that such
expenses should not be an item of cost to constituent Lodges but
should be absorbed by the Masonic Homes as such expenditures are
productive of contributions by Masons to the Endowment Board which
produces income to cover the expense of operation of our Homes. We
accordingly recommend that the action taken at our 1968 Communication be reconsidered by the Grand Master in due course."

58

59

I find no legislation or action by Grand Lodge since 1932 affirmatively
defining a policy as to which entity should ultimately bear these expenses,
namely those incurred by the Endowment Board and the usual expense of bus
transportation and lunches for the annual Wednesday trip to Union City. In
1932 the Fund presumably was owned by Grand Lodge. Since 1953 the ownership thereof has been vested in the Masonic Homes. Allocation of the foregoing expenses has been in a state of flux and historical review does not provide
anything more than changing, in fact alternating, precedents.
Bearing in mind that the Homes corporation owns the Fund and is the
sole beneficiary of the income therefrom; that the expenses of the Board and
the annual trip to the Home at Union City are natural and essential incidents
to the growth of the Fund; and that these costs represent an insignificant percentage of the contributions which are obtained, I am in accord with the
opinion held by the 1970 Finance Committee.
I have therefore directed the Finance Committee, in presenting its budget
1971 Annual Communication, to offset appropriations for the Endowthe
at
ment Board and the expense related to the visitation to Union City by reimbursement by the Masonic Homes corporation.
This will realign the factors in their proper relationship.
The membership is already contributing by a portion of its per capita to
supplement the income needed for maintenance and operation of the Homes.
There is no justification to increase that per capita in order to pay the cost
of obtaining additional contributions for the Endowment Fund.
I therefore recommend: 1. That my directive to the Finance Committee
be approved. 2. That Grand Lodge by affirmative expression adopt the policy
of appropriating funds for the expenses of the Endowment Board and for the
annual visitation to the Home at Union City only on condition that reimbursement to Grand Lodge be made by the Homes corporation.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

CALIFORNIA MASONIC FOUNDATION
Assets of the Foundation, among others, include proceeds from the sale of
the Masonic Clubhouse at Berkeley and ownership of the Masonic Clubhouse
at U.CL.A.. Efforts to dispose of the latter have been and are under way.
Meanwhile, the expenses of maintaining the clubhouse, though unoccupied,
continue. Real . property taxes, utilities, and custodial cost amounted to
$14,679.31 for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1970. Grand Lodge advanced
the funds for this purpose. The Board of Trustees of the Foundation authorized reimbursement to Grand Lodge, which was made.
The expenses for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1971 amounted to approximately $16,165.26. In the absence of the President and in line with
the policy established last year the Accounting Office was authorized to
reimburse Grand Lodge in this amount, which was done.
As advised to date the Board of Trustees of the Foundation has taken
no action to ratify this reimbursement. Moreover, scholarships have been
granted and funds for the same disbursed in excess of monies available from
earnings.
Obviously a solution should be manifest when the U.C.L.A. Clubhouse is
disposed of. Meanwhile, I am of the strong conviction that the Foundation
should live within its own financial ability. If this means drawing from capital,
it may be unfortunate, but it is conceivable that under the Federal Tax Laws
such practice might even become essential.
Irrespective of any legal requirements under the tax laws, the principle
involved is the same, namely, the Foundation should be self sustaining.
If the Board of Trustees holds to a different view, Grand Lodge nevertheless, if in accord with the principle stated, can refuse to make any further advance of funds; in which case the Foundation can look to its own resources.
I am aware of Resolution No. 29 presented by Brother Frederick Bolte,
P.M., proposing that Grand Lodge contribute $50,000.00 annually to the
Foundation. Brother Bolte asserts that this was the policy set by Grand Lodge
when the Foundation was created, and should be re-affirmed.
What actually occurred was this - The Report of Special Committee on
Programs For Students made at the 1967 Annual Communication contained,
among other topics, the following recommendation:
"4. That the annual appropriations formerly devoted to the clubhouses be
standardized at $50,000.00 and added to the educational foundation each year
as an appropriation from Grand Lodge." (1967 Proc. p. 159). The Report was
adopted, without reference to any specific provisions. At that time, of course,
the Foundation had not been created, the Clubhouses had not been sold, and
no $50,000.00 appropriation was included in the budget.
At the 1968 Annual Communication, Grand Lodge approved and authorized
the establishment of The California Masonic Foundation ( 1968 Proc. pp.
235-237). The resolution did not re-affirm the policy of an appropriation of
$50,000.00. It made no mention of same.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

61

The budget, as presented by the Committee on Finance, and adopted by
Grand Lodge, contained no $50,000.00 appropriation to The Foundation. (Use
of the clubhouses had been discontinued, and the one at Berkeley had been
sold.)
This action by Grand Lodge constituted revocation of the policy, if indeed
it had been made a policy in 1967, to make an annual $50,000.00 contribution
to the Foundation.
Brother Bolte's Resolution in effect simply reopens the subject of an annual
appropriation which would increase the per capita by approximately $~.21. I
do not regard this as justified, when the Foundation holds assets valued m the
general neighborhood of $1,000,000.00. Contributions should be made on a
voluntary basis.
·
In order to focus the questions for positive disposition, I recommend 1. That the Foundation be requested to take appropriate steps to ratify
reimbursement to Grand Lodge for funds advanced during the fiscal year ending June 30, 1971.
·
2. That Grand Lodge make no further advance of funds for the use or
benefit of the Foundation unless the Foundation agrees to make reimbursement.
DECISIONS IN GENERAL
Numerous questions were propounded during the year calling for a ruling
by the Grand Master. Most of them could be answered by reference to the
California Masonic Code or recalling a precedent or tradition. It is not deemed
necessary to report them all.
A few of interest or requiring analysis and interpretation will be detailed
in succeeding sections.
DECISION -

ExPENSE REIMBURSEMENT

A question arose late in 1970 which may recur, and which can be put to
rest by a sitnple decision. The question is: When a Master and a Warden
from the same Lodge both attend the Annual Communication, the Master
serves on a Committee and his presence is required in committee sessions
during a substantial portion of the Grand Lodge Communication, and the
Warden is in regular attendance on behalf of the Lodge on the floor of the
Grand Lodge, what mileage payment or reimbursement for expenses is
authorized?
The answer is that the Officer or Elected Representative who is in attendance on the floor of Grand Lodge representing his Lodge is entitled to reimbursement for mileage under C.M.C. Sec. 17 4.
The other Officer who is in attendance as a Committeeman is entitled to
reimbursement for his necessary expenses in attending the Annual Communication as a Committeeman if his duties require his presence there. Such
reimbursement is made upon presentation and approval of a request for reimbursement, in compliance with C.M.C. Sec. 176 and Item H of the "Instructions and Regulations" pertaining to expense claims.

DECISION - EXPENDITURE OF LoDGE FUNDS
FOR PUBLIC SCHOOLS EVENTS
I was asked the following questions:
1. Is it a permissible expenditure of Lodge funds to give prizes in the
form of U.S. Government bonds to winners of essay contests during or related
to Public Schools Week? The essays are written on the Public Schools Week
Theme.
My answer was yes, providing the cost is available from, an? is paid out
of, the Lodge's Refreshment Fund, and the bonds are of nonunal amount.
Public Schools Week Observance is a program required by the Grand Lodge,
and encouragement to students to participate in the manner de~ned, is directly
related to the Observance. Requiring the funds to be provide_d out of ~e
Lodge Refreshment Fund is a desirable limitation, to automati~ally rest~1ct
the expenditures so they do not interfere with the normal costs m operating
the Lodge.
2. Is it proper expenditure of Lodge funds to make .a contribution of
cash to the library of a school in the name of a c~ntest winner? My a~swer
was no, irrespective of use of a donor's name. It 1s not a necessary adjunct
of Public Schools Week Observance.
C.M.C. Annotation 409 m states that a Lodge cannot c;ont?bute its funds
to a non-Masonic charity. In that case, the proposed contribution was to The
Salvation Army.
C.M.C. Annotation 409 n states that a Lodge cannot contribute to a
"Chimes Fund" in memory of a departed brother. It is not stated what the
"chimes fund" was, but apparently it was an outside charity. Co!1trib~tions
to a Public School Library would fall in the same general classification of
non-Masonic enterprises.
3. Is it a proper expenditure of Lodge funds to award a cash scholarship
to a deserving student? The answer was no.
The 1967 Grand Lodge Proceedings, page 255 to 257, show that two
resolutions, one for Lodge scholarships and the other for Grand ~dge
scholarships were defeated by Grand Lodge. The reports of the Co1D1lllttee
on Policy a~d General Purposes recommended a "no" vote with the statement that this should be done because the Grand Master had recommended a
scholarship foundation. The recommendation of the Grand Master was
adopted, and the California Masonic Foundation is the result.
Annotation 412 y states that a scholarship program cannot be financed
from the refreshment fund of a Lodge.
Scholarship recommendations may be made to the California Masonic
Foundation. The only way Lodges would be able to set up or awar? scholarships would be by future action of Grand Lodge, upon presentation of an
appropriate resolution.

DECISION -

63

VOTING BY THE TILER OF A LoDGE

The question of when and by what procedures the Tiler who is a member
of the Lodge can cast a ballot or vote has arisen on a number of occasions.
My considered decision, and the grounds supporting it are as follows:
If the Tiler is a member of the Lodge he has the privilege of debating
and voting on questions before the Lodge ( C.M.C. 3 23 ( c)) ; and every
member of a Lodge, when present, must vote upon a ballot for the degrees
or for affiliation (C.M.C. 534).
The Tiler is present at a Lodge meeting even though he is not in the
Lodge room but is at his post in the Tiler's room. (C.M.C. 320(d)). Consequently he must vote upon such a ballot last mentioned.
As to others than the Tiler, I construe the term "present" to mean actual
attendance in the Lodge room. The Tiler's room (C.M.C. 534(c)), or the
Lounge, or the cardroom, or dining room or kitchen are not part of the
Lodge room.
Moreover, if members have gone to such areas, the Master in his discretion may require them to return and participate in the ballot. ( C.M.C.
534(d)).
The Master should require the Tiler to come into the Lodge room and
participate in the ballot for an applicant; "and he should be relieved of
his duties for the purpose." (C.M.C. 323(c)).
Of course if a visiting brother is present, or even a member of the Lodge
who has not been present at the meeting, is willing, by arrangement in
advance, to relieve the Tiler, he can be in the Lodge room for the entire
balloting procedure.
The Grand Lecturer comments that this arrangement must be made
prior to the opening of Lodge or before the commencement of business. He
further states that this is the instruction which the Inspectors have been
told to give their District members, but almost invariably they are challenged
with the question: "What happens if there is no visitor, and none of the
members will volunteer to relieve the Tiler?"
In this case we turn to an alternative. Someone from the Lodge room
must be designated to perform this service. The proper time and procedure
is next discussed.
The fact that the Master should not permit any member to enter or
leave the Lodge rciom proper after announcing the report of the committee and
directing the ballot, and during the ballot (C.M.C. 534(a) and (c)) "unless
sickness or some other imperative reason should be pleaded" would appear
to have two primary purposes: First, to prevent a newly arrived brother to
ballot without being properly informed and, second, to prevent a brother
from escaping his obligation to ballot. I can see no other harm which would
result from his departure.
This brings me to the conclusion that there can be no valid reason to
prevent a brother, after he has cast his ballot, to go out and relieve the

64

PROCEEDIN GS OF THE

Tiler. The circumstance demanding this procedure, in the light of the requirement and the Tiler vote, constitutes an "imperative reason."
This should be done by order of the Master, after all in the room have
cast their ballot. Upon entrance of the Tiler, the Master should repeat the
purpose of the ballot, and the announcement of the report. of the investigating
committee. Thereupon, the Tiler votes, and returns to his post. Re-entrance
of the brother who relieved him may be optional with him.
Similar procedure should be employed in inst~ces where th~ Tiler,
being a member of the Lodge, desires to vote on motions or resolutions.
DECISION -

EXPENDITUR E OF LoDGE FUNDS
FOR PAST MASTERS DINNER

I was requested for a ruling on the following question: Whether it is a
permissible expenditure of Lodge refreshment funds to provide dinner on Past
Master's Night to Past Masters and their wives wilh;out charge when all other
members and their wives will be charged for such dinner.
The answer as to Past Masters is Yes. This has become a custom in
various Lodges, and it falls within the definition of "promotion of fraternal
intercourse." (C.M.C. Sec. 412).
As to the wives of Past Masters the answer is No.
RELIEF FOR A PHYSICALLY OR MENTALLY

IMPAIRED ADULT CHILD OF A MASON
The Master and Wardens of Redondo Lodge No. 328 have presented a
problem and requested a decision concerning eligibility of a person for
relief.
The facts in brief are: The daughter now aged 56 years of a deceased
member in good standing of the Lodge has been ~eriously. defoi:m~ .sin<;e
birth, her physical impairments have increased dunng her ~1fe, disability is
such that she cannot possibly support herself. Her mother 1s long deceased
and she has no living relatives.
•
She lived with her father during his lifetime, and for a penod the
Masonic Homes of California granted outside relief to the brother in the
amount of $215.00 monthly.
Upon the recent demise of this brother, such relief was discontinued and
the daughter has received no relief from the M'.'5?nic Homes ~presuma~ly on
the premise that Section 601(i) C.M.C. prohibits the granting of relief to
an orphan over the age of 21).
.
The majority orphan's remaining financial resources probably will soon
be exhausted. Redondo Lodge has been contributing toward her support, and
is hopeful that the Masonic Homes will assume this responsibility.
Section 601 C.M.C. requires that a Lodge must relieve its own members,
their widows and orphans, when m
· distress. Annotati"on """
1 defi nes an
"orphan" to mean the son or daughter under the age of 21 years of a de-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

65

ceased Master Mason; and "no man or woman over 21 shall be entitled to
relief as a matter of right as the son or daughter of a Master Mason." This
is predicated on 1928 Proc. pp. 163, 245, and 263.
I hold that the words "matter of right" do not exclude the granting of
relief in the discretion of a Lodge if the circumstances justify.
Some support for this conclusion is Sound in statements of principle in
the 1928 Proceedings. Moreover, Annotation "h" of Section 601 states that
a Lodge may relieve a brother by extending relief to a helpless or incompetent son, sister or mother of a Mason if they are dependent on him and he
is unable to relieve them. A daughter obviously must be read into this.
It is unthinkable that relief should be cut off upon the demise of the
father. Such would be repugnant to the basic principles of Masonic relief.
I therefore expressly rule that a Lodge may in its discretion, provide
relief in exceptional circumstances to the adult child of a deceased Mason
where a need arises by reason of physical or mental impairment.
In my view the same principle should be applied to outside relief granted
by the Masonic Homes. The pertinent section contained in the C.M.C.
Appendix, pp. 369-370, provides that outside relief may be granted to "(b)
Those who are otherwise qualified but who are ineligible by reason of
disease or physical or mental infirmity."
This would appear to exclude any afflicted adult orphan because an
adult orphan is not listed in the "Rules Governing Admission," consequently is not "qualified." I consider this to be unduly restrictive. Moreover,
we are confronted by the limiting statement in Annotation "a" of Section
601 C.M.C.
I recommend that the Board of Trustees be requested to take appropriate steps to amend its requirements whereby outside relief may be granted
under the exceptional circumstances defined above authorizing a Lodge to
provide relief.
Further, I recommend that when such an amendment has been implemented, the Board review the file and history of the case in point, as it
may be updated by Redondo Lodge, and consider the subject of outside
relief for the adult daughter referred to.
STUDY oF PRIORITms

During each Masonic year and frequently at the Annual Communications
various programs or projects are suggested by letters or resolutions or actions
by Boards or Committees.
Examples by way of illustation, but not of limitation, are Masonic Homes
Redevelopment, addition of a Library and Museum to the Memorial Temple,
acquisition of ffistorical Sites, possible grants to the Youth Organizations.
These and others have been put forth and consideration solicited individually and without any general order of priority, some without a plan of
funding.

66

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Long range planning suggests that a careful and thorough survey should
be made and priorities allotted.
Therefore, I recommend that the incoming Grand Master appoint a
special committee for the Study of Priorities. This committee should invite,
from all other pertinent committees and boards, and from all interested
Lodges as well as individual brethren, suggestions for programs and projects,
evaluate their importance, study probable costs together with funds currently available or possible sources to provide the same. The committee should
report in detail its findings and recommendations, with particularity as to
priorities which should be accorded.
SUGGESTION OF FLOAT FOR ROSE PARADE
I have been informed that Virgil J. White, a Brother and President of the
Pasadena Tournament of Roses Association is willing to recommend the entry
of a Masonic Float in the January 1973 Parade; and he thinks we have an
excellent chance of being accepted.
This would afford an opportunity to boost Public Schools, DeMolay, Job's
Daughters and Rainbow for Girls all in conjunction with the Masons of
California and Hawaii. As we all know, television coverage of the parade is
viewed by millions.
A float of which we could be proud would cost, according to advice
received, about $25,000. This would not be an annual commitment, as we
would not be considered eligible again for perhaps ten years.
It is necessary for me to present this subject to Grand Lodge at this
Communication, because if we favor this our application should be made as
soon as possible. Announcement of float selections will be made about April
1972; and funds would have to be expended during 1972.
I conceive no legislation to be involved, and no advance Resolution to be
necessary. It would be covered by a direction of Grand Lodge to the Finance
Committee to include the necessary appropriation in the Budget. ·
In order to bring the subject before Grand Lodge for consideration I
recommend:
1. That the Finance Committee be directed to include an appropriation
of $25,000 in the Budget for the purpose specified.
2. That if such an appropriation be authorized, an application be
promptly made for permission to enter the float.
3. That if items 1 and 2 are authorized, the incoming Grand Master
appoint a Special Committee to collaborate with the Pasadena Tournament
of Roses Association, design a float, and attend to the details connected with
its appearance in the Parade.

FEBRUARY 9TH EARTHQUAKE DAMAGE AND !TS EFFECTS ON TEMPLES
As most of the country now knows and the majority of Southern Californians will verify, the earthquake that rocked Southern California on the
morning of February 9, 1971 caused many deaths and extensive property
damage throughout the area. Fortunately, only two Masonic meeting places
were damaged seriously enough to deserve a description.
Although the epicenter has been described in relationship to Newhall, it
lies at a point some seven miles north and east of San Fernando, where the
greatest amount of damage was done. The damage in the Newhall area was
also extensive; however the absence of taller buildings and the lighter density
of population resulted in less total damage.
The meeting place of Old West Lodge No. 813, in Newhall, was the
Fellowship Hall of the Presbyterian Church on Newhall Avenue in the town
of Newhall. The damage to the building was sufficiently heavy to require the
city engineers to designate it unfit for occupancy. The primary damage was
separation of the exposed beam ceiling rafters at the apex of the roof, with
minor plaster separations. After searching diligently for another meeting
place, the Master of Old West Lodge, Worshipful Harold Kempel, was
prompted to request the Grand Master for a dispensation to meet in Granada
Hills Temple for a three month period. This being agreeable to Granada Hills
Lodge No. 790 the dispensation was granted. The Master of Granada Hills
Lodge, Worshipful "Whitey" Webster, and all of the Brethren of that Lodge,
extended full fraternal consideration. Their own meeting nights, as well as
all of the Masonically affiliated bodies that met in their Temple, were reduced
to a minimum to alleviate the emergency.
It is gratifying to report that the church was repaired and Old West
Lodge was able to return to its regular meeting place within the period of
the dispensation.
The San Fernando Masonic Temple sustained heavy damage from the
earthquake. To place things in the proper perspective, we are informed that
in a distance of approximately one half mile Maclay Street on which the
Temple is located is now one foot higher at Foothill Boulevard, tapering down
to Glenoaks Boulevard. The San Fernando Masonic Temple is on Maclay
between the two boulevards. We are further told that Hubbard Street, approximately one-half mile to the west, is now a full five feet higher than before
the earthquake. It is not difficult to understand, then, how the San Fernando
Temple sustained some thirty-five thousand dollars estimated damage.
The Master of San Fernando Lodge, Worshipful John Winslow, lives
between Hubbard Street (mentioned above) and two hospitals which were
destroyed. The damage to his home was moderate; however his wife suffered
a cut over her eye which required eight stitches to close.
The city engineers surveyed the damage to the Temple and placed a
notice of "unsafe for occupancy" on the door. The building is basically a brick

The Building Association held an emergency meeting. Services of a professional structura l engineer were obtained. With the information he provided,
volunteers, mostly Past Masters and Officers of the Lodge, proceeded to tear
out carpeting, remove seats, cut huge holes in the floor in order 'to get to
ground level, and shore up the steel girders and brace the outside bowed wall
of the Main Lodge Room. If this had not been done, the largest aftershock
about a week later probably would have leveled the building.
Subsequently, permission was obtained from the city engineer to meet in
the dining room. A temporary Lodge Room was set up and properly secured
for tiling. Consequently, it was unnecessary to obtain a dispensation to meet
elsewhere. Subsequent events included requests to the Committee on Lodge
Financing for permission to restore the Temple and accomplishment of that
effort.

PROPOSED GRAND LoDGE OF HAw AII
RECOMMENDATION No. 2 (pg. 37)

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
We believe that the Grand Master has discharged his duties and responsibilities relating to this matter in a most commendable manner and one that
is in keeping with both the general policies of this Grand Lodge and the high
purp0ses of the institution of Freemasonry.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
There was referred to the Jurisprudence Committee for review the edict
of the Grand Master and the guidelines on which it was based regarding the
attempted formation of a Grand Lodge of Hawaii.
The issuance of an edict is an exercise of executive power. Under Section
16 C.M.C. the Grand Lodge of California has "all the executive powers of
sovereignty" and Section 50 C.M.C. provides that between Annual Communications the Grand Master may exercise all the executive powers of Grand
Lodge except the granting of charters.
In issuing the edict, therefore, the Grand Master acted within the scope
of his authority.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

73

In order to put the edict and advisory guidelines in proper perspective a
brief review of the law governing formation of new Grand Lodges is advisable.
Among Grand Lodges in the United States it is universally recognized as
the law of Masonry that whenever there are three Chartered Lodges in any
state or territory in which no Grand Lodge is established those Lodges have
the absolute right to meet in convention and organize a Grand Lodge for such
state or territory.
The Grand Lodge of California has acknowledged and subscribed to this
law since 1875.
While procedures are not specified under this rule, it does contemplate that
the participating Lodges meet in convention to form a new Grand Lodge.
The steps taken by several of the Lodges in Hawaii to act through Commissioners appears not to be in accordance with such procedure.
It is the opinion of the Jurisprudence Committee that the Grand Master
acted within the scope of his executive powers with regard to Paragraph A
of the edict, which reads as follows:
"A. That no further action be taken by any Lodge in Hawaii or by any
officer or member thereof or by any commission representing a Lodge
having as its objective the formation of a Grand Lodge of Hawaii, except
for submission to its entire membership of an opportunity to give written
assent or dissent to the proposal."

Paragraph B. of the edict presents a more difficult question. It reads as
follows:
"B. That no Mason, a member in another jurisdiction and not a member
of a California or Hawaiian Lodge, shall participate in the movement for
a Grand Lodge of Hawaii or interfere or intervene in the affairs of a
Lodge in Hawaii."
Sojourning Masons who are members of Lodges of a foreign jurisdiction
are subject to the Masonic law of the Grand Lodge of California while residing within our territorial jurisdiction. While they may visit our Lodges, the
right of visitation does not include any right to participate in the business
of the Lodge.
The Grand Master had the power, therefore, to forbid any such sojourner
to "interfere or intervene in the affairs of a Lodge in Hawaii."
We are, however, of the opinion that that portion of Paragraph B which
requires that no such sojourner "shall participate in the movement for a Grand
Lodge of Hawaii," since it pertains to his activities outside as well as inside
a Lodge, would preclude him from even engaging in conversations with his
Brethren on the subject, and is overly restrictive.
It is evident from the Grand Master's Message that the intent of the edict
and guidelines is not to infringe upon any legal right of our Lodges in Hawaii
to form a Grand Lodge, but rather to assure that the formation of such a
Grand Lodge is in fact the will of the members of the Lodges involved, and
also to assure that such Grand Lodge when established will receive favorable
consideration of its request for recognition by this Grand Lodge.

ARREST oF CHARTER OF MOJAVE LODGE No. 783
RECOMMENDATION No. 9 (pg. 54)
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence reports that, under Section 128 of the
California Masonic Code, the Grand Master has the authority to arrest the
charter of any Lodge, for good reasons shown, and suspend the operations
thereof until the next Annual Communication.
The recommendation that the charter of Mojave Lodge No. 783 remain
in arrest until the succeeding Grand Master is satisfied that a line of officers
are qualified for certification, and that thereupon the charter be restored to
the Lodge is a matter to be decided by Grand Lodge and does not involve a
question of law.
Adopted by separate action of Grand Lodge the recommendation of the
Grand Master that the charter of Mojave Lodge No. 783 remain in arrest
until the new Grand Master is satisfied that the officers are qualified.
SusPENSION oF MASTER OF LODGE No. 819
RECOMMENDATION No. 10 (pg. 54)
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
The following items of the Grand Master's Annual Message have been
referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence:
Suspension of the Master of Frank S. Land Lodge No. 819.
Under the provisions of Section 129 of the California Masonic Code the
Grand Master had the power to suspend the Master of said Lodge until the
next Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of California. The question
of whether or not such suspension is to be made permanent is a matter for
the Grand Lodge to decide. It is not a legal question.
(NOTE: By separate action of Grand Lodge, Suspension of the Master of
Frank S. Land was made permanent.)

RELmF FOR A MENTALLY IMPAIRED AnULT CHILD oF A MASON
RECOMMENDATION No. 15 (pg. 64)
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
We urge that immediate attention be accorded to the present problem
facing Redondo Lodge No. 328, as outlined in the Grand Master's Message,
and we approve the Grand Master's recommendation that the Board of
Trustees of the Masonic Homes undertake a study for possible amendment
of its requirements whereby outside relief may be granted under exceptional
drcumstances. The Board of Trustees should make its report on this to the
Grand Lodge at the 1972 Annual Communication.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
The matter of Relief for a Physically or Mentally impaired adult child
of a Mason, appearing on pages 38 and 39 of the Grand Master's Annual
Message has been referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence.
The Grand Master ruled that, in exceptional circumstances, a Lodge may
grant relief to an adult orphan child of a deceased Mason.

78

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The Committee unanimously agrees with this ruling. We hold that a
proper and Masonic interpretation and application of Section 601 of the
California Masonic Code and the annotations thereto requires that the
relief be granted in the instance cited.
We also hold that the Grand Master's recommendation that the By-Laws
of the Masonic Homes of California be amended to provide for outside relief
under exceptional circumstances presents no legal problem.
The Committee therefore, moves that the Grand Master's ruling be
approved.
Adopted.

DECISIONS

STUDY OF PRIORITIBS:
RECOMMENDATION No. 16 (pg. 65)

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
We endorse the Grand Master's recommendation concerning the need for
a Study of Priorities. We suggest that the first step in such a study program
might properly be a request to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes
for a determination and proposal as to basic priorities and categories thereof,
prior to the appointment of a special committee and/or the issuance of a
general invitation for the submission of suggestions for particular programs
and projects. To do otherwise provides the possibility of priorities being set
on the basis of proposals at hand whether timely or not. At the proper time
the Grand Master should issue the invitation for the submission of programs
and projects.
Adopted.
SUGGESTION OF MASONIC FLOAT FOR ROSE PARADE
RECOMMENDATION No. 17 (pg. 66)

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Master's proposal for the entry of a Masonic float in the
January 1, 1973, Pasadena Tournament of Roses Parade is exciting and
appealing, and your Committee has no doubt as to the message that might be
conveyed or as to the pride with which such an entry would be viewed by the
total Masonic Family of our jurisdiction. However, we feel compelled to
recommend against participation. We believe that there are other requirements •
and necessities of the use of general Grand Lodge funds that are of greater
priority and of more lasting benefit. In a period of declining membership and
increasing costs we feel that we cannot approve a one-time expenditure of
this magnitude with its resultant increase in the per capita tax for the Lodges
of this jurisdiction. Perhaps financial sources other than the general fund of
Grand Lodge might be discovered or secured, in which case we would most
heartily approve the proposed Tournament of Roses Parade participation.
Adopted policy not to expend funds.

LoDGE OFFICERS - EXPENSE REIMBURSEMENT
DECISION No. 1 (pg. 61)

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
We concur with the Grand Master's decision.

,

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
The Grand Master, during his term of office, ruled that where a Master
of a Lodge and a Warden of the same Lodge both attended the Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge and the Master was also and at the same time
attending as a member of a Grand Lodge committee, and served on such
committee during all of the time while there, and the Warden attended the
session of Grand Lodge as the representative of the Lodge, then each was
entitled to reimbursement for his expenses.
This decision of the Grand Master was referred to the Committee on
Jurisprudence. The Committee finds that the Grand Master was correct in
his decision under the provisions of Sections 174 and 176 of the California
Masonic Code.
The Committee, therefore, moves that the Grand Master's decision be
approved.
Adopted.
EXPENDITURE OF LoDGE FUNDS FOR
PuBLIC SCHOOLS EVENTS
DECISION No. 2 (pg. 62)

The Ct>mmittee on Policy and General Purposes:
We concur with the Grand Master's decision on points 1 and 3. On Point
2 we have reviewed the report of the Jurisprudence Committee and we will
concur in that report.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
There was referred to the Jurisprudence Committee for review the decision
of the Grand Master set forth in his message under the heading of "Expenditure of Lodge Funds For Public Schools Events".
Three questions were presented to the Grand Master for his ruling. We
will take the third one first.
Is it a proper expenditure of Lodge funds to award a cash scholarship to
a deserving student? His answer was no. The ruling was correct.
.
To the question "Is it a permissible expenditure of Lodge funds to give
prizes in the form of U. S. Government bonds to winners of essay contests
during or related to Public Schools Week?" The Grand Master correctly
replied in the affirmative.
Section 410 of the CMC provides that the expenditure of funds for any
program required by Grand Lodge or the Grand Master shall be deemed to be

80

81

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

a part of the necessary expenses of the Lodge. Expenditures in connection
with the required observance of Public Schools Week fall within this section.
However, we question the Grand Master's requirement that the expenditure come out of the refreshment fund. His stated purpose is to keep such
expenditures within reasonable bounds. We think this is accomplished by
the limitation in his ruling that the prizes must be of nominal value. The
refreshment fund is "for purposes of refreshment and the promotion of fraternal intercourse". (Section 412 CMC)
To the question "is it a proper expenditure of Lodge funds to make a
contribution of cash to the library of a school in the name of a contest
winner?", the Grand Master's answer was "No", based upon Section 409
CMC and the annotations thereunder.
While the question is not explicit as to whether the contest winner referred to is in connection with the Lodge's observance of Public Schools
Week, on the basis of the Grand Master's statement that it is not a "necessary adjunct of Public Schools Week" we assume this is the purport of the
question. So construed, we doubt the correctness of the ruling. If the giving
of a prize for winning an essay contest in connection with the observance is
permissible under Section 410 CMC, we fail to see that it makes any legal
difference whether the prize goes directly to the winner or to the school library
in his name. Under these we are of the opinion that Section 409 CMC does not
apply.
Adopted as amended in Committee on Jurisprudence report.

governing this matter. We know that the question of having the Tiler enter
and retire from the Lodge room while the ballot is in progress has been a
problem which has confronted the Masters of Lodges intermittently for many
years.
Sections 534 and 323c are in conflict regarding this problem of the Tiler
voting and we feel that the Grand Master ruled correctly in the matter.
We recommend the approval of Decision No. 3.
Adopted.

EXPENDITURE OF LODGE FUNDS
FOR PAST MASTERS DINNER
DECISION No. 4 (pg. 64)

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Your Committee believes that the Grand Master has drawn too sharp a
line in his application of the definition of "promotion of fraternal intercourse."
We believe that the determination as to whether or not the wives of Past
Masters of a Lodge should be guests of the Lodge at a Past Masters Night
dinner should be left to the discretion of the Lodge. The "promotion of
fraternal intercourse" should include the concept of the gracious host.
I move the adoption of this report.
Adopted as amended by Committee on Policy and General Purposes.

GRAND LODGE
FREE AND ACCEPTED MASONS
OF CALIFORNIA
PROCLAMATION
YOUTH ACTIVITIES WEEK

MARCH 14-21, 1971
This year is the Fiftieth Anniversary of DeMolay in California. Many
activities throughout California and Hawaii have been planned to celebrate
this event.
The International Supreme Council of DeMolay has proclaimed March
14 through 21, 1971, as DeMolay Week.
The Masons of our Grand Jurisdiction should accord fraternal and parental recognition to this program. Also we should bear in mind that Job's
Daughters and Rainbow for Girls are sister organizations to DeMolay, and
that all three Orders have been assured of our support, our blessing, and
.
our encouragement.
Their ideals are our ideals, and the nation's future is in their hands.
These young folks are moral, and intelligent, and patriotic. The time will
come when they will support, bless, and encourage us.
Therefore, to complement and supplement the DeMolay observance, I
hereby proclaim the week of March 14-21, 1971, to be Youth Activities
Week. During that period, Masons everywhere are urged to display visible
manifestation of their purpose in furthering the interests of our three Youth
Orders. Invite a Chapter, a Bethel, or an Assembly to exemplify their work
in your Lodge. As Lodge groups or as individual Masons, visit one of their
meetings. It may surprise you how important you are to them. They will
never presume to suggest the truth, how important they are to you.
I direct that this Proclamation be read at the Stated Meetings of each
Lodge in March and, if convenient, that a copy be sent to each member
of the Lodge.

Dated: February 10, 1971
HERBERT A. HUEBNER

Grand Master

Attest:
EDWARD H. SmMs
Grand Secretary

PROCLAMATION

PROCLAMATION

PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK-APRIL 26-30, 1971

MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT MONTH

In observing the Fifty-first Anniversary of the founding of Public Schools
Week, we recognize that the most vital force in equipping this Nation's youth
to meet the many challenges of the future is the American system of free
public education. We firmly believe that the strength of the United States of
America lies in its public schools and those dedicated men and women who are
the teachers and administrators of our public schools.
This system of universal public education provides the opportunity for
fulfilling the greatest potential of American ideals by educating our youth to
become responsible citizens versed in the practice of self-government and
informed in the ways and means of preserving freedom.
We should ever be alert to danger signals which appear on legislative
or organizational horizons by whatever real or synthetic designations they
are known, which warn us of attempted trespass on the principles of our free
public educational system, which should always be devoid of partisan influence or religious dogmas.
I, therefore, proclaim the week of April 26-30, 1971, to be the Fifty-first
Annual Public Schools Week and the theme of this annual event to be "Our
Public Schools - Pillars of Wisdom, Strength and Beauty." I further direct:
That all Constituent Lodges in California and Hawaii actively participate
in an appropriate Public Schools Program.
That the suggestions offered by the Public Schools Committee be followed
whenever possible.
That no Lodge or prerequisite body programs or meetings be held during
this period for purposes other than this observance, with the exception of
Stated Meetings.
That publicity be given Public Schools Week in the trestle boards of
Constituent Lodges.
That this Proclamation be read at each of the Stated Meetings for
March and April and, if convenient, that a copy be sent to each member
of the Lodge.

The Masonic Homes Endowment Fund has been building through the
years by the contributions of the Masons of California and Hawaii, and by
gifts and bequests. Its principal is never touched. Onl~ the income, fro~
conservative investment, may be used toward the operations of our Masoruc
Homes.
Since the income does not yet fulfill these needs, the deficiency is supplied in part by the per capita tax. Rising costs and depreciated money must
be met in our calculations. Our goal is to increase the fund so that some day
the per capita tax may be discontinued;
None of the Endowment Fund income can be diverted to redevelopment
costs of the Covina Home and none will be used for the projected redevelopment of the Decoto Home. Other sources provide for those great projects.
The care of the children at Covina and of the elderly at Decoto has been
so firmly established as a manifestation of Masonic Relief that no reminder
of that is really necessary.
But we do remind every Brother that the culmination of the year's ·
efforts to secure contributions and to welcome gifts for augmenting our
Endowment Fund comes into full realization at the end of each Spring.
To emphasize this, I hereby proclaim the month of May, 1971, to be
Masonic Homes Endowment Month. I direct that this Proclamation be read
at the March and April Stated Meetings of all Lodges in California and
Hawaii. Also I request that copies, which are being furnished to the Lodges,
be sent to every member of the Lodge.

Dated: February 10, 1971
HERBERT A. HUEBNER
Grand Master

Attest:
EDWARD H. SIEMS

Grand Secretary

Dated: February 16, 1971
HERBERT A. HUEBNER

Grand Master

Attest:
EDWARD H. SIEMS

Grand Secretary

The period of the audit covered the year ending June 30, 1971 and contains a record of income and expense for the prior year. These official audit
statements are on file in the Grand Secretary's office for your perusal. All
are in proper form; and as stated by Touche Ross & Co., were made in
accordance with generally accepted accounting practices.
The statement for the Grand Lodge indicates a surplus after expenses of
$32,802.00 for the current year.
The statement of the Masonic Homes of California indicates a surplus
after expenses of $123,482.00.
The statement of the California Masonic Memorial Temple indicates an
excess of expenditures over income of $146,527.00, which includes depreciation of $146,950.00.
In the statement of appropriations the Grand Master was requested to
approve supplemental expenditures of $21,300.00, some of which are nonrecurring.
Your Grand Treasurer is deeply indebted to the Most Worshipful Herbert
A. Huebner, Grand Master of Masons in California for his fine leadership and
outstanding cooperation. California Freemasonry was indeed blessed with his
service. The Grand Treasurer also acknowledges with sincere appreciation the
close liaison maintained with the Most Worshipful Edward H. Siems, Grand
Secretary; the Worshipful Vern W. Hendrix, Assistant Grand Secretary and
the entire office staff who have assisted the Grand Treasurer in the performances of his duties.
Special appreciation is extended to the Assistant Grand Treasurer, Worshipful Arthur Linsk, who faithfully fulfilled his every responsibility with
dignity and exceptional ability.
Respectfully submitted,
CHESTER R. MACPHEE, Grand Treasurer

AccoUNTING REcoRDs
Over the years, your Grand Secretary's office has handled the fi~anci~
accounting records for Grand Lodge, the Masoni~ .HoI?es, ~e Califo.rma
Masonic Memorial Temple and other related entities m this conve.ment,
central office. This has been so, in part at leas~, because of th~ conuty of
interest in the sources of income and relationship o_f areas of disbursement
of the funds handled. The propriety of these practices has been confirmed
by our Auditors the Finance Committee and, if approved by Grand Lodge
at this Communlcation, the In-Depth Study Co~tt~ in the report on our
operations presented at the 1970 Annual Commurucatlon. .
•
Progressive steps in mechanization of our recor?s continue cautiously.
To avoid the pit-falls inherent in too rapid conversion ~ step has b~
analyzed, carefully programmed, and dry-run before ~mg made effective.
During this year we have ~echanized cash r~ceipt and disbursement records,
in addition to the accounting areas noted m the Report o~ the In-Depth
Study Committee last year. Application of s~ch methods, i~ general, are
no cheaper, but greater possibilities of analysis are made available and, as
practical, are being effected.
.
Our Accounting Office continues to make all poS&ble effort to accurately

101

reflect the financial condition of each of the separate entities. In view of
various governmental regulations, particularly in areas of taxation, caution
is exercised and professional advice is followed. The requirements of our law
are fully met while, at the same time, the best interests of the Fraternity
are served.
During the last year our office has worked with sub-committees of the
several entities. Improvements in the types of analyses and statements have
been made more convenient for their uses, more accurately reflecting the
factors of cost and income. Progress continues toward simplication or amplification as requirements dictate and our systems improve.
TAX REFORM Acr-1969
Taxation legislation has been far-reaching and has directly or indirectly
affected all units of our operations. Because of the complexities of the new
laws and their applications, we have sought the professional counsel of the
management section of our auditors (Touche Ross & Co.) and in addition,
with the full concurrence of the Elective Line Officers of Grand Lodge and
the assistance of the Grand Master, tax counsel has been employed on an
advisory basis. Our Staff members have attended seminars and studied the
law, giving special attention to its application to our operations. The subject
is complex. Because much of the law is new, the extent or nature of its
provisions as they pertain to our interests have not yet been fully clarified.
As yet, its actual extent is not clear as there have been few tax rulings or
decisions in applicable areas. The Trustees and Directors of our several
Masonic interests, together with our Staff, are keeping abreast of the
requirements of the law so that all may be in full compliance therewith.
VETERAN BUTTONS
The effect of the increase in Masonic membership for several years after
World War I is now bearing fruit. Presentation of Fifty Year Veteran Buttons
to eligible members continues at a heavy pace. The same factors have
increased the courtesy presentations to fifty year Masons from other
jurisdictions.
We have been reminded by Grand Lodge Officers of other jurisdictions
that the presentation of fifty year awards to California members, now
living in other jurisdictions, should be handled by Grand Secretaries of the
respective jurisdictions. You are asked not to request presentations directly
through the Lodges. The same procedure is used by California when the
situation is reversed. If we follow this method the eligible veteran member
is more certain of receiving his award without delay.
Because of the recognition by Lodge Officers of the significance attached
to these awards, many meaningful and heartwarming presentations have
been and continue to be made.

MASONIC CONFERENCE S

Your Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master and Grand Secretary, together
with Past Grand Master Guy B. Mize, again attended the National Conferences of Grand Masters and Grand Secretaries, and The George Washington Masonic National Memorial Association held in Washington, D.C.
Past Grand Master Eugene S. Hopp attended also as a member of the
Philalethes Society and chaired group discussions relating to the physical
qualifications of applicants for the Degrees.
Past Grand Master Henry C. Clausen, Sovereign Grand Commander of
the Scottish Rite, Southern Jurisdiction, was also present. He hosted a
luncheon and tour through the House of the Temple for all delegates to
the Conferences.
The work ~ons, however, were the significant part of the Conferences.
Each covered areas of interest which related to the particular Masonic offices
of the delegates.
The Grand Master has commented in his Message on some of the
activities. Past Grand Master Mize, later in this Communication, will report
on The George Washington Masonic National Memorial.
The program as it related to the Grand Secretaries consisted in part
of papers and discussions on the following topics:
1. Membership Transfers, Dimits, Resignations and Certificates
2. Simplified Forms
3. Grand Representatives
4. Liability Insurance for Lodges
5. Automated Record Keeping for Grand Lodges
6. Memorial Practices for Sojourning Masons
7. View of the Membership Situation.
Interchange of thought on such practical matters is of value to Masonry,
and the results of each Conference have been helpful to Masonry in
California.

As in the past, your Committee suggests that the Lodges review Article X
of their by-laws which sets forth the maximum authority of the Charity
Committee of the Lodge during the interval between Stated Meetings. This
year four Lodges increased the authority of the Charity Committee and we
commend them for doing so.
Your Committee while reporting favorably on the increases, wishes to
remind all Lodges of the President's order of August 13, 1971, which froze
increases. This law should be complied with and should be postponed.
Even though all of the amendments reviewed were approved, your Committee found that the matter of designating holidays in the By-Laws remains
troublesome. Article III of the Uniform Code of By-Laws, which permits
exceptions to the regular date of the Stated Meetings of a Lodge, limits the
exception to legal holidays and during the Annual Communication of Grand
Lodge.
With regard to legal holidays, these should be specifically named so that
there will be no misunderstanding as to whether a particular day is or is not
a holiday. Further, the particular legal holiday should be identified by
NAME and NOT by date; that is, New Year's Day is preferable to J~­
uary 1 and Independence Day is preferable to July 4, because such description
leaves no doubt that the exception applied when these days are celebrated
on Monday in a year when January 1 or July 4 falls on a Sunday.
Particular attention should be paid to this point of designation of holidays and most especially for Monday night Lodges, because commencing
this ~ear of 1971, by action of Congress, several holidays will be celebrated
on Monday even though they fall on another day of the week.
Also, a Lodge should provide for an alternate date in case its Stated
Meeting falls during the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge. While only
those Lodges whose Stated Meeting is during the second week of the month
are affected, the date of any Annual Communication may be changed for any
year, so the contingency should be provided for.
In reviewing the resolutions having to do with the change of meeting place
by various Lodges, your Committee found that in several cases a Lodge
moved to a new location without following the formal procedures set forth
in the California Masonic Code, and when the Lodge notified Grand Lodge
it was meeting at the new location, such notice was the first knowledge that
Grand Lodge would have of a move having taken place. Thereafter, the
Lodge would have to take the necessary procedural steps that it should have
completed prior to any move. The procedure for changing the meeting place

The Committee on Grievances:
The Comittee on Grievances reports as follows:
Twenty-nine trial records have been referred to your Committee. Eight of
those records are petitions for restoration and will be dealt with separately.
This year as in years in the past we have found that many of the problems
that arise in connection with the processing of trials in the subordinate Lodges
are caused by the failure to use the forms provided by Grand Lodge. We
have urged the use of these forms for some years and again most earnestly
suggest their use as they are the result of a good deal of experience and study
and are designed to prevent errors in procedure and guarantee proper notice.
In Trial Records Nos. 1980, 1981, 1982, 1983, 1984, 1985, 1987, 1988,
1990, 1991, 1992, 1993, 1995, 19%, 1997, and 1999 your committee has

TRIAL REcoRD No. 1973
An application for restoration has been received from a member of Barstow Lodge No. 682 who was suspended by this Grand Lodge last year.

111

PROCEEDIN GS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The application · for restoration shows that the applicant has completed
his psychiatric treatment and been discharged by his doctors. His probation
officer reports excellent progress and his probation while originally for three
years has been terminated.
At the original trial the Lodge fixed the penalty at reprimand. In its
report last year your Committee stated that in view of the fact that the
Accused was not cured and that treatment was continuing the penalty should
be raised to suspension, leaving to the Lodge the determinatio n as to when
the Accused is rehabilitated and entitled to be restored. The Lodge has received notice of the application for restoration but has not indicated its
attitude.
Your Committee still feels that the Lodge is in the best position to determine when the applicant is rehabilitated and entitled to restoration and should
express their opinion. In view of the short time since the suspension and the
fact that no report has been received from the Lodge your Committee offers
the following resolution:
RESOLVED , That in Record No. 1973 the application for restoration to
Barstow Lodge No. 682 be denied without prejudice and that in any future
application the Lodge be urged to express its opinion.
Adopted.

TRIAL REcoRD No. 1994
of Oak Grove Lodge No. 215, was arrested and
member
a
The Accused,
charged with grand theft for having taken money in excess of two hundred
dollars from each of three national banks. He plead nolo contendere to the
first count and the other two counts were dismissed. He was sent to the
California Medical Facility at Vacaville for diagnosis and recommendation.
On his return sentence was suspended and the Accused was granted probation.
Charges were filed by a Past Master of the Lodge. The Accused did not answer
and the Trial Master after investigation found him guilty and fixed the penalty
at expulsion. The forms furnished by Grand Lodge were not all used. The Accused has appealed and states that he talked to the Trial Master on a number

fixing the penalty at suspension. The word suspension was crossed out and
expulsion written in its place. Your committee feels that if the Accused did
not answer in reliance on statements made to him by the Master that he
should have the opportunity to answer the charges and present his case. We
therefore offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED , That the action of the Trial Master in Record No. 1944 be
reversed and the matter be sent back to Oak Grove Lodge No. 215 for
further proceedings.
We would further suggest that the Grand Lodge forms be used in their
entirety.
Adopted.
TRIAL REcoRD No. 1998
The Accused, a member of Frank S. Land Lodge No. 819, who had recently been removed as Master of that Lodge, was charged with unmasonic
conduct supported by eleven specifications. The specifications generally allege
that the Accused mishandled, or allowed to be mishandled, funds of the Order
of DeMolay and for a short period of time concealed assets of the Order of
DeMolay and disclaimed any knowledge thereof.
He was tried by Pentalpha Lodge No. 202 and found not guilty by that
Lodge.
Your Grievances Committee has carefully examined the transcript of the
Trial, 477 pages in length. The record indicates that Accused was charged
with the fiduciary responsibility of DeMolay funds, solely as to certain
amounts and jointly as to others. During a period of approximately fourteen
(14) years large sums of these moneys were improperly used for personal

112

113

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFSRNIA

expenses and uses. The Accused denied knowledge of any improper expenditures. While the record indicates that the Accused did not personally make
the expenditures nor gain therefrom, he had knowledge of some of the transactions, if not all. It is unquestioned, for example, he knew of the purchase
of three automobiles from DeMolay funds, which automobiles were used,
for the personal use of another DeMolay executive. One of those automobiles
was subsequently purchased by the Accused, who paid the purchase money
to that other DeMolay executive. The Accused co-signed all the checks for
other improper expenditures. While he claimed that he signed the checks in
blank, there is ample evidence which seems to belie that fact.
The record clearly indicates guilt to your Grievances Committee and we
can only feel that the manner in which the Trial Master handled the trial
caused a miscarriage of justice. For example, the Trial Master mistakenly
believed that the proceedings were penal in nature and not only ruled on
evidence under that belief but instructed the Trial Commissioners improperly
as to the burden of proof.
Your Grievances Committee unanimously determined that it was clear the
Accused mishandled the funds entrusted to his care as supported by the
evidence presented, the admissions of the Accused, and his concealment of
assets - including $31,000 in cash at various times held in his office, his
home, and the trunk of his car. In view of the fact that these funds were
those of a concordant body in which Masons have a special interest and the
clarity of the impropriety of the actions of the Accused who was especially
trusted by these young people, your Grievances Committee believes that the
findings of the Trial Commission should be reversed and the Accused expelled.
We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption.
RESOLVED, That the findings of the Trial Commission in Record No.
1998 be reversed, the Accused found guilty, the penalty be set at expulsion,
and that the member be expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry.
Adopted.

RESOLVED, That the finding5 of the Trial Master in Record No. 2001
be approved but that the penalty be raised to expuwon and that the member
be expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry.
Adopted.
Respectfully submitted,
ALFRED J. McComTNEY, Chairman

TRIAL RECORD No. 2001
The accused, a member of Mt. Wilson Lodge No. 794, was charged with
two counts of misapplication of funds, a felony, from the Citizens Commercial Trust & Savings Bank of Pasadena, of which he was the Auditor. Upon
being questioned by the bank officers the accused admitted the theft of
sums in excess of $200.00.
The Trial Master found the accused guilty of all specifications and of
unmasonic conduct and imposed the penalty of suspension.
On review of the record it was found that the accused was originally
charged with six counts of misapplication of funds by the Federal Court. He
pleaded guilty to two counts and the court dismissed the other four counts.
Your committee feels that the theft of funds from a bank by one of its
officers is serious enough to warrant the penalty of expulsion.
We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER

passing that the Assistant Grand Lecturers and myself are in complete accord
not only with respect to the wording, but also to the mechanics of the Ritual'.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
As the restless sands of time pursue their relentless course through the
hour-glass of life, we come once again to the time of accounting for the
happenings of the year late past.
It has been a year of decisions; matters of greatest concern have been
dealt with by this Ritual Committee, and the final disposition of some has
required diligent study and prayerful deliberation on the part of your Grand
Lecturer. In all decisions of this nature, the best interests of our order has
been my sole consideration, and the propriety of my acts is herewith commended to you, the Brethren of the Grand Lodge.
The year has also been one of great happiness for me, and it is with a
feeling of deep pride and humility that I now stand before you, to render
an account of my stewardship as your Grand Lecturer.
Section 156, paragraph fourth of the California Masonic Code sets forth
the duties of the Grand Lecturer, one of which is: "to render to Grand Lodge
at each Annual Communication a full and detailed account of his services
during the year, and to set forth therein a report of ~e con~i~o~ of the
Lodges throughout the Jurisdiction." In order to be qmte expliot m every
detail I shall categorize this report, but before so doing, permit me a moment
in whlch to pay tribute to the memory of a treasured friend: the late Elbert
W. ""Bill" Davis, Past Grand Lecturer, who passed from this earthly life on
Friday, August 6, 1971. Brother Bill was a truly good man; a ~on. of
very great stature, he was endowed with a depth of understanding which
transcended the comprehension of all but the most astute observer. He was
indeed a true friend of this Ritual Committee, and to his memory is lovingly
dedicated this report.
RITUAL

It is my happy privilege to report that the Ritual of this Grand Jurisdiction continues to be the finest anywhere in the World. Great strides have
been made this year in the continuing quest of total uniformity in the Ritual.
Much of the credit for these gains must necessarily be given the hard working
Inspectors and Assistant Grand Lecturers who have all given of their time
far in excess of the mere call of duty. There exists among this dedicated
group, a marvelous spirit of cooperation which s:rike~ a very f~vorable
impression in the minds of the Lodge Officers and inspires them with that
noble spirit or contention, of who best can work and best agr~.
The Ritual Committee has studied the Ritual very closely this year, and
in some cases minor changes have been effected in the mechanics of the
work in order to have it remain as it was handed down from time immemorial.
The Ritual Committee met twice this year, first at Palm Springs where the
esoteric work of the three degrees was completely reviewed. The second
meeting in Long Beach dealt mainly with matters of administration. Both of
these meetings were greatly productive, and it is noteworthy to mention in

During the Spring months the Inspectors Conferences were held as
follows:
Division 1-At Santa Rosa, April 16, 17 18 Conducted by Worshipful Bertram C. vonKonsky, Assistant Grand ~lurer Division 1.
Division 2-At Lake Tahoe, June 18, 19, 20 Conducted by Worshipful Edward E. Seagle, Assistant Grand Lectur~r, Division 2.
. Division 3 -At Los Gatos, March 26, 27, 28, Conducted by Worshipful Ulysses G. Patropulos, Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division 3.
Division ~-At Twain Harte, June 4, 5, 6, Conducted by Worshipful
Wallace H. Fiske, Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division 4.
Division 5 -At Twin Peaks, May 14, 15, 16, Conducted by Worshipful George W. Perkins, Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division 5.
• Division 6-At Pomona, February 26, 27, 28, Conducted by Worshipful Ernest M. Newton, Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division 6.
At each of these Conferences, the Brethren were greatly inspired by the
presence and counselling of the Grand Master and his Elective Line Officers
and they were further encouraged by the words of the Deputy Grand Maste;
as he shared with them, his thoughts and plans for the coming year. The
Ritual and lectures of the three degrees were very ably demonstrated by
the Inspectors of the various Divisions, and it was most gratifying to obse~ve the efforts of these Inspectors as they strive for perfection in the
Ritual. They are truly a dedicated group, and their common interest is the
great !ove ~hi?i they all share for their work in Masonry; that of teaching
the Ritual m its purest form, thus assuring a close uniformity of the work
throughout the entire Jurisdiction.
Schools of instruction for the Inspectors were held at regular intervals
by the Assistant Grand Lecturers, and during the year the Inspectors held
an average of nine schools per year for the Officers of their individual Districts. In some cases, the Inspectors held individual schools of instruction
when deemed necessary to the proper qualification of Lodge Officers.
Culminating the year's activities of the Ritual Committee the Grand
Lecturer's School of Instruction for the Inspectors will be held tn this auditorium on Saturday following the close of Grand Lodge. At this school, legislation enacted at this Communication will be discussed1 and the Ritual of
the three degrees will be exemplified by the Inspectors of the several Masonic
Districts.
Two changes occurred within the Ritual Committee this year. Following
the resignation of Worshipful William A. "Lon" Fishback in January this
year, Grand Master Huebner appointed Worshipful George W. Perkins Assistant Grand Lecturer in Division Five. Effective September 1 1971 Worshipful Burton 0. Young was appointed to succeed Worshipfui Beri:am C.
vonKonsk.y as Assistant Grand Lecturer of Division One. Brother vonKonsky
