FuNERAL SERVICE QuALIPICATION
This program, which requires certification of all who deliver the California

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

133

Masonic Funeral Service, has been in effect less than one year, yet, the
advantages of such a program have already been clearly demonstrated. The
many complimentary remarks which have come to me from all over the
Jurisdiction would indicate that this program is indeed serving the purpose
for which it was intended, and that the solemnity and dignity of our Funeral
Service is being adequately maintained. With the cooperation of all the
Brethren, we may be assured that this beautiful service will continue to
provide comfort and solace to the widowed, the orphans, and all who meet
to mourn the loss of a Brother.
With further regard to the Funeral Service I have come to the conclusion
that some clarification should be given as to the requirements for Funeral
Certification. It has been apparent in the past few years that a great number
of the Brethren do not agree to total memorization of the Funeral Service as
a prerequisite to qualification.
In all fairness I must admit that your Grand Lecturer feels that no good
purpose is served by this requirement. However, Past Grand Lecturer Warlow
in January, 1944 made total memorization of the Service mandatory for all
Masters-Elect, and proficiency certificates for these Brethren were signed
only upon proof of that capability.
I most heartily agree with Brother Warlow's desire to maintain proficiency in the manner of delivery the Funeral Service; I do not feel that
total memorization is required to accomplish this purpose. I have therefore
counselled with the present Grand Chaplain, an ordained Minister, who
advises that proficiency can be maintained without that requirement. I have
further been supported in this contention by the members of the Ritual
Committee, and I now wish to place the situation in its proper perspective.
Effective immediately, the following policy shall be observed: a total
memorization of the Funeral Service shall not be required of Master-Elect,
but rather the requirement shall be "proficiency of Delivery;" this to be
determined by the Inspector of each District previous to qualifying said
officer for a proficiency certificate or qualifying a Brother for a Funeral
Service Certificate.
I should hope that none might mistake the foregoing statement as a policy
of abandoning the controls which assure proficiency in the delivery of our
Funeral Service.
On the contrary, as I have reported, the program of Funeral Certification
is our one great hope of maintaining the dignity and decorum of this Service
and will continue in full force and effect.
We say only that total memorization of the Funeral Service will no longer
be required, but each Master-Elect or any Brother who desires to be certified
to deliver our Funeral Service will still be required to give proof to his
District Inspector that he is entirely familiar with this Service, and that he
is fully qualified to deliver same assisted by presence and use of the printed
Service.

135

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

It is respectfully hoped that all who perform the Funeral Service will,
at all times, have the Funeral Service book open before him except in those
instances where the officiant is required to be away from the Lecturn, and
which still must be committed to memory.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The report of the Grand Lecturer contains two matters which require
policy consideration by the Grand Lodge. Your Committee on Policy and
General Purposes comments as follows:

134

VISITATIONS TO OTHER JURISDICTIONS

During the year it was my privilege to visit the Jurisdiction of Nevada
and Oklahoma, and study at first hand some of the varied systems of control
used by these Jurisdictions to teach the Ritual.
In November 1970, I was in attendance at the Annual Communication
of Nevada in Las Vegas, and in February of this year I attended the Grand
Lodge of that great State of Oklahoma in Guthrie. In my opinion much was
gained from these visitations as they afforded excellent opportunity to consult
and compare practices and procedures employed by my counterpart in these
Jurisdictions. I am greatly indebted to our Grand Master for permitting me
the Honor of acting in his behalf at these visitations.
BUDGET

The high cost of living has been keenly felt by the Ritual Committee
this year. In spite of determined efforts on the part of the Assistant Grand
Lecturers to minimize expenses, costs for the Inspectors annual Conferences
have continued to rise. Even higher costs are anticipated for the coming
year due to greatly increased travel requirements for the Inspectors and
members of the Ritual Committee. Accordingly, we have requested that the
Finance Committee approve a budget in the amount of $47,500.00 to cover
expenses incurred in teaching the Ritual for the year 1971-72.
CONCLUSION

In closing I would like to thank all those who have so greatly assisted
in making the programs of this year successful. The Inspectors for their
dedication to duty, and their determination to maintain high standards of
excellence in the several Masonic Districts. The Assistant Grand Lecturers
for their warm friendship and their steadying influence in matters of policy
determination. Grand Secretary Siems and his wonderful Staff for their
complete cooperation during the year, and to Grand Master Huebner, .1
extend my personal gratitude for his kindness and understanding; for his
many acts of courtesy, and for his complete and unwavering support throughout the entire year. And finally, to you my Brethren, for permitting me the
great honor of serving as your Grand Lecturer.
Respectfully submitted,
H. DouGLAS LEMONS, Grand Lecturer
Referred to Committee on Distribution.
(NoTE: See also Report of Committee on Ritual Ceremony for Removal

of Cornerstone.)

1. The Grand Lecturer stated that the Ritual Committee has prepared

a suitable ceremony for the removal of Cornerstones in accordance
with Grand Master MacPhee's recommendation at the 1970 Annual
Communication. Although the Grand Lecturer's report states that such
a ceremony was approved at last year's Annual Communication, the
Proceedings show that the matter was deferred for possible action at
this Communication.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes it is proper
to have a prescribed ceremony for this purpose available for use when
desired, but that it must be clearly understood that use of the ceremony
is completely optional.
I move that the Grand Lodge permit the use of a special ceremony,
as prepared by the Committee on Ritual, for the opening of Cornerstones.
2. The Grand Lecturer has recommended that a special committee be
appointed to review the Cornerstone Ceremony with the intent of
adopting certain optional phraseology which will better fit the ceremony to modern circumstances.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes that a very
few changes would be required and that these should be only in the
form of alternate words, in order that the time-honored and unique
character of the Masonic Cornerstone Ceremony may be retained with
as much fidelity as possible. Your Committee also believes no special
committee is required for this purpose and that the Ritual Committee
be requested to provide the few simple alternate words which may be
needed.
I move that the Committee on Ritual be instructed to modify the
Cornerstone Ceremony in order to provide the use of alternate words
where deemed necessary and appropriate.
Adopted.

MEETINGS
The Board has continued to hold its meetings monthly near the San Francisco or Los Angeles airports, except for meetings held over a two-day period.
These were held in January at Decoto, in March at Covina, in July at Newport
Beach and in September at Camp Masonic, the Covina Home's summer camp

FINANCIAL

In any private business, it is essential for management to know the cost of
doing business and the results obtained for its expenditures. Failure to do this
will inevitably result in bankruptcy. We view the operation of your Homes in
the same light. If we do not know costs in the various departments of our
operation, with inflation and resultant price and wage increases, it is easy to
have operational chaos. Our continuing endeavor is to prevent this and to maintain your per capita contribution at its present low figure of $1.00 per member.
As a consequence of this, the Budget and Operations Committee, under the
able leadership of R.W. William H. Price, met many times during the year
with the Secretary, Edward H. Siems, and the chief accountant, Miss Birma
Roush, to pinpoint areas of possible saving. The cooperation of the office staff
is gratefully acknowledged.
The comments of this Board on matters affecting its operations in its report
of the In-Depth Study evolved from Chairman Price's committee and were
unanimously adopted as the Board's position relative thereto.
It is timely here to congratulate the Homes Endowment Board and its
Chairman, Wor. Kermit A. Jacobsen, on their splendid record of achievement.
With increasing understanding of our challenges and opportunities carried to
the Lodges by these brethren, there should be a renewed spirit on the part of
the Lodge officers and members. It was a pleasure for the Homes Board President to meet with the Endowment Board and, more frequently, Brother Jacobsen. Out of these meetings comes cooperation of the finest sort in the spirit of
"who best can work and best agree". Our thanks must, however, go particularly to those dedicated Chairmen within the Lodges, the Masters and Secretaries, who, starting the Endowment drive immediately upon their return from
the Grand Lodge Communication and getting contributions in with dues payments, remembered that Masonic Charity is a twelve-month, not a one-month
virtue.
Again, we believe that with your generosity, the gifts made either in life or
by will, and with business-like administration, there will be no need for an increase in per capita, and we therefore recommend the continuance of $1.00 per
member for the support of the Homes.
COVINA

We reported to you in 1970 concerning the progress made in the redevelopment of this truly Masonic Home. The eight cottages, completed in August
of 1970, became home to our young people with the advent of the school year.
The shift from dormitory to true home environment made possible the uniting
of families formerly split off from each other by both age and sex. The expan-

139

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

sion of the concept of couples as houseparents has given a balance of family
living and a resultant feeling of stability noticeable in its effect upon the
children.
We reported the demolition of the dormitories, the site and landscape work
then in progress. With their completion, an entirely new atmosphere pervades
the grounds. The many Lodge visitations bear testimony to the expanded
interest of our membership in Covina. As an example, the annual get-together
of Eastgate Lodge No. 290 and King Solomon's Seaport No. 260 this year
centered on Covina in an outing and visitation not soon to be forgotten.
Now we are engaged, under the guidance of our Master Plan Architects, A.
Quincy Jones & Associates, with Brother William G. Laffin, Cahuenga Lodge
No. 513 continuing in charge of the project, in the erection of the new Community Center. A contract with Samuelson Brothers Constructors of Los Angeles
in the amount of $712,596 and with Kitcor Corporation in the amount of
$43,710 was approved by the Board on March 13, 1971 and construction commenced in May after final approval of plans by the various authorities to which
we are subject. Work is progressing on schedule and occupancy should be
expected in early Spring of 19 72.
The following summer should complete demolition of the fifty-five year
old Administration Building, the Infirmary and a shop building, all now to be
contained in the new Center. Site repair and landscaping will bring this phase
of Covina Redevelopment to final fruition. We will then have a Home, not only
in the forefront of Masonic, but of all child-care facilities throughout the world.
We stress again that these changes, as well as those to come at Decoto, have
cost the membership, as such, not one cent. Every penny going into these improvements has come from individual donors who thought enough of Masonry
and its place in God's world to give and bequeath a portion of their worldly
goods that God's work, through Masonry, might go on after them.

DECOTO REDEVELOPM ENT
Our greatest concern last year, and doubly so now, is the question of Decoto
Redevelopment.
At the 1970 Communication, we reported to the Grand Lodge on the study
made by the Board itself through the Decoto Redevelopment Steering Committee. This Committee consisted of Alfred W. Odle, Laurence E. Dayton,
P.G.M., Myron E. Smith, P.G.M. and William H. Price, then Junior Grand
Warden. Their report, made after long investigation, became a part of our
report under the heading:

A Reaffirmation of Masonic Relief."

purposes, the ravages of time, the change of environment from pleasant countryside to heavy industrial, the rising age of our guests, and the lack of level
ground had all mitigated against the present site.
Not satisfied with this and in order to safeguard the orderly proces.5 of
redevelopment, the Board ordered two entirely independent studies to be made
of our present facility to determine if, based upon present requirements of law
and building regulations, use could be made of the present site and the existing
buildings. One study was made by our Master Plan Architects, A. Quincy
Jones and Associates, who have done such a superb job at Covina. This firm is
presently engaged by Palo Alto Clinic as its Master Plan designers. Since Palo
Alto Clinic and Stanford University Hospital furnish all medical care for our
Decoto guests, a happy circumstance of close collaboration exists to our benefit. The second study was made by Community Health Planning Corporation
of San Francisco under the able direction of Mr. John Y. James, its President,
who personally directed the project.
Underlying each study is a thread of fact of great concern to this Board.
The Hayward Fault, a major branch of the San Andreas Fault extends directly south down the western face of the Hayward Hills through the present
site of the Home. This Fault was the center in 1868 of one of the largest earthquakes to hit Northern California. In the face of the devastation wrought at

which have stood for generations but we would be derelict in our duty

proceed with the orderly planning, acquisition and erection of the kind

the prohibitive cost and practica l impossibility of bringing the present buildings up to prevailing code, notwithstanding the earthqua ke hazard, but with
this as an acknowledged fact of life, our removal to another site becomes
imperative.
To this end, we are proceeding with the search for a site, meeting the criteria laid down in these studies.
We are, at the same time, looking to the engagement of an architec t so that
the site chosen may be properly utilized for the high purpose intended.
We are grateful to the firms who engaged in these studies with vigor, understanding, and, above all, a feeling for the work here being done by the Fraternity through this Home. In each case, the spirit of Superintendent Herring and
his staff was transmit ted to and became evident as a part of each report.

Masonic Home in Union City, for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1971.

There were 157 men and 208 women, and the average age was 83.43. For the
first time, the average age of our men residents, 83.56 years, slightly exceeded
the women residents average age of 83.29 years.

Our !tfaso~c H?me register ~as signed by 3,748 visitors, repr~nting 392
Lodges m Califorma and Hawan, 25 states and 4 foreign countries· Japan
Newfoundland, Finland and Holland. Visitors included the Grand Master of
Kansas and the Grand Master of Oregon .
One of the highlights of our Masonic Home year was the visitation of our
own ~ost Worship.ful Grand Master, Herbert A. Huebner on January 23, 1971.
On this same date It was our fraternal pleasure and privilege to have the entire
Board of Trustees of the Masonic Home, here for their meeting .
We express our appreciation to the many Lodges and Masonic Affiliated

Bo~es, and .to each individual for their various contributions to the Home.

The total capacity of our hospital, including the 5th floor Adams Annex is
16 7 and as of June 30, 1971 the hospital census was 15 5 patients of which 131
were considered permanent. There also were 60 semi-ambulatory residents
requiring nursing care and 59% of the total population of the Home was under
nursing care. Because of the advanced age of the new residents entering the
Home and the gradual increase in the average age of residents, we can expect
an even greater percentage of our population requiring nursing care in the
future.
We have been very fortunate in the past year in not having any major
repairs, but because of the age of the buildings and equipment, maintenance has
been very costly and we can be assured that costs will increase greatly each year.
Most of our buildings and equipment have passed their useful expectancy.
Much enthusiasm has been generated by our residents since the announcement last Fall by the Board of Trustees that studies for a new Masonic Home
are under consideration. Although much nostalgia is attached to our present
Home, the majority of our residents are excited about the possibilities of a new
home.
Many new pleasures for the residents have been instituted in the past year.
We have enlarged our Arts and Crafts classes and increased shopping trips. A
continental breakfast is served on Sunday mornings for those who wish to sleep
late. These are only a few of our new activities. We have a new coffee shop and

Their donations of money, clothing, Christmas gifts and many other items
have all been put to good use. Our special thanks to the Order of Eastern Star
the East Bay Past !datrons Ass?Ciation, for their many projects, Jam and Jell;
Day, cancer dressmgs, entertainment, etc., which are very beneficial to the
Home.

as.sistance you have g1ven me; for the many hours of labor you have given to
make our residents' today and tomorrow as pleasurable as possible.
Also, to o~r sta~ at Union City and San Francisco, my personal thanks foe
your cooperation this past year.
Respectfully submitted,
HUGH B. HERRING, Superintendent

REPORT OF SUPERINTEND ENT-COVINA HOME
It is a pleasure to submit the annual report of the Masonic Home for Children for the year 1970-1971.
. At year's end our population .c.onsisted of 62 children, 38 boys and 24
girls - ages from 5 - 18. Our high school graduating class of 1971 conSISB. tebd of Mike Jenner, 18, Wilshire Lodge No. 445 and Stuart Kausrud, 18,
ur ank Lodge No. 406.
Throughout the year we had three young men reunited with their
families by means of parental withdrawal - Larry Knauer, 16, Ashlar

The children and staff at Covina would be most happy to have you
come visit us. We have picnic facilities, including softball field, picnic
tables and benches, athletic equipment, shade trees, lots of grass, a tennis
court, badminton facilities and an unlimited amount of enthusiasm and

"Our tum over" has been a consistent one - children reunited with
their families, seniors graduating and going on to college, plus new members coming to live with us. Life at Masonic is meaningful, interesting
and ever changing.
The "cottage plan" of living for the children under our care at Covina
has exceeded all expectations. In many instances brothers and sisters are
together as a family unit for the first time in their lives. The "big
brother" - "big sister" concept has become a reality, inasmuch as we no
longer group our children solely by age. All cottages have an age differential which is more closely oriented toward family living.
With our new cottages, each child has a degree of privacy due to
his having his own individual room. Psychologically, he has something
of his own and with this privilege he also has the responsibility to care
for it.
Each child, in all eight family groups, has the opportunity to plan,
buy, and prepare an occasional meal under the supervision of houseparents.
Each child has an opportunity to learn and develop skills which are
going to be neces.sary for him to use when he graduates and leaves the
home. These same experiences can be applied to his purchasing, caring
for, washing and ironing his clothing, inasmuch as each family cottage unit
is equipped with a washer-dryer combination. Education and training for
tomorrow is one of our passwords.
By using couples as houseparents, our children are exposed to a more
normal, happy, living, family relationship. To some of our children this
is a new experience. In some instances our houseparents have had babies
born to them while employed here and this experience has been a thrilling
one for our boys and girls. Our children have been exposed to a normal
family situation where "mama" becomes pregnant, carries the baby and
delivers a new "little brother or sister" to the family group. In most

During your visitation our children will be happy to serve as guides.
Arrangements for visitations can be made by calling the H<~me or writing
to arrange for dates.
The key to successful operation is a combination of philosophy, method
of work, and personnel. The fraternity can be extremely proud of the personnel who are meeting the needs of the children under our care.
Brother J. Burt Brown, Assistant Superintendent of the Masonic Home
for Children is a most dedicated Masonic brother and brings a very rich,
meaningful background to his position. Burt has been a successful business
man, an assistant pastor in a local church and brings an experience of some
25 years of working with people. He is an excellent organiur and has the
ability to relate with our boys and girls. Part of Burt's immediate responsibilities deal with the redevelopment project and working with architects, contractors, and subcontractors as we continue the Covina redevelopment
program.
Mr. Bill Hamner serves as Director of Child Care. Bill has just completed his professional training and is soon to be a registered social worker.
His primary responsibility is to help in the selection, orientation, supervision and evaluation of houseparents and child care staff that deal directly with our children.
Mr. Walt Schaeffer supervises our tutorial-educational program. I't
is his responsibility to see that each child is tested as to his capacity and
is encouraged to work up to maximum capacity in the area of education.
Walt has graduate degrees in psychology and education and is extremely
well fitted and experienced for his job. Walt's skill and sensitivity aids us
in helping the children accept the type of counseling and guidance which is
necessary for them to reach their maximum potential.
Mrs. Ruth Whittenberger, our head cook, serves a variety of well planned and prepared, and well served meals. For those who need the same,
special diets are prepared. She and her staff are extremely important persons in our staffing structure.
All personnel, engineers, gardners, nurses, administrative personnel, bookkeeper and maintenance people contribute patience, love and understanding
into the lives of all our children. They are all very important people.

ANNUAL REPORT OF THE
MASONIC HOMES ENDO WMEN T BOARD
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Masonic Homes Endowment Board hereby submits its 39th Annual
Report covering the fiscal year ending June 30, 1971. We welcome this
opportu nity to examine the records with you and to express our deep appreciation for your wonderful support.
INCOME FROM THE ENDOWM ENT FUND

It is interesting to note that our permanent Endowment Fund earned
$1,167,969.49 during the past year which has been transferred to the operating account of our two Masonic Homes. If we did not have the endowment fund, that amount converted into terms of a per capita tax would be
an additional amount of $5.06 per member.

BEQUEST S, GIFTS AND MEMORI ALS

Bequests in the amount of $517 ,42 2.6 7 were received into the Endowment
Fund during the past year. In addition, $902,678.05 were received in bequests
by the Homes from estates wherein the Endowment Fund was not specifically
mentioned in the will.
Gifts through organizations and individuals amounted to $9,651.45.
Memorials added $26,091.59 to our funds, thus a total of $1,454,843.76 was
received during the fiscal year in the form of bequests, memorials, and gifts
from individuals and groups. One can readily see the importance of stressing
the value of bequests and wills for the benefit of our two homes.
INDIVIDU AL CONTRIB UTIONS THROUG H LoDGES

We are always anxious to know how well we have done in the area of
individual contributions through our lodges. We are very pleased to report
that individual contributions through Lodges in California and Hawaii totaled
$936,637.66. This is $17,245.50 more than was contributed last year. The
average per contributing member is $8.36 per member as compared to $8.12
in 1970. The percentage of participants was 48.5% or .1 % over a year ago.
The average donation from the entire membership increased from $3.91 to
$4.06 this year. This is a fine record in spite of the problems of rising unemployment and a poor economic climate.

CONCLUSION

It is obviously impossible to give due and adequate credit to' all who

participated in the Homes Endowment Program this past year. We realize
more and more that this program receives the support of every active member
of California Masonry.
Our Grand Master, the Most Worshipful Herbert A. Huebner, has given
his full support to every phase of our program. We gratefully appreciate his
leadership, suggestions and wise counsel.
The Grand Lodge officers, Past Grand Masters and Grand Lodge comniitteemen all did their share to assist us; to them we extend our thanks.
The Grand Lecturer, Assistant Grand Lecturers, Inspectors, Masters and
!Wardens, Lodge Secretaries and Endowment Committee men of the Lodges
ifepresented a solid front and total effort for which we are deeply appreciative.
Finally, our thanks to the 112,019 brethren who contributed the $936,637

156

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

for our permanent Endowment Fund and to the dedicated members of thia
Board who contributed unselfishly in time and effort.
To all, thanks for helping to insure the continuance of love, care and
security for our elderly at Decoto and our children at Covina.
Respectfully submitted,
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD
KERMIT A. JACOBSON, Chairman

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

REPORT OF BOARD OF CONTROL

pretations which could affect the operation of Boards of Relief, particularly
those receiving bequests and gifts.
The Board of Control has been in contact with the Grand Master, other
Grand Lodge Officers, and Tax Consultants to determine our area of responsibility.
Based on advice received, all Boards of Relief have been advised that they
must collect and pay certain Federal, State and Local Taxes such as Withholding, Social Security, Unemployment and Local Payroll Taxes. Boards
have been advised to obtain professional assistance if there is any doubt as to
complete compliance with all aspects of the Laws.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Since the last Communication of Grand Lodge, your Board has met in
Los Angeles on December 19, 1970 and May 28-29, 1971. Also in San Francisco on January 13, March 20, and August 7, 1971. Meetings were spaced to
avoid unnecessary travel expenses due to the geographical location of the
Board Members. Interim business was handled by postal communication
and individual contact.
Copies of communications from the Board of Control to and from Lodges
and Boards of Relief, as well as minutes of our meetings, were directed, as
in the past to the Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master, Grand Wardens,
and Grand Secretary.
All Official actions of the Board of Control were submitted to the Grand
Master.
The Right Worshipful Raymond A. Ebbage, Junior Grand Warden, was
appointed by the Grand Master as Liaison Officer to your Board, and was of
most valuable assistance.
POLICY

At our meeting on January 13, 1971, in the Grand Lodge Office, policies
were formulated, and concurred in by the Elective Grand Lodge Officers,
effective until otherwise legislated by Grand Lodge whereby:
1. Boards of Relief publishing Clearing House or Concurrent Jurisdiction
Reports may continue this practice.
2. Funerals for Sojourners shall be conducted in accordance with CMC
Sections 604 and 605, and Policy heretofore adopted by Grand Lodge.
3. Funds of a Board of Relief shall not be expended for social purposes.
If The Grand Master is the guest of honor, the function is considered an
Official one.
4. All other activity of a Board of Relief shall be in accordance with
the CMC, AND THE October 1, 1969 Rules and Regulations governing the
operation of Boards of Relief.
5. Any special problem will be considered individually.
NEW FORMS

To simplify and standardize the information required of the Boards of
Relief by the Board of Control, new forms were developed and put into use.
Report of Election Form 6-71, Annual Reports Form BC 1-71, Statement of
Income and Expenses Form BC 2-71, Balance Sheet Form BC 2-71, and
Annual Statistical Report Form BC 4-71.
The Board of Control expects to develop a new form for the reporting
of Estimated Budgets to bring about uniformity for required information
and expedite approval of the same.
TAXES

The Board of Control has been concerned over recent Tax Law inter-

RULES

Due to tum-over in Lodge Officers and Board of Relief Officers and Representatives, requests have been made for additional copies of the Rules and
Regulations governing operations of Boards of Relief. Copies may be obtained
upon request directly to the Office of The Grand Secretary.
Clarification was requested of Article VIII of the Rules and Regulations
governing Lodge representation in Boards of Relief. The term of a Representative shall be one year, and shall run concurrently with the term, and
with the will and pleasure of the Master who appoints him. Each succeeding
Master may or may not, as he chooses, re-appoint the Representative for an
additional term. However no Representative shall serve more than three
consecutive terms (Three Years) from the effective date of the Rules,
October 1, 1969.
This Board cannot over emphasize the importance and responsibility of
the Master in selecting competent and active Representatives to their Board
of Relief. These Representatives are responsible for the administration and
operation of a Board. This responsibility cannot be delegated to their
employees.
.
The Board of Control has, on a few occasions, received complaints from
various Boards of the failure of member Lodges to remit their per-capita
assessment. As in all such cases of non-compliance with the Rules and Regulations, this Board has communicated with the offenders and sought correction of the situation. Certain cases have been referred to the Grand Master.
Operation of Blood Banks by Boards of Relief have been continued
pending the formation of Jurisdiction or Statewide Blood Banks as per
Recommendation No. 10 of the 1970 Proceedings.
Boards of Relief have been directed NOT to accumulate Blood Bank
Cash surplus until such time as the revised Blood Bank Plan is accepted by
Grand Lodge.
WITHDRAWAL FROM BOARDS OP RELIEP

Several Lodges have inquired regarding methods for withdrawal from
Boards of Relief. The Board of Control, recognizing that many requests were
of a bonafide nature, established the following procedure:

178

179

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

1. The Lodge should direct their written request to the Chairman of the
Board of Control, including therein their reasons, with a copy to the Board of
Relief.
2. The Board of Relief should state in writing, to the Board of Control
approval or disapproval.
3. The Board of Control will rule on each case according to the facts
submitted or obtained.

REALIGNMENT
Previous Board of Control Members recognized that many inequities
existed in Board of Relief memberships due to rapid changes in communities,
relocation of meeting places, and endless other situations. This Board felt
that the time had come for action and was long overdue, and further that a
plan for realignment should be put into effect this year. After considerable
time and effort, a program was drafted based on simple jurisdictional responsibility guidelines, that is,
If there is more than one Lodge meeting in the same City or Town,
they should all be members of the same Board of Relief, or not members
of any Board. In making recommendations for transfers and withdrawals,
your Board was particularly careful not to force the creation of any new
Boards of Relief.
Based on this Jurisdictional responsibility formula, your Board made the
following decisions and recommendations:
REQUESTS BY LoooEs FoR WITHDRAWAL DENIED

Board. Fruitvale No. 336, Orinda No. S21, Diamond No. 603 from the East
Bay Board. Alamo No. 122 from the East Bay Board, San Gabriel No. S46
from the San Gabriel Board.
REQUESTS BY LoooEs FoR TRANSFER APPROVED

All transfers were made subject to the completion of the necessary forms,
payment of per-capita obligations, and approval of the Grand Master.

REPORT OF TRUSTEES
CALIFORNIA MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:

The Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple
herewith submits its Seventeenth Annual Report. At the close of the 1970
Annual Communication, the Board of Trustees held its Annual Meeting and
the following officers were elected:
IRA W. COBURN, P.G.M.•••.••.••..•.... ....... . President

The President, at the first meeting, reported to the Board that the work
on the Auditorium, as outlined in the report of 1969, was completed with the
exception of a few minor items. A year has passed and the Auditorium has
been put to test and found to be in excellent working order.
The raised stage has proved most adequate and functional. The drapes
and side wings have not only added to the beauty of the Auditorium but the
wings have made the entrance to the stage more functional.
All lighting defects observed during the past year have been corrected.
The lighting and sound consoles are operated from the new booth in front
of the balcony. They are efficient, effective, and give the operator great
flexibility of operation.
The new dressing room back stage has provided a great convenience to
the artists.
The acoustics in the Auditorium are excellent. The acoustical work, designed by Dr. Vern Knudsen Ph.D., Sc.D. of UCLA, in 1962 and refined in
subsequent years, has been the basis of our present outstanding and publicly
accepted sound system.

Our Auditorium has become well-known nationally as one of the finest
facilities on the Pacific Coast and it is recognized as a cultural center for
our locality.

In accordance with the instructions of Grand Lodge the Board of Trustees
held two meetings with Robert D. Lintner, Chairman of the Board of Library
Commissioners, as to the needs of space for an adequate Masonic library,
study rooms, periodical rooms, rooms for research and study and offices for
a librarian, together with rooms for bookbinding, mailing and cataloging.
The Board of Trustees then engaged the services of Milton T. Pflueger,
A.I.A., a prominent architect in San Francisco, to make a thorough study of
the properties we acquired and to make recommendations as to how best to
utilize the site.
The Trustees held several meetings with Architect Pflueger and his son,
who is also an architect, and it immediately became apparent that it would
not be practical to erect a structure solely for a library and museum. Present
construction costs for such a structure would be very substantial and would
not provide us with additional income. In addition, in our present Temple
there is a considerable shortage of storage space and there is much need for
space for additional offices of the Grand Lodge and for the Masonic Homes
of California. Our present facilities are totally inadequate as far as office
space is concerned. Furthermore, since we are now renting the Auditorium
for cultural events and other purposes, it is extremely desirable and, in fact,
almost necessary to have a freight elevator to bring equipment to the main
floor of the Auditorium. At the present time our freight elevator only goes
up to "G" floor where our Exhibit Hall is located. This necessitates moving
heavy stage and other equipment through the main foyer of the Temple.
In addition, the Board of Trustees was extremely concerned about erecting
a structure without providing additional sources of revenue. Our present
Exhibit Hall has many shortcomings primarily due to the spacing of the
concrete pillars throughout the whole area, and many prospective tenants
have refused to rent the hall because of this disadvantage. There is a great
need for exhibit space in San Francisco and increased revenue could be
obtained if the new addition contained one or more exhibit halls. At the same
time the new structure could provide additional garage space which would
also give us increased revenue. The architect states the expansion of our
garage facilities would result in a better flow of traffic and likewise provide
additional revenue.
Since the mandate of the Grand Lodge was to present plans for a Grand
Lodge Library and Museum, the Board of Trustees feels that it should
have some direction from Grand Lodge as to the erection of a structure
Which would not only house a library and museum but would also provide
for expanded facilities of our present Temple and facilities which would

At the 1969 Annual Communication of Grand Lodge the following resolution was adopted:
"RESOLVED, That the Temple Board Trustees be requested to
acquire at the most reasonable price the two properties needed to
complete the area behind the Temple window and that said
Trustees prepare plans for the development of the property which
shall be presented to Grand Lodge for approval prior to any
construction."
At the 1970 Annual Communication of Grand Lodge Most Worshipful
Grand Master Chester R. MacPhee made the following recommendation:
(Recommendation No. 2)
"It is my recommendation that this Grand Lodge instruct the Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple, together with the
Library Commission, to continue working on the plans for the
development of our Library and Museum as a part of this building
and present a finalized report for consideration at the Annual
Communication in 1971. The report should include consideration of
feasibility, suggestions as to contents, size and location, estimates
of cost, as well as a possible modest per capita tax increase, if
needed, to effect the program. We should take specific steps to
achieve any goal and our Library Museum is such a worthwhile
goal."
At the same · Communication the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes reported as follows:
"Recommendation number two is that the Trustees of the California
Masonic Memorial Temple and the Library Commission continue
working on plans for the development of a Grand Lodge Library
and Museum and present a finalized report at the 1971 Communication. I so move and the Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a 'yes' vote."
This motion was adopted by Grand Lodge.

bring additional income. The architect states that his fee for the study that
he had made to date was $14,000, $7,000 of which would be credited against
any fee for a feasibility study that he would be called upon to make, and
the balance of $7,000 would be credited against a graphic report, including
slides and illustrative material that he would be called upon to prepare. If
he were called upon to make a feasibility study, including an economic
report, his total fee would be $20,000, less the credit of $7,000. No part of
this $20,000 fee would be recoverable. To make a graphic report, including
slides and illustrative material, his fee would be an additional $30,000, less
the credit of $7 ,000. This latter fee of $30,000 would be credited against
his total architectural fee if he went forward with the project. The architect
further proposed that a model be made of the proposed structure for a cost
of approximately $3,500, which sum would not be recoverable. The new
structure envisaged by the architect would be a beautiful and attractive
building with a large open area behind the endomosaic window, and the new
building would become an integral part of our existing Temple.
The architect estimated that the erection of a new structure, such as that
proposed by him, which would not only house the Library and Museum but
provide us with the additional space needed for our own operation as well as
revenue-producing facilities, would involve a total expenditure of approximately $6,000,000, including furnishings.
Your Board of Trustees did not desire to incur the additional architectural
expenses for a feasibility study or for the graphic report, illustrative material,
etc., until Grand Lodge expressly authorized such expenditures.
This action of the Board is not in any way to be construed as opposing
the erection of a structure to house a library and museum but, in view of
the additional architectural expenses involved and the total approximate
cost, it desires to have specific authorization from Grand Lodge to incur
such additional expenses, it being understood that no construction will commence until specifically approved and authorized by Grand Lodge.
Your Board of Trustees is only anxious to carry out your wishes and
will instruct the architect to proceed with his studies as above outlined if
specifically authorized by you.
The Board expresses its thanks to Brother George D. Gavin, Executive
Manager of the Temple, for his untiring efforts in behalf of the complete
efficient operation and management of the Temple. Appreciation is also
extended to the staff for their conscientious effort in maintaining the building.

Referred to Committees on Policy and General Purposes and on Finance.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes: The Report of the California Masonic Memorial Temple Trustees has been referred to your Committee on Policy and General Purposes because of two policy determinations
requested in the report.
First is a request to the Committee on Finance to include a per capita
tax of not less than 50 cents per member to accelerate liquidation of a present
bank loan. We have discussed this with the Committee on Finance and we
will concur with its report.
Second is a request for Grand Lodge authorization to the Memorial
Temple Trustees to proceed with a proposal calling for a feasibility study,
plus illustrative material, for the development of our Library and Museum
on property which was procured behind the Temple for needed expansion.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes the Memorial
Temple Trustees should proceed with the proposed study and report, with
the understanding that authorization for preparation of final plans will not
be made until such study and report has been received and approved by
Grand Lodge.
I move that the Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple
be authorized to proceed to secure a feasibility study and such related
reports as in their judgment are necessary to enable this Grand Lodge to
make a ·careful decision in the future concerning the development of the
Pine Street property owned by Grand Lodge, and that the costs of the study
and reports be provided from Temple funds.
The Committee on Finance: The Trustees' Report of the California
Masonic Memorial Temple was referred to your Committee on Finance. We
have reviewed this report and we find two areas therein in which we are
particularly concerned.
The Trustees have recommended a per capita tax of not less than fifty
cents per member in order to liquidate all or a portion of the existing bank
loan in the amount of $198,278.00.
Your Committee on Finance has reviewed the cash flow and the revenue
and expenses of the Memorial Temple and, after projecting a normal year of

199

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

operation, it is our opinion that sufficient funds will be generated to retire
this bank loan in a reasonable time.
On the subject of the architectural fees and other initial planning costs,
which have not been resolved at this writing, we further project that such
costs could also be borne by the Memorial Temple.
Your Committee on Finance, therefore, recommends that the suggested
per capita tax of fifty cents not be added to the current budget.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes has indicated its concurrence in this recommendation.
(NOTE: By separate actions of Grand Lodge the recommendation of the
Committee on Policy and General, Purposes and of the Committee on Finance
were adopted.)

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON TAXATION
To lhe Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of CaJ,ifornia:
Since filing our report for 1970, there have been changes in the payroll tax
laws which apply to our various Masonic Organizations.
As has been our custom in the past, we present, for reference purposes,
the usual schedule of tax rates and wage bases for the various payroll taxes
which will be in effect during the calendar year 1972 and thereafter.
FEDERAL WITHHOLDING (INCOME) TAX
All wages paid to employees of a Masonic Lodge are subject to Federal
Income Tax withholding. In order to determine the amount of income tax
which is to be withheld from wages paid to its employees, the Lodge should
ask each employee to complete and file with the Secretary of the .Lodge a
Federal Form W-4, "Employee's Withholding Exemption Certificate".
Reference to current withholding tax tables furnished by the Treasury
Department will enable the Secretary to determine the amount to be withheld.
These will be revised as of January 1, 1972, due to a change in the personal
exemption amount.
CALIFORNIA WITHHOLDING {INCOME) TAX
There is legislation pending which may require withholding of California
State Income Tax. You will be advised if such legislation is enacted.
FEDERAL INSURANCE CONTRIBUTIONS (SOCIAL SECURITY)

As the law now stands, an employee of a Masonic Lodge is subject to
tax for each calendar quarter during which he earns $50.00 or more. The
tax rates shown below are applicable to the first $9,000.00 of wages paid
to each employee during the calendar year. These rates are to be paid by
both the employer and the employee.

Masonic Lodges will be subject to this tax if they qualify as an "employer"
by employing on each of twenty days (each in a different calendar week)
during the preceding or current calendar year, at least one employee for some
portion of the day, or pay wages of $1,500 or more during any quarter in the
current or preceding calendar year. For this purpose, all paid employees of
the Lodge, including the Secretary and those who are performing ritualistic
services (Tiler, Organist, Soloist), should be counted. Federal Unemployment
Tax at the rates shown below will be applicable to the first $4,200.00 of
wages paid to each employee during the calendar year. However, Lodges which
are subject to the California Unemployment Insurance Tax Law, and which
meet certain requirements, will be entitled to a credit up to 2.7%. Only the
employer pays Federal Unemployment Tax.

The Federal Unemployment Tax Liability is computed quarterly and the
tax due is deposited in authorized banks, provided the amount exceeds
specified limits. The Lodge should obtain from the Internal Revenue Service
detailed instructions to implement the deposit procedure.
CALIFORNIA UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE TAX
Masonic Lodges will be subject to this tax if the total wages paid during
a calendar quarter to taxable employees are in excess of $100.00. For this
purpose a taxable employee is one who is paid $50.00 or more per calendar
quarter. However, whether or not elected or appointed officials of a Lodge are
to be counted as taxable employees will depend upon whether or not the
lodge is subject to the Federal Unemployment Tax Act.
If the lodge is not subject to the Federal Unemployment Tax Act, then

202

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
REPORT oN HISTORIC 'fEMlPLE OF BENICIA LonGE No. 5

The Chairman of your Committee on Masonic History met with a special
committee from Benicia Lodge to determine the situation concerning this
historic building and has been able to gather the following information:
This Masonic Temple was the first built as a Masonic Lodge in California.
Construction was commenced in March of 1850 and was completed later that
same year. The first meeting held there by Benicia Lodge was on October
14th, 1850. It was officially dedicated on St. John's Day, December 27th
of that year. The building was in continuous use by Benicia Lodge until
March 10th, 1888, when they moved into their new Temple building erected
on the adjacent property.
Benicia Lodge lost title to the historic Temple from shortly after its
removal until January 3rd, 1950, when it was reacquired by the Lodge by
purchase from Solano County.
It is now being maintained as a Masonic Shrine by Benicia Lodge No. 5.
From 1950, when the Lodge was reacquired, until the present time many
Lodges have performed degrees there. It is one of four sites where this can
to be done without special dispensation. The four being:
1. In the Lodge room at the Masonic Home at Union City.
2. In the Historic Masonic Temple at Columbia.
3. In the Old Masonic Hall of Los Angeles Lodge No. 42.
4. At the Benicia Historic Temple.
This according to Section 324 of the California Masonic Code.
At the Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge in 1949 the reacquisition of this building was discussed by various Committees. It was agreed
that Benicia Lodge should be helped in regaining their former temple.
Benicia Lodge did reacquire it but needed no financial help at that time. Title
to the property is now held in the name of the Lodge and is free and clear
of all liens and encumbrances.
Now, after standing for 120 years against the elements, this historic
building is now in need of large scale reconstruction. The foundation particularly is showing signs of erosion.
The special committee on the preservation of the building, appointed by
the Master of Benicia Lodge, has been working with the city building inspector of the City of Benicia. They have also contacted several building
contractors in the area for bids to repair the building. It has been agreed
that to bring the building up to code and to keep it as a Masonic Shrine
the following should be done:
A. Move the building back 10 feet toward the rear of the lot and plant
grass and shrubs in front for beautification.
B. Rebuild the entire foundation.
C. Bring all plumbing and electrical work up to code.
D. Sand blast and repaint exterior and repaint interior of the building.
E. Repair all windows and sash that may be broken in the move.
Benicia Lodge has received two bids from licensed contractors for this

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

203

work. One from the R. & K. Construction Co. of Benicia is in the amount of
$10,188.00. The second bid is from R. E. Bradley of Vallejo in the amount of
$11,740.00. At the request of this Committee Benicia Lodge obtained a third
bid for comparison. The third bid, from Siri Construction Co., is in the
amount of $14,400.00.
For Benicia Lodge to expend this much money would entirely deplete their
total resources.
We then come to the crux of this matter. What can be done with this
historic Temple. There are three alternatives to which we can tum:
1. Reject any request of Benicia Lodge for financial aid in this matter
and let them either raze the building or find their own means with
which to fix it up themselves.
2. Have Grand Lodge make them a loan at little or no interest with
which to repair the building.
3. Have Benicia Lodge deed the site over to Grand Lodge and have
Grand Lodge make all the repairs on the building.
In our discussions with the members of Benicia Lodge on this matter
your Grand Lodge Committee has reached the following conclusion:
1. If the request of Benicia Lodge is ignored it will, in the near future,
have to raze the building for lack of compliance with the building code.
This would be a tragedy in the perpetuation of the history of Masonry
in our State.
2. A loan to Benicia Lodge would create a hardship on their financial
resources. Their ability to repay such a loan would be impaired by
the rising cost of maintaining their own meeting place and paying
their own incurred bills.
3. The deeding of the property to Grand Lodge seems to be the best
solution. It can be accomplished in the following manner: Benicia
Lodge deeds the property to Grand Lodge who will then expend the
funds needed to put the building into the proper condition. Grand
Lodge can then lease the building back to Benicia Lodge for a determined period. Benicia Lodge will then operate the Historic Temple
and will be responsible for its upkeep, including taxes, insurance, any
minor repairs, etc. They will also be responsible for maintaining it
as a Masonic Shrine.
In this way the history of California Masonry will not suffer another
broken link in its chain.
We are enclosing with this report graphs showing the income and expenditures of the Historic Temple over the last six years. Also enclosed are
the minutes and the final report of the special committee appointed by the
Worshipful Master of Benicia Lodge No. 5.
Portions of this report are referred to the Committee on Finance and
to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
There was a dissenting vote from Brother Ralph E. H. Cooper, of this
Committee.

This Committee would like to acknowledge a gift from Brother Morris C.
Guss, P. M. of Los Angeles Lodge No. 42 of a volume of the "Western States
Jewish Historical Quarterly." The lead story in this volume concerned Rabbi
Abraham Wolf Edelman, Past Master of Los Angeles Lodge No. 42 in 1868,
'81, '83 and '84. He was also the Charter Master of Wilmington Lodge
No. 198. We thank Brother Guss for this presentation.
In order that your Committee on Masonic History may continue its work
for the coming year we submit the following budget:

We are planning on having a dimmer switch installed in the Lodge Hall.
Because of some cracks in the ceiling of the museum, five hundred dollars
was budgeted last year for constructional examination of the building. After
examining the blue prints of the Temple, the State Construction Inspector
told us that there is nothing to worry about, but he did recommend that two
coats of Thompson's Water Bar be applied to the outside of the building.
This was last done in 1962. The cracks in the ceiling have been repaired and
painted and the floor in the foyer has been painted. The cost of these projects
is included in our budget.
Sixteen lodges from various parts of the state have conferred degrees in
the Temple during the year. We hope that more of the Orders will make use
of the Temple next year.
During the June conference held in Sonora, the Most Worshipful Grand
Master of the State of California, the Deputy Grand Master, and other
Grand Lodge Officers visited the Columbia Temple.
The Worthy Grand Matron and the Worthy Grand Patron, of the State
of California, Order of the Eastern Star, with some of their staff, families
and friends also were shown the Lodge Hall and Museum.
We would welcome anything of historical interest, pertaining to the early
days of Masonry in California, to exhibit in the Columbia Museum.

Infractions of our laws, rules and regulations under the jurisdiction of
this committee have been minor in nature. No Masonic trial resulted from
any matter of violation.
The infractions or violations have been handled through discussion and
an understanding with those in violation that said violations will cease and
desist. Several examples of items referred to the Commercialism Committee
are as follows:
One of the members of the Clandestine Bodies was in violation of using
the Square and Compass, with the letter "G" cente~ed the~ein, in. h;i~ advertising. Communication with officers of the Clandestine Bodies was xrutiated
and the matter was ftnally referred to the Grand Secretary for further investigation. Since the Square and Compass are the property of the Grand
Lodge of California, its use must be by permission of the Grand Master
of this Body.
Permission was recommended to the Job's Daughte rs and Rainbow Girls
to sell birthday calendars, as long as the calendars gave no indication of the
sponsoring organization.
One of our Brethren .wanted to open a gift shop and turn the proceeds
over to a Masonic Lodge. By law, the Lodge could not enter into such an
enterprise whereby commercialism was used to raise funds.
A number of charitable athletic events were reviewed by the Committee.
The audited fi.nancial reports of the Shrine football games conducted in
California and Hawaii were submitte d by the Most Worshipful Grand Master
and examined by the Committee, with recommendations and conclusions
reported to the Grand Master. In general, all of these events have been well
conducted, the costs and expenditures were within reason and the net proceeds
have been paid to the Shrine Hospitals.
One charity football game for 1971 was approved by the Committee with
the recommendation to the Grand Master that a defi.nite directive be established at the annual Communication regarding the percentage of expense
that should be allowed for such events.
The Associated Students have requested that a minimum fee against a
percentage of gross ticket sales be paid by the Shrine Temple. The Committee
believes that this type of expense removes the proposed event from the
character of charity and that the Associated Students are, in effect, making
a substantial profi.t from .what should be a charitable event. The Grand
Master concurred with the Committee's recommendation and bas requeste
d
the Committee on Commercialism to prepare a special report with recommendations concerning the above problems for the 1972 Communication.
Your committee does not initiate investigations. Its activities originate
with complaints which are referred to the Committee. A member of the
Committee is assigned each complaint and after investigation the fi.nal report
is forwarded to the Grand Secretary. Continual education of the Brethren
will help to reduce the number of complaints. If in doubt as to the legality

Your committee appreciates the helpful cooperation of the Grand Master
the Grand Secretary and the Grand Lodge Officers. It has been a privileg~
to have worked with each of them.

What effect real property taxes may have on the building and operation
of temples, is, of course, subjeet to future consideration. However, at this
time the matter is receiving much attention from many sources. For instance,
there is at the time of preparation of this report a petition in circulation to
prohibit a real property tax greater than one per cent of . the value. This
petition is calculated to be placed on the ballot as an initiative measure.
Considering further the problems presently facing Lodges and Temple
Associations with regard to taxes it will be recalled that both the Federal and
State governments have recently revised the exempt status of certain organizations such as religious, educational, fraternal and charitable, or those
identified therewith, with a particular endeavor to see that there is not a
connection that results in the consummation of a business which is in fact
a commercial venture properly subject to taxation. This is referred to in the
so called reform legislation of 1969 as unrelated income. While this matter
is presently receiving a great deal of attention there has not, as yet, developed
any rulings or decisions which will with any degree of assurance determine
for Lodges and Temple Associations the precise amount of tax, if any.
These problems indicate the need for those interested to make a determination whether a temple should be a single purpose facility or one which
might in part, be properly used for rent or lease to any person or company
with an outside interest. The question as to whether the use is substantially
incident to Lodge requirements is dependent on the purpose for which used
and tax rulings to be expected in the future.
Notwithstanding the increased cost of construction it is to be noted that
due to urban development, earthquake and old age it is increasingly necessary
to rebuild, repair or demolish old established temples. Many of the older
Lodges are finding it necessary to establish new quarters. As a consequence
there is a constant drive to accomplish what appears in some cases to be
almost an insuperable problem.
The Committee expresses its appreciation to the Grand Master, Most
Worshipful Herbert A. Huebner for his consideration of Temple and kindred
problems, to the Deputy Grand Master, Worshipful Lester S. McElwain, who
has served in a liaison capacity, and to the Grand Secretary, Assistant Grand
Secretary and their staff for their unfailing efforts to assist in any way
possible.
The work of this Committee is continuous and demanding, requiring constant application and effort and in some situations requiring specialized consideration and knowledge usually under conditions requiring fast action.
The efforts of the members, therefore, require diplomacy, tact and great care.
We trust that those efforts have proven of value to those requiring assistance.
There is attached hereto an appendix indicating the action taken on
requests processed since the last annual report. Other matters are pending
and will be reported on at a future date.
In view of the necessity for stationery, mailing costs, travel and expenses

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee this year, consisting of twenty-five members and two
consultants, wish to extend to the Grand Lodge Official Line, including the
Grand Secretary and Assistant Grand Secretary, our gratitude for their
counsel and assistance to the Committee during the past Masonic year.
Three committee meetings were held during the past year: October 13,
1970, January 16, 1971 and May 1, 1971. It is interesting to note that 80%
of the committee members and consultants attended all three meetings and
that the average attendance was twenty-two members. Many guests were
also present during these meetings and their contributions were of great help
to the Committee.
Once again a special recognition must be given, because of their great
devotion and contributions, to our two consultants Brothers Richard R. F.
Lehmann and Oscar E. Anderson.
PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK APRIL 26-30, 1971

"The Public Schools - Pillars of Wisdom, Strength and Beauty" was
the slogan selected by the Most Worshipful Herbert A. Huebner, Grand
Master of Masons in California and Hawaii for this year. The slogan, with
its Masonic connotation, was extremely well accepted and utilized by Masonic
groups. Many non-Masonic groups particularly those in the public school
system also adopted the slogan and used it extensively.
Your Committee is extremely proud of the results of our Annual Public
Schools Week - a partial list follows:
Thirty thousand official posters and bus cards, printed at Los Angeles
Trade Technical College under the direction of Brother Pete Florio, were
distributed through the office of the Grand Secretary.
The pamphlet "The Masons of California and Hawaii Salute Their School
Administrators and Teachers" gained its highest degree of popularity this
past year when it was again offered to the Lodges at no cost. The demand
necessitated three printings and a distribution of 75,000 copies. A new
pamphlet is now on the drawing boards and it is hoped that it will be
available early in 1972.
The media of radio and television were very generous with their time.
The Grand Master, several Committee members and other prominent Masons
appeared on radio and television programs.
In excess of eight million milk cartons carried a panel promoting Public
Schools Week. This project has been in effect for many years and has always

SPECIAL RECOGNITION

The concordant bodies of Freemasonry, through their generous contributions again this year, made it possible for the Committee to perform additional important activities and they have our everlasting gratitude.
Our "thanks" also goes to the teacher groups and many school systems in
California and Hawaii for their help and cooperation during and prior to our
Public Schools Week Observance.
NEXT PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK APRIL 24-28, 1972

"Keep The Public Schools Strong, The Basis For Freedom and Democracy" is the slogan for the 1972 Observance as announced by the Deputy
Grand Master. Your Committee feels that the slogan is an excellent one and
will be widely acclaimed.
WHAT Is AHEAD?

Your Committee, for the past several years, has functioned as a yeararound Committee, without de-emphasizing Public Schools Week concen~ting on the problems of our public schools. Not the least of these 'problems
this last year has been the over abundance of anti-public schools legislation
that has been submitted to the Legislature. Some of this legislation has passed
committee and is awaiting action of the floor. Each member of your Committee and in particular those members of our sub-committee on legislation have
fought the battle and done a yeoman job in getting the word out to the
Brethren in our jurisdiction concerning our problems in Sacramento. The

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
HAITI

Last year Grand Lodge accepted this Committee's recommendation that
the petition for recognition of the Grand Lodge of Haiti be held over. From
information we have received, we can report that the Grand Master, Carnot
Adrien, and the Grand Secretary, Gerson Alexis, are regular, and individually,
of the highest character. Since Haiti has a French background, it is quite
natural that this Grand Lodge is strongly influenced by and continues in
relations of amity with the Grand Orient of France, which we in California
consider to be irregular. Additional information is being sought, and at the
moment I do not want to close the door to eventual recognition, nor do I
want California to be only the second Grand Lodge in the United States
to grant recognition.
So, the recommendation of our Committee is to again postpone action on
this matter.

are

GRAND LODGE ALPINA OF SWITZERLAND

Since I have already touched on the Grand Orient of France, perhaps I
should now mention the Grand Lodge Alpina of Switzerland, with whom the
United Grand Lodge of England has severed relations. We leam from the
latter's quarterly Communication that there is substantial evidence of
visitation by irregular masons, presumabl y from Lodges under the jurisdiction
of the Grand Lodge of France. The Grand Lodge Alpina has issued a Bulletin
by which we are informed of its adherence to basic Masonic principles and
that any particular contacts, such as ritualistic work in their temples, with
any pseudo-masonic or para-masonic bodies not under the control or direction
of a Grand Lodge which has been recognized by the Grand Lodge Alpina
of Switzerland, "must be uncompromisingly avoided."
In the confidence that the edicts of the Grand Lodge will be obeyed, your
Committee sees no need at this time to disturb the amity which presently
exists between our Grand Jurisdictions.
CHILE

In connection with recent political and economic events in Chile, the
President of that Country, Senor Salvador Allende, has been variously
described in our news media as a Marxist, an atheist and a mason. To
resolve this seeming contradicti on, our Grand Secretary queried his opposite
member in Chile and we are informed that Brother Allende was made a
mason in 1935, served as W. M. of Hiram Lodge No. 65, and has been active
in the Craft during his masonic life. Also, that he has never declared himself
to be an atheist but has publicly reiterated that he is a mason, and finally

218

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

that since Allende's younghood he has been a member of the Socialist Party
and never of the Communist Party, those parties being antagonistic to each
other. The Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of Chile adds that Communists cannot be members of Chilean Freemasonry.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE

MExrco
There seems to be increasing interest among the Lodges of the United
States of Mexico in obtaining recognition from foreign Grand Lodges. Your
Committee has before it petitions from the Gran Logia "Occidental Mexicana"
whose seat is in Guadalajara, and whose jurisdiction includes the States of
Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan, and the Grand Lodge "La Oriental
Peninsular" seated in Merida and claiming jurisdiction over Yucatan, Quintana, Roo and Belize.
At the present time, we lack sufficient information to justify recommending
recognition of either of these Grand Lodges.

BRAZIL
We have also been requested to exchange representatives with the Grand
Orient of Brazil.
Two years ago I devoted most of my Report to Brazilian Masonry, so it is
only necessary now to remind the Brethren of Grand Lodge that there are
two powerful Masonic Powers in Brazil: the Grand Orient, claiming jurisdiction over the entire country, and the State Grand Lodges claiming jurisdiction over the particular state in which they exist.
We recognize seventeen of these Grand Lodges.
At the present time there seems to be Treaties of Amity between the
Grand Orient and all the state Grand Lodges, but our letters from the Grand
Orient indicate that they are to be considered the only regular Masonic
power in Brazil.
Until we have further information as to their fraternal inter-relations, we
recommend that the Grand Lodge of California does not extend recognition to
the Grand Orient of Brazil.
Respectfully submitted,

WILLIAM RHonEs HERVEY, JR., Chairman
J. NEn. HANSON

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Constitution of the United States has been a bulwark for freedom for
184 years, and guides a Nation that has survived while most of the other
}eading Nations of the world have deteriorated or collapsed. This government of the people and for the people has existed as a polestar of guidance in
a turbulent and changing world, because its citizens fundamentally believed
in and followed the tenets of our Constitution.
It will continue to exist only as long as the principles and bases of the
document are fully understood and correctly interpreted, and as long as a
free people have the courage to stand firm against aggression.
Your Constitution Observance Committee is pleased to report to the
Grand Lodge that, through the splendid support, enthusiasm and efforts of
the Craft as a whole, we are able to report an outstanding year of accomplishment on this most important program.
Your committee on Constitution Observance consisted of thirty-one
members and one Advisor. Four meetings were held during the Masonic
year. The Committee has endeavored to implement and carry out the theme
for this Masonic year as set forth in the Grand Master's Constitution Observance Proclamation, proclaiming the month of September, 1971 to be
Constitution Observance Month in the Jurisdiction of California and Hawaii;
and directing all Lodges to arrange and perform, or actively participate in,
pitriotic exercises, to which the public is invited, with the objective of demonstrating faith in our Nation, intensifying our allegiance to it, denouncing its
enemies within or without, and pledging that justice without undue delay
or unconscionable interruption will always prevail.
The ultimate success of this year's program must certainly be ascribed
to the mass communication coverage, through radio and television announcements particularly in the Metropolitan areas of Los Angeles, San Francisco
and San Diego.
Because of the disappointing results in previous years, many Lodges do
not put forth the enthusiasm they should because of a feeling of "What's
the use? No matter how hard we work, we still can't get the response we
desire."
Following a lengthy discussion by this Committee at a meeting held on
March 14, 1970, in San Francisco at which time twenty-three members were
present, your Chairman appointed a sub-committee of five members headed
by Brother Richard Hopelain to examine alternate methods of presenting
our Constitution Observance Program.
'
The purpose of this study was to reach the largest possible number of
people with the message of Constitution Observance. Through our Lodges,
Newspapers, Radio and Television. On June the 29th of this year, Your

It is the unanimous recommendation of the Committee that a charter
be granted and number assigned to Tustin Lodge No. 828 in the City of
Tustin, County of Orange.
There has been assigned to our Committee that portion of the Report
of the Grand Secretary listing changes of meeting place of a number of
Lodges, and also that portion relating to the following consolidations:
York Lodge No. 423 and Florence Lodge No. 649, to be known as
Florence Lodge No. 423; also Pacific Lodge No. 136 and Lebanon Lodge
No. 495, to be known as Lebanon-Pacific Lodge No. 136.
We recommend that the Grand Secretary be authorized to properly
endorse the above charters to carry out these changes.
This would normally conclude the report of the Committee on Charters,
however, I have received permission from the Grand Master to add a few
remarks. I have been studying the minutes of the Committee on Charters
covering the past fifteen years and I would like to share the results of this
study. (I might insert at this point that I have to be careful of what I say
because our Grand Master was chairman of the Charters Committee during
most of this time and would qualify as an expert witness.)
During the 15 year period, 88 Lodges have been chartered. There were
3,751 charter members, of which about 2,500 were California Masons and
the rest sojourners. The 1970 Proceedings show the total membership of
these 88 Lodges to be 14,453. In other words, the 2,500 California Masons
in the new Lodges had brought in 11,953 new members.
Now lets look at the total membership of Grand Lodge for this same
period. In 1955, the membership was 224,887, rising to a peak of 244,586 in
1965 and dropping to 233,855 in 1970 - a net gain of about 9000 members
over the fifteen years. In other words, in the past 15 years, 2,500 California
Masons in the 88 new Lodges attracted 11,953 new members while the other
approximately 220,000 Masons in the other 614 older Lodges showed a
net loss of about 2,900 members.
There is an old saying that figures don't lie but that liars do figure and
I hasten to add that this is probably an oversimplification of our membership
situation, but it does point up beyond question that our total membership
trend is strongly influenced by the formation of new Lodges.
The point of all this is that our laws and regulations, (and I would not
change them), prohibit the solicitation of new members - but there is
nothing Masonically illegal or Masonically improper in actively encouraging
and assisting the formation of new Lodges. Other organizations attach great
honor to the Club or Chapter which actively sponsors a new club, yet in
many cases the only problem is to find a certain number of worthy people
willing to sit down at an established eating place and have a meal together.

Respectfully submitted,
HERMAN R. Moou, Chairman

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The only new Lodge formed since our last communication has been
Tustin Lodge U.D. which received a Dispensation dated July 2, 1971, was
instituted on July 28, 1971, and has now applied for a charter.
Tustin is an incorporated city in Orange County just south of the City
of Orange and east of Santa Ana. The area was mainly agricultural until about
1960 but has since become a residential community for the rapidly growing
surrounding areas which include the extensive Irvine Development. Despite
the population explosion, this is the first new Lodge in this part of the country
since 1925 and will be the only lodge in Tustin.
An unusual aspect of this Lodge is that it meets in the parish hall of St.
Cecelia Catholic Church. The Lodge has had enthusiastic support from
Father John Sammon, Pastor of St. Cecelia's, and has also had complete
cooperation from the Knights of Columbus who share the building.
The officers and representatives of Tustin Lodge have submitted the
required records and have met with the Committee on Charters. Both the
records and interviews have been most satisfactory and all the requirements
of our ordinances have been fulfilled. While the time under dispensation has
been short, we feel that this is compensated for by the wealth of Masonic

224

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

A Masonic Lodge has a more difficult birth! The members who start it must
already belong to the Craft; a suitable meeting place must be found; the
officers must be proficient in both the ritual and our laws; and the new candidates must come of their own free will and accord. All of these problems
can be solved but sometimes a new group needs some help.
There are 10 Lodges in our jurisdiction with over 1,000 members; there
are 125 Lodges with over 500 members; there are Lodges adjoining fast
growing areas - too far away to adequately serve the new community, but
near enough to help form a Lodge. I am appealing to these Lodges; to the
Masters, the Officers, and the Past Masters, to consider as a project, the
formation of a new Lodge. This does not mean robbing an existing Lodge
of its members, but it does mean helping find the nucleus of a new group,
helping them find a meeting place (and it is surprising what ingenuity will
do in solving this problem), and giving them assistance and advice in solving
their problems. In case you are thinking that this sponsorship might furnish
competition to older Lodges and hurt them, I can say that it has been
the experience of the Charters Committee, that the activity and enthusiasm
of a new Lodge attracts a new group of potential candidates and sojourners
and that there is little effect on the growth pattern of existing Lodges.
The Charters Committee stands ready to help whenever called upon.
There is a manual available that details each step in forming a Lodge and
I am sure the Inspector Corps will cooperate as they always have.
And so I am urging that this jurisdiction take a new approach to the
formation of Lodges - that we actively and aggressively sponsor and assist
them and that we pay due honor to the Lodges and members who accept
this challenge. Instead of depending on "Spontaneous Combustion", let's
light the match and then fan the flame so that when a worthy young man
considers joining our fraternity, there will be a door upon which he can
knock and a brother there to say, "Let him enter!"
This concludes the report of the Committee on Charters.
Respectfully submitted,
KENNETH HEMPHILL, Chairman
