REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Correspondence Committee of the Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California, respectfully submits the within Review covering Masonic Jurisdictions,
other than California, and with whom California maintains Masonic recognition.
It has been said that all Masonic Grand Lodge Jurisdictions, as well as
their constituent Blue Lodges, are maldng surveys in an attempt to learn the
cause of lack of growth of Masonic Lodges, including membership losses. Some
have increased youth organizations, promotions; some have expended efforts
of increasing Masonic news in newspapers, radio and TV; more scholarship
programs are being developed and such activities as non-realistic programs joint programs with other organizations, which have a prerequisite Masonic membership discussion group meetings, increased social meetings, more
public installations of officers and meetings for presentation of SO-year emblems, etc., are becoming more common.
It has been said that the young man is not joining any fraternal order. Do
not worry about it. Petitioners in their early twenties are very few. Instead,
young men are in the military service of their country. Others, including those
in military service are either going to be, or are married, buying a home with
a 20 or 30 year mortgage, or deed of trust - buying a sports car, a television
set, have children, hospital bills and the worry about education of their children. All this will take time and money - a lot of both. When the young man
gets in his early 40's, or later, he will become a good prospect for petitioning
a Masonic Lodge.
Here are some gleanings from the various books of proceedings which your
committee received.
Alabama started an "Endowment Pennies Program" and ten lodges participated the first year, contributing $2,101.85. Florida has had this program
for a number of years, which is named "Let your pennies make Good Cents",
and in 1970 Florida's contributions totaled $224,027 .63.
What is known as "St. Luke's Program" is a new venture of Connecticut,
developed by a physician and named after St. Luke, the physician, its intent
being to bring a feeling of brotherhood, unity, involvement and consideration
for the needs of others, primarily to older men aand women to make them
feel that they belong and that Masonry is interested in their welfare.
The Grand Lodge of the District of Columbia has a Grand Lodge Physician whose duties it is to attend all Grand Lodge meetings to administer
emergency or first aid attention to anyone requiring it.
Georgia adopted the District Deputy Grand Master System.
Idaho Lodges are asked to provide the Grand Chaplain with the name and
address of a Brother's widow immediately following his death so that he can
express the sympathy of the Grand Lodge.
The Illinois Medical Center started in 1921 with 53 available beds, now
has grown to a 620-bed capacity.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND ORATION -

1971

"THANK GOD I AM AN AMERICAN"
BURTON MEYER, JR., Grand Orator

Most Worshipful Sir, Grand Lodge Officers, Distinguished Guests and
Brethren:
"I believe in the United States of America as a government of the people,
by the people, for the people; whose just powers are derived from the consent
of the governed; a democracy in a republic; a sovereign nation of many
sovereign states; a perfect union, one and inseparable; established upon those
principles of freedom, equality, justice and humanity for which American patriots sacrificed their lives and fortunes. I therefore believe it is my duty to my
country to love it; to support its Constitution; to obey its laws; to respect its
flag; and to defend it against all enemies."
Nearly 200 years ago, at the Constitutional Convention of 17 8 7, after many
months of careful deliberation and many heartaches, there was engrossed upon
parchment a document unique in the history of mankind. Of the 39 signers of
our Constitution 23 were Freemasons. From that time forward, the fabric of
our nation has b~en woven with the golden threads of Masonry always evident,
creating a tapestry that has been the centerpiece of admiration for nearly two
long centuries. This great nation was born out of the agonizing existence of
oppression of a foreign nation. It is the oldest continuous form of government
in existence today. Freemasonry is also the oldest continuous fraternity in existence today - the two go hand in hand because the principles upon which
each were erected are the principles which have made each of them a shining
light in the history of mankind. The basic principles of Freemasonry and the
basic principles of our Constitution are inseparable. The members of our Fraternity therefore played an important part in the creation of the United States
of America.
Today we should, as Masons and as Americans, be concerned with the
events in our history during the past few years. Our country was founded in an
atmosphere of turmoil but in a spirit of excellence. Throughout our history,
trouble has come and gone but our high purposes have remained intact. Today,
the standards we raised are still vital in a complex and changing world. We are
being challenged to hold to our high ideals and to share in the great American
dream - freedom and justice and equality for all; the pursuit of happines.5
and the absence of fear; where man's loyalty is to God and to his country.
It is inconceivable that it should be necessary to have an "Honor America
Day". We should, each day of our lives, thank God that we have the rare
privilege of living in this great country and to be Americans. We should be
concerned about those who would seek to destroy our way of life, seek to
destroy all that this nation stands for and what it has meant to the millions of
persons over the years - and to those who have fought and died to preserve
the very things that made this country great - our cherished ideals and our

229

dreams of an ever improving tomorrow. Our nation was conceived in liberty
and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal. This nation
has survived and endured events in our history that have destroyed other
nations. Today, we are being tested as to whether this nation or any nation so
conceived and so dedicated can long endure; whether our form of government,
as we know it today, will survive yet another crisis; whether this nation dedicated to freedom and dedicated to almighty God will continue to exist.
Yes, my Brethren, we are being challenged by a group of young radical
revolutionaries, dedicated to the destruction of the establishment and the overthrow of OUT form of government. Let us pray to God to give us the wisdom, the
strength and the courage to meet this challenge.
Can we succeed? I am sure that we can. We can succeed because, as Masons,
we have always had the desire and the determination to uphold our Masonic
principles - the Brotherhood of Man under the Fatherhood of God; because
the foundation stones upon which our nation and our fraternity were erected
are as strong today as the day they were laid. No other nation on the face of
this earth or any other nation in the history of mankind can match the progress
and the accomplishments of these great United States of America. Let's look at
some of these accomplishments:
Let's look at education - Today there are more children attending more
schools, with more facilities, receiving a better education than at any other time
in our history.
I look at these accomplishments and say, "THANK GOD I AM AN
AMERICAN."
Let's look at medicine - The life expectancy of Americans has increased
by 50% in the past 50 years. We no longer fear the diseases of the past. Polio,
typhus, diptheria, smallpox, scarlet fever and T.B. have virtually been eradicated. More Americans enjoy longer and healthier lives than at any other time
in our history.
I look at these accomplishments and say, "THANK GOD I AM AN
AMERICAN."
Let's look at science - In the past few years, American scientists have
enabled us to have a world wide communications system; launched satellites to
forecast weather conditions; perfected nuclear energy for the benefit of all
mankind; put men in orbit in outer space; succes.5fully landed men on the
moon and dramatically returned them safely to earth.
I look at these accomplishments and say, "THANK GOD I AM AN
AMERICAN."
Let's look at civil rights - In the past few years, more has been done in the
field of civil rights than was done in nearly 200 years. While more remains to be
accomplished, today, the minority groups have more advantages, earn more
money and have made more social progress than at any other time in our
history.
I look at these accomplishments and say, "THANK GOD I AM AN
AMERICAN."

231

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Let's look at labor - More Americans support our free enterprise system
by owning more stock in more corporations than ever before. Today, there are
more persons employed, working shorter hours, working under better conditions, earning more money, enjoying more leisure hours with more luxuries
than at any other time in our history.
I look at these accomplishments and say, "THANK GOD I AM AN
AMERICAN ."
The list of our accomplishments and our contributions to world progress is
not only impressive - it is endless. But what about the future? We need not
be afraid of the future for the future will be in our own hands. We shall need
courage, energy and determination but above all, we shall need faith- faith in
ourselves, faith in our communities, faith in our country and faith in Almighty

we do indeed practice the tenets of Freemasonry and so impress the outside
world of the goodness of this Institution and prove to them that we are proud
to be ~asons an~ proud to be Americans. By our acts and by our deeds, shall
we be Judged. It httle matters what we say or what we do if our words and our
actions do not subscribe to the highest of our principles.
Remember the solemn obligations that each of us took at the altars of
Freemasonry and make them a part of our daily practice - so to live and so to
act. Th.ere is no pla~e in ~~n~ for less than our very best. Strive always for
perfection because if we fail m this regard, we have failed not only Masonry we have failed ourselves as well.
Our heritage dictates that we must, on all occasions, uphold the traditions
of our Fraternity. Let our principles become a part of the daily lives of our
youth groups and, in particular, of our DeMolay. These are the persons who
l<>?k .up to us as examples of virtues upon which they will erect their lives. They
will Judge us as examples of excellence or examples of failure. If we can be the
guiding light in some young person's life, we will have fulfilled an important
mission in our Masonic life.
You, who sit out there today, are the representatives not only of your Blue
Lodges but the representatives of Masonry in your local areas. You are the
Grand Lodge of California and, as such, you will be judged by your fellow man.
If t?e principles of Freemasonry have instilled in you a strong will and a strong
desire to be better men and better citizens in your communities, you will have
added another important and vital link in the golden chain of Freemasonry. I
hope that each of you will leave this Annual Communication desirous of rededicating your lives to Freemasonry and to better citizenship.
Let each of us have the unbounded determination and the burning desire
that our forefathers had to make the American dream come true. Let each of us
light a candle of faith and hope and the glow from that flame will truly light the
world. Let each of us unite in a common goal, as Masons and as Americans to
insure that future generations will realize that American dream· not an impossible dream but a dream come true; that same dream our ~erican forefathers had nearly 200 years ago when those 23 Freemasons affixed their
signatures on that piece of parchment, our priceless heritage known as the
Constitution of the United States of America.
Let each one of the 200 million Americans of this great nation climb that
highest mountain and whether it looks out on the windswept plains of Kansas
or the snow capped mountains of Montana; or the sand covered deserts of California or the rock bound shores of Maine; we should climb that highest mountain and- standing erect - at the very summit - shout in a voice for all the
world to hear - "THANK GOD, THANK GOD I AM AN AMERICAN ."

230

God.

We must place our faith in the youth of this great nation and while some
groups of our youth are testing and challenging our form of government, I
believe that those who would divide us will have united us. Someone once said,
"What a pity to waste youth on the young." I disagree. Youth need not be
wasted - it cannot be wasted. It is our greatest natural resource.
Young people must have someone or something to identify with- let that
be Freemasonry and the Master Mason. The youth of our nation today will be
the leaders of tomorrow. Herein lies our challenge. We can take the youth of
our nation and help mold them into better citizens. What better place to begin
our program than with our own youth groups - Jobs Daughters, Rainbow for
Girls and DeMolay; our own youth groups who are dedicating their lives to the
Brotherhood of Man and the Fatherhood of God; young Americans who believe
in and practice the basic philosophies of Freemasonry. In each of the past few
years, we have had representatives of our youth groups appear in this magnificent auditorium and address this Grand Lodge; outstanding examples of
what the overwhelming majority of our youth really stand for and what they
truly represent. America's future is in their hands and since these young adults
are in the majority, then we can be confident that America's future will be safe
and secure. We can be proud that they believe in what we believe in - that
Freemasonry does, indeed, serve the Brotherhood of Man under the Fatherhood
of God; that the foundation of this great and glorious nation was built upon
those Masonic principles which we hold so dear; that these youth groups will
safeguard and protect this country against the groups of radical revolutionaries
and thus insure that this nation, under God, shall not perish from the earth.
The youth of our nation have an awesome responsibility placed in their
hands and they must learn that responsibility is the price of freedom. Let us not
forget that we, too, have a responsibility, a duty and an obligation to support
these fine youth groups by showing them that we have a genuine interest in
their programs and in the goals which they have set for themselves.
The hallmarks of our Fraternity have always been brotherly love, relief
and truth. Let us insure and safeguard these principles not only for ourselves
but for the entire world. Let us display to the public, not by mere rhetoric, that

the active cooperation of many of our Inspectors, to whom we owe a great
debt. It is essential in any such program that dates to be scheduled be worked
into local planning to avoid conflicts, and this year there was a minimum of
misunderstanding.
Two problems have developed with this program as originally conceived:
1) some of the panel subjects constructed for the assistance of the Inspectors
in carrying out their charge in the California Masonic Code, 161, 3rd (" ....
for instruction in the proper administration of the affairs of the Lodges, and
such other matters as may be for the welfare of the Craft.") have been misunderstood as to purpose, and have required to be withdrawn until a lawful
method of agreed operation can be developed to permit such assistance to
our Lodges; and 2) it is apparent that most of the Brethren who attended
the Workshops are officers of their Lodges. This is good in the sense that a
very high percentage of the members of Grand Lodge is in this group. But
it is not good in that the program has reached just over 1% of the members
of the Fraternity in this jurisdiction, or about one half of our active Masons,
who number only about 6000 I
Question: how can we activate the inactive member? How can we make
them Masons in more than name?
It is the contention of this Committee, derived from its organizational
instructions from this Grand Lodge that any meetings should be voluntary
in nature, and that if they cannot reach the general membership on that
basis they will render no service to the Fraternity. It is our conviction that
a few men cannot impress a regulation or a regime on a voluntary organization of free and intelligent men. Any such attempt loses sight of the causes
of our ancient Brethren banding together as a Brotherhood. We need for
the welfare of Masonry, broad participation and personal concern with the
health of our Lodges and the interest and interests of their component members. We have too few of our Brethren so concerned. It is a fact that those
active in our Grand Lodge organization number only 650 Masons.
It is not the intent of this report to find fault with the necessarily small
number of officers and other influential members of this Grand Lodge. It is
our intent to draw your attention to this fact, and to advance the concept
that it would be desirable to encourage and create wider participation in the
activities of the Craft.
Not to leave an imponderable thought with you, with no consideration
of a solution, we call your attention to the concluding list of panelists who
have participated in the above programs of the Committee on Masonic
Information and Responsibility this past year without official appointment,
and at considerable self-sacrifice and personal expense out of their love for
the Fraternity and its ideals. This is the kind of selfless participation that
made possible the formation of this Grand Lodge some 120 years ago.
Masonic ideals are not obsolete.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON CEMETERIES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Cemeteries submits the following report of their
activities for the Masonic Year 1970-1971.
As most of you already know, Grand Lodge has, for a number of years,
owned the Masonic Cemetery in the Columbia State Park at Columbia the
Jamestown Masonic Cemetery in Jamestown and the Fiddletown Cem;tery
at Fiddletown.
Columbia: Located in the Columbia State Park near Sonora is in good
condition. The weeds were sprayed by the Future Farmers of America of
Sonora and some other clearing was done. It has been noted that several
headstones in the cemetery are in need of repairs and we are requesting a
sum in our budget this year for that purpose. We do not know the exact

237

amount of restoration work that will be required but we are requesting an
additional $200.00 for that purpose. A Square and Compass wreath was
placed in the Cemetery on Memorial Day and many favorable comments
were made by visitors to the park.
Jamestown: This cemetery, also located near Sonora, was again sprayed
for weeds and some hand cleaning was done. This cemetery is graced with
a number of large beautiful oak trees. We have reported the past two years
that one dead tree had to be removed and a number of dead limbs removed
from others. We were unable to get anyone to do the work but this year
Brother Buck Nelson succeeded in getting the job done at a cost of $100.00
which we consider most reasonable. Unless we have some bad storms this
type of work should not have to be done again for a number of years. It has
also been noted that some work should be done on several of the headstones
and we are requesting $100.00 to start this project. These headstones, like
the ones in the Columbia Cemetery are well over 100 years old and do
require almost constant attention.
Fiddletown: Brother Vincent Lake, because of a back injury and surgery,
was only able to make one trip to this Cemetery and that was in February.
He has in the past been doing much of the clean up work himself. He does
report however, that all is well at the cemetery. Weed spraying was again
done by the Amador County Agriculture Department. We are most fortunate
to have this service and at such a low cost. Amador Disposal Company does
some of the clean up work and leaves a large container there for those who
do work on their family grave sites. Their charge is usually about $20.00.
Peter Lassen Grave: This grave site of Peter Lassen, well known in
Masonic history, is located near Susanville. We do not own this property
but have taken over the responsibility of caring for it. Your chairman made
an inspection of this grave site in late February and found it to be in good
condition. The original marker is well protected by a redwood shake roof
and a chain link fence. Two new redwood picnic tables have been installed.
It is our hope that several more can be put in this next year. This site has
become quite a popular place for travelers who are interested in early California history to stop for a picnic lunch and take pictures of the monuments.
Michigan Bluff: For several years Grand Lodge has been working to
acquire title to the Michigan Bluff Masonic Cemetery in Michigan Bluff,
Placer County. This property consists of approximately one acre and has
been known as the Michigan Bluff Masonic Cemetery for well over 100 years.
There are only a few headstones in this cemetery and all bear the Masonic
Emblem. A few years ago these stones were set in cement pads to prevent
further damage to them and a minimum amount of clearing was done. On
December 4, 1970, Judge Ronald Cameron of Placer County issued the
necessary certificate and a deed to the property dated July 4, 1971 was
delivered to the Grand Secretary. This will be an entirely new project for us
and we are requesting the sum of $250.00 for work to be done during the
1971-72 year.

SUPPLEMENT TO REPORT OF
SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON CEMETERIES*
Edward H. Siems
Oct. 6, 1971
% Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California
1111 California St.,
San Francisco, Calif. 94108
Dear Brother Siems:
This is my report of a meeting with the elective officers of Fallbrook

239

Lodge No. 317 and the president and directors of the Mai<>nic Cemetery
~ciation of Fallbrook.

Meeting held in the offices of Oceanside Savings and Loan Association in
Fallbrook and started about 10:15 A.M. and adjourned at approximately
2:30 P.M. on Saturday, October 2nd, 1971.
Fallbrook Lodge was represented by Jack R. Levitt, Attorney at Law,
1906 U. S. Bank Building, San Diego, Calif. 92101, phone (714) 232-6211.
Brother Levitt is a member of San Diego Lodge No. 35.
Mr. Donald Anthony, president of the Masonic Cemetery Association of
Fallbrook, and he claims others that he would not name, was represented by
Arlie W. Bergman, Attorney at Law of 309 S. Maple Street, Escondido,
Calif., phone (714) 745-1641. Brother Bergman is a member of Consuelo
Lodge No. 325 of Escondido.
Mr. Anthony has apparently been circulating a report that the Grand
Lodge and Fallbrook Lodge now want to gain control of the Cemetery and its
bank accounts so that they could do with them as they see fit.
My opening remarks were to the effect that Grand Lodge wanted no part
of their cemetery or the accumulated funds. That I was in Fallbrook to
attempt to bring all sides together and see that Fallbrook Lodge did not
loose control of their property.
Much discussion was then centered on who had title to the land, how
much money was on hand and who were the stockholders.
The Master of the Lodge reported that a title search was being made
and that as of Friday night, October 1st, everything appeared to be free
and clear.
I talked with William Alford, Master of Fallbrook Lodge, Tuesday night,
October 5th, on the phone and he told me that the title search was made by
First American Title Company of San Diego and that everything was free
and clear and that title was vested in the name of Masonic Cemetery Association of Fallbrook. During the same conversation Mr. Alford stated that
the shares of stock that were to be delivered to him for safekeeping by
2 :30 Tuesday afternoon had not been delivered. He told me at the same
time that Mr. Anthony made the remark to the man sitting next to him at
our meeting that, "I will turn over nothing to Fallbrook Lodge or to the
Grand Lodge."
Mr. Anthony claims to own one share of stock because he purchased
200 square feet of the cemetery property. It is his claim that some judge told
him to buy the plots so that he could be on the board. He failed to give the
name of the judge. It was later brought out that at one time 1997 shares
were supposedly held in trust for the lodge by a brother now in bad graces
with the lodge. His name is Vick Westfalls and is now supposed to be in
Australia. These shares were later transferred to James Robinson, a present
member of the board. Mr. Robinson claims the shares were put in his name
a number of years ago and that he paid nothing for them. He admits that
he is supposed to be holding them in trust.

240

241

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The association has two reserve accounts in the Oceanside Federal Savings
and Loan of Fallbrook in the amounts of $20,227.94 and $12,155.27 as of
June 1, 1971. Two names appear on these accounts, Donald Anthony and
Dave Glick. They also have in the Bank of America of Fallbrook what they
call the maintenance account of a little over $3000.00. Two names are on this
account, Donald Anthony and Zane McAnear. McAnear is a treasurer of the
Association.
Mr. McAnear claims his name was on the two reserve accounts when they
were transferred to Fallbrook. He does not know how nor when his name
was taken off and the name of Dave Glick added. There appears to be very
little, if any, communication between Mr. Anthony and Mr. McAnear.
It was brought out that regular meetings of the Association are very
seldom called or held and when they did have meetings, proper minutes were
not kept. Bills to be paid were in a number of instances just handed to the
treasurer on a plain piece of paper with instructions to issue a check for the
amount and give it to Mr. Anthony. I saw a couple of these bills and they
did not explain in detail what they were for.
Very poor records are kept and it is very doubtful that they have a
proper set of books.
There is an apparent attempt by a small group to take over the cemetery
and its assets and run it exactly as they see fit with no regard what-so-ever
for the lodge.
Mr. Anthony claims there are approximately 50 to 300 shareholders but
that stock certificates have not been issued. He claims to have the book of
stock certificates with some stubs and certificates in it. He has not produced
the book and apparently is unwilling to do so. He would name no other
stock.holders other than himself and James Robinson. He said the figures of
50 to 300 shares was an estimate.
Lots in the cemetery are 5 feet by 10 feet and are sold for $200.00 each.
Half of the money received is put in the reserve or perpetual care fund,
the other half goes to the maintenance fund. According to the original by-laws,
any person buying 4 lots (200 square feet) is entitled to one share of stock
and one vote. He also claims that single lot owners can pool their interests
in multiples of four and have a vote but not a share of stock.
It was pointed out by several members of the lodge that the taxes on the
cemetery property were paid out of lodge funds for many years. More
recently these taxes have been pa.id out of cemetery funds.
A number of years ago, the cemetery had $4000.00 in the bank. Fallbrook
Lodge borrowed $3000.00 to help finance their temple. The lodge did not give
the cemetery association a note for the amount borrowed. About 15 years later
the money was repaid but with no interest. Mr. Anthony was quite disturbed
that the interest had been lost over the years. One member present pointed
out that the money was actually borrowed by the Fallbrook Masonic Temple
Association and not the lodge itself. It was also mentioned that Mr. Anthony
was on the temple board during a part of this time and that he made no

attempt to see that the money was repaid to the cemetery and also made no
mention of interest.
The Articles of Incorporation of the Masonic Cemetery Association of
Fallbrook expired on September 13, 1971. The attorney, Mr. Levitt, stated
that the association was no longer in existence and that new articles would
have to be filed and a new set of by-laws drawn up.
It is my understanding that the attorneys for both sides plan to get
together and see if they can come up with some solutions that will be satisfactory for all concerned. Mr. Levitt has agreed to keep me posted. The
attorney for Mr. Anthony, Arlie Bergman, appears to be a very reasonable
and understanding man.
About two o'clock in the afternoon it appeared that we were getting
nowhere and that Mr. Anthony was unwilling to cooperate in any way, so I
issued the following directives:
To the Master of the Lodge, William G. Alford:
1. That he instruct the attorney to draft a new set of Articles of Incorporation and file them with the Secretary of State.
2. That he appoint at the next stated meeting of Fallbrook Lodge on
October 7, 1971, a committee to draft a new set of by-laws that would
comply with the Grand Lodge rules as set forth in the Masonic Code,
and that they be acted ui>on as rapidly as possible.
To Donald Anthony (President of the Cemetery Board)
1. It is ordered that all shares of Masonic Cemetery of Fallbrook be
given to the Master of Fallbrook Lodge No. 317 within 72 hours,
and that such shares be placed in a safe deposit box for safe keeping.
2. The names of all stockholders of the Masonic Cemetery Association
of Fallbrook and the number of shares owned by each be sent to me
within 10 days of the above date.
3. An audit of the books of the Masonic Cemetery Association of Fallbrook be made and sent to me within 10 days of the above date.
4. A complete financial statement of the Masonic Cemetery Association
of Fallbrook be sent to me and to the Grand Lodge Committee on
Lodge Finance within 10 days of the above date.
Dated October 2, 1971 at 2:20 P.M., Fallbrook, California, and
signed by Basil R. Gillett, Chairman, Grand Lodge Committee on .
Cemeteries and by Milo A. Ensminger, Inspector of District No. 636.
In a letter dated May 7, 1971 from Mr. Donald Anthony to the Master
of Fallbrook Lodge he stated, "Neither Grand Lodge nor Fallbrook Lodge
has any jurisdiction in our cemetery business."
Mr. Anthony admits the cemetery records are incomplete and have been
very poorly kept for a number of years.

REPORT OF BOARD OF LIBRARY COMMISSIONERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
In response to our appointment by Grand Master Herbert A. Huebner,
your commission has endeavored, with his assistance and support, and with
the full cooperation of the Grand Secretary and his staff, to carry out the
Grand Master's expressed wishes with regard to the administration of your
Library and Museum.
With regard to additions to our ever-expanding library, we beg leave to
report that over 390 volumes were donated by members of Grand Lodge,
members of constituent lodges, and the families of deceased brethren, as well
as by non-Masons. Eighteen articles were donated to our museum by the same
source, and these aquisitions likewise take their place alongside a growing collection of Masonic memorabilia. In addition your commission has purchased
38 volumes of Masonic significance from our modest budget allotment.
In-so-far as use of facilities is concerned, we are pleased to report that
during the year 160 books were loaned through our mailing service or to members who visited our library to do research or to borrow volumes. Our register
indicates that 1,206 visitors acquainted themselves with our facilities, and it is
safe to say that many times that number were made aware of our existence
as a result of having been in the building or as a result of some other attraction.
During the year we were able to install 2 additional sets of book shelves
to relieve some pressure on our crowded shelves, and make more orderly use
of our ever decreasing wall space. Your library and museum are quite literally
coming to the point in time when we will in fact be "Bursting our seams". In
this regard, and in response to a recommendation of Grand Master Chester R.
MacPhee in his message in 1970, and further in response to the action of
Grand Lodge as recorded on page 54 of the 1970 Proceedings, the Chairman
of your commission has worked closely with the Trustees of the Masonic
Memorial Temple, as well as joined them in their meetings when matters
concerning the possible future development of our library and museum were
discussed and acted upon. The Trustees of our Temple will make an adequate
report of this phase of our joint efforts in their report, therefore we will not

REPORT OF THE SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
YOUTH ACTIVITIES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & A. M. of California:

The members of the Youth Activities Committee would like to begin this
report by expressing our gratitude to the Most Worshipful Herbert A. Huebner, Grand Master of Masons in California and Hawaii, for his appointments
of the members to this committee. These appointments have given each of
us a first hand opportunity to continue our work and association with future
Masons and leaders of the country.
We wish also to extend our thank yous to Worshipful Brothers John L.
Wixson and Melvin A. Pixley, Executive Officers of the Northern and Southern Jurisdictions of California of the International Order of DeMolay, to
Miss Barbara Campbell, Supreme Deputy of the International Order of
Rainbow for Girls in California, and to Mrs. Dorothy Halstead, Grand
Guardian of the International Order of Job's Daughters in California and to
their assistants for the cooperation and courtesy extended to the members of
this Committee during this past year.
We also extend our thank yous to the Fresno Masonic Temple Association; The Sunset Mizpah Masonic Temple in Los Angeles, and the Safeway Stores Facility in Oakland for providing meeting places during the
year at no expense to this Grand Lodge.
MEETINGS

Your Youth Activities Committee held four (4) meetings during the
past year. Some of the items under discussion were a continuance of last years
committee efforts and some items will obviously be recommended for continued action by next year's Youth Activities committee.
As an expedient and an economy measure, the committee was divided
into two sub-committees, one for the northern half of the state under Vice
Chairman Robert J. Matheison and one for the southern half under Vice
Chairman Arnold G. Brocksen, Sr. Meetings were held by their respective
sub-committees in their areas culminating in a final joint meeting at Fresno.
It was again decided to present a Youth Activities display in the exhibit
hall for this annual communication. This display is to be prepared by the
Youth Groups of the San Francisco Bay area. All present at this annual
communication are urged to examine this exhibit and view the activities of
the Youth Groups.
In addition to the four Committee Meetings, this Committee was represented at the Grand Assembly of Rainbow for Girls at Fresno on April 4th
through April 7th, with the invitation of Miss Barbara Campbell, Supreme
Deputy. Members of the Committee were also present at the Grand Bethel,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

245

International Order of Job's Daughters in California, in Long Beach on
June 25th and 26th. Members of this Committee were also present at both
the Northern and Southern California Jurisdictional Conventions of DeMolay
held at Redding in November 1970 and Palm Springs in August 1971.
Your Youth Activities Committee extends a hearty thank you to Newcomb Condee, Editor in Chief of the California Free Mason for the publication of the very informative information on Youth Orders. It is hoped
by this Committee that a reprint of those pages be prepared for presentation
to each newly raised Master Mason.
In order to establish a closer relationship between the Master Mason
and the Youth of Job's Daughters, Rainbow Girls and DeMolays, this
Committee recommends to the Masters of the several constituent Lodges
the following: When the Lodge has a Stated Meeting dinner or similar function, that an invitation be extended to the Master Councilor, to the Honored
Queen and to the Worthy Advisor. This Committee suggests that they
be offered a place of honor at the head table and given the proper introduction. Why not ask them to say a few words?
This Committee further recommends that the Master of each Lodge
make space available in his Trestle Board for news of the DeMolay Chapter,

In fact, this Committee now requests your attendance, you the members
of this Grand Lodge, to attend as many of these Youth Meetings as possible.
You are the leaders of Masonry in this Jurisdiction and it is up to you to
set the example. Let all of us make a real effort. Let all of us lead the way
to our Rainbow Assembly meeting, our Job's Daughters Bethel meeting and
DeMolay Chapter meeting. See you there!
The members of this Committee wish to thank those Building or Temple
Associations for heeding our recommendation to adjust the rental rates for
the Youth Groups. However, there is still need for improvement in a few
isolated instances. To you few, please reconsider.

I have been asked by the Grand Master to introduce the report of the
Special Committee on Physical Qualifications chaired by Most Worshipful
Eugene S. Hopp, Past Grand Master.
The Committee has met, discussed the matter at length, and has prepared an excellent report. There are members of this committee who favor
modification of our law respecting the physical qualifications of a candidate
for the degrees of Masonry in this jurisdiction. There are members of the
committee who do not. Actually, the committee was evenly divided (6 to 6)
on the issue.
The result is that this highly important report consists of two reports one by the proponents of change, and the other by those opposed. Both reports are carefully written and very well done.
My purpose in appearing before you to introduce the presentation of the

the reports to the Committee on Policy and General Purpose, which committee will propose a plan of usage of this report which we believe will be of
important and far-reaching benefit for the Lodges of this jurisdiction.

The Chairman then asked each one to speak freely and to give his general
impressions on the subject. During the discussions which followed, the
Chairman expresed his belief that we were charged to study and report on all
physical requirements, including women, eunuchs and those under 21 years
of age.
Such subjects as the C.M.C. secs. 511 and 512 pertaining to the word
"substantially" as well as the possible deviation from the "Ancient Landmarks" were discussed at length.

Several references were made respecting what should be considered "substantial" compliance to the ritual, and also, as to whether the Ancient Laws
should be applicable to the ritual and whether they should be held binding
upon our present procedures as far as physical qualifications are concerned.
The~e was not sufficient time to take into consideration at length, any
!8.lternative methods of our present procedures of conferring the degrees
wh~reby it might be possible for physically-handicapped persons, who might
deSire to apply for the degrees of Masonry, to do so, and if elected, to be
able to have the degrees conferred upon them without embarrassment to themselves or to the Lodge.
Realizing the importance of a study of this phase of the question 1 we have
directed our main efforts to the research of a method which could be practical
and acceptable.
In the letter of the appointment of this committee, the Most Worshipful
Grand Master Herbert A. Huebner requested the c.ommittee to make a
thorough study of the subject and to submit a report, containing its observations, conclusions, and recommendations, and that the report should be full
and fair. This would in our opinion justify a thorough study of all phases of
the subject.
Prior to meeting, various materials were submitted to the Committee for
study. Much information, not generally known to the average Mason, was
contained in the materials distributed. Among this material, there was one
paper called the "Doctrine of the Perfect Youth," printed by the Masonic
Service Association, 700 Tenth Street N.W., Washington 1, D.C. The first
edition was issued December, 193 7 and a revised edition was issued September 22, 1950. This publication contained a summary of the procedures of
handling physically-handicapped candidates of the 49 Grand Jurisdictions in
the United States, including the District of Columbia.
It was noted in this summary that, at that time, there were 42 Grand
Jurisdictions that did accept physically-handicapped persons using various
procedures for accepting them.
Seven of the 49, including California still adhered to the strict rule of the
"Perfect Youth".
Of the 42 that were accepting applicants, 30 of them left the decision to
the discretion of the Lodge, 11 were left up to the Grand Masters, and 2 were
left up to the Master of the Lodge to decide.
It was apparent that there were some irregularities in some of these procedures, from the standpoint of the conferring of the degrees, and there was
some indication that they were straying from the ritual, especially as we
know it in California where we are accustomed to the highest quality ritual
available anywhere, and are desirous of keeping it that way.
There was one plan, however, adopted by the Grand Lodge of Indiana
which appears to have solved the problem and with certain variations we feel
it could be very applicable to our situation here in California.

(A) POSITION - FAVORING CHANGE
A copy of the minutes of the meeting held on the date and place noted
above are hereby attached and made a part of this report.
As indicated in the minutes, most of the alloted time for the meeting was
consumed by disct1$ions, regarding physical qualifications, including women,
eunuchs, and eighteen-year-olds.

252

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

In 1961 - the Grand Lodge of Indiana plWOO legislation to create an
Occasional Lodge to operate Under Dispensation, for the sole purpose of
conferring the degrees of Masonry upon Candidates of other Lodges who were
under physical handicaps, and whereby they were unable to literally conform
to the ritual.
Prior to this time Indiana had been accepting physically-handicapped
candidates and each individual Lodge was conferring the degrees upon them,
thus more or less adapting their own ritual to the case at hand. This was not
proving satisfactory to those who wanted the ritual preserved, so they set out
to find a better way to accomplish the purpose without returning to the "Perfect Youth" theory.
This was accomplished in the establishmen t of an Occasional Lodge Under
Dispensation named Bartimaeus Lodge in reference to blind Bartimaeus
receiving his sight and being made whole as stated in the New Testament.
Ref: St. Mark 10:46 through 10:52.
Although the name Bartimaeus may seem to some to have a significance
to the situation, it is not n~ily so and any applicable name would be
appropriate. Such as, Realization Lodge, Ritualistic Lodge or Occasional
Lodge. For identification purposes we shall use the name Occasional Lodge
Under Dispensation.
Although the mechanics of such a Lodge cannot be fully described in this
report we can consider most of the basic ideas.
The idea was conceived by a group of men who wanted to see the ritual
preserved, yet who wanted to allow the degrees of Masonry to be conferred
upon those who were physically handicapped, and, who were otherwise worthy
and well qualified.
To do this, they suggested the formation of a Lodge that would consist
only of "Blue Ribbon" ritualists, who would meet occasionally solely for the
purpose of conferring the degrees of Masonry upon physically-handicapped
candidates of other Lodges. Those receiving the degrees were not made members of the Occasional Lodge, but were members of the Lodge which they
petitioned.
It must .be remem~ered that this Occasional Lodge was not a Lodge to
accept physically-handicapped persons. Its only function was to confer the
degrees upon physically-handicapped candidates of other Lodges. In other
words it performs a special function, to guarantee that the degrees are conferred upon physically-handicapped candidates in a manner distinguished for
'
its perfection.
Without further details as to the workings of this arrangement which we
consider hig~y commendable, we wish to summarize by offering the following
recommendations.
It is thought by those making this summary that legislation should be
introduced to establish the creation of a Special Lodge in the State of California and Hawaii, for the sole purpose of conferring the degrees of Masonry

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

253

upon candidates of Constituent Lodges who are under physical handicaps
whereby they are unable to conform to the present ritual.
The creation of such a Lodge, would by no means represent a change in
policy with respect to petitioners who are physically handicapped (except as
it shall be later stated). This would allow all present safeguards to be retained for the ritual, and in addition, the Grand Lecturer and his staff would
have the sole control over the manner in which the degrees would be conferred.
Our recommendation would be to establish three such Lodges all of the
same name, and in the same manner, one in the North, one in the South and
one in Hawaii for the convenience of the officers and candidates.
As heretofore mentioned, these Special Lodges would operate under Dispensation, having no charter, not owning property, nor having a vote in Grand
Lodge, and having no other powers except the sole purpose of conferring the
degrees of Masonry upon physically-handicapped candidates of constituent
Lodges in this Jurisdiction, all of which would be under direction of the
Grand Lecturer.
It is recommended that the Grand Lecturer should appoint the officers of
the respective Special Lodges each year and before such officer may be installed he must qualify himself before the Grand Lecturer or his appointee.
The above recommendations would, we feel, qualify for the proper conferring of the degrees and would lend to the control and dignity appropriate
to the occasion.
In order to make this possible we would recommend certain changes in
C.
to M. C. To wit:
1. That the physical qualifications of a person shall be no bar for application if he is otherwise worthy and well qualified. Ever remembering
that the physical sufficiency of the apr>licant shall be left to the sound
discretion of the Lodge, and if elected, the degrees must be conferred
by qualified ritualists.
2. Sec. 511, is proposed to be amended to read:
An applicant for the degrees of Masonry must be a man;
a believer in God and a future existence; of moral conduct; capable
of reading and writing; of supporting himself and family; having no
maim or defect in his mind or body that may render him incapable of
lear:ning the art, and physically able to conform sabstantially to what
the several degrees respectively require of him, provided however that
if an applicant who is unable to comply with the physical requirements
by virtue of a physical disability or disabilites, the application may
be received and voted upon by the Lodge in accordance with Sec. 512
(as proposed for amendment) .
3. Sec. 512 Proposed to amend:
Before an applicant, who has a physical handicap, may apply for the
degrees, it will be necessary for him to appear before a special committee of not less than 5, appointed by the Master of the Lodge to

254

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

which he wishes to make the application. This committee shall consist
of not less than two of the principal officers of the Lodge, and other
members whom the Master may appoint. The committee shall request
that the proposed applicant appear before them at the lodge hall in
a private room suitable for the occasion and with dignity, to view the
extent of the proposed applicant's disability and determine whether or
not the proposed applicant could substantially conform to the ritual.
Upon conclusion of the interview if in the opinion of the committee,
that the proposed applicant could not substantially conform to the
ritual it would be their duty to inform him that he could not qualify
and therefore, to relieve him of the possible embarrassment of being
rejected, would recommend that he not make an application to the
lodge.
If it was the opinion of the committee that the proposed applicant
could substantially qualify, they would advise him that if it was his
decision to proceed with an application that this preliminary investigation would in no way be construed as a guarantee that he would be
elected to receive the degrees.
If the proposed candidate be elected, the degrees must be conferred
upon him according to Sec. 512-1 (to be established)
4. 512-1 To establish:
Conferring of degrees upon physically handicapped applicants.
The Lodge must request the Grand Lodge to have the degrees conferred upon the candidate and get permission thereof. The conferring
of the degrees upon a physically-handicapped candidate shall only be
done by a Specially Dispensated Lodge created by the Grand Lodge
for the specific purpose of conferring the degrees e>f Masonry upon
physically-handicapped candidates without undue deviation from the
ritual, by Brethren trained and proficient in their work, in surroundings and under. ci~cumstances which will contribute to the solemnity,
decorum, and d1gruty of the occasion.
5. 512-2 To be ~tablished:
Change of ritual.
There shall be no deviation or change in the ritual in any respect
except in those instances where the candidate cannot literally conform
to the ritual. At this point, another, who may be qualified may be
directed by the Master to conform as a proxy for the candidate. None
of ~e ritual may be omitted. It must be given in its entirety. The
candidate shall be allowed to wear or use any aid or aids that he
would normally use in the daily pursuit of his livelihood or social
activities, and for the purpose of receiving the degrees such aid will
be considered a part of the person, of which he cann~t be divested.
Therefore, it shall be said where applicable "Except that which is
considered a part of your person" and "Ex~t that which was considered a part of your person."

These are the changes we recommend and we feel this can be done without
violating our Ancient Laws, Regulations, or Landmarks.
In substantiation of this, we would like to make certain references regarding the above, i.e. the Landmarks.
LANDMARK 18. States only, quote, "The qualification of candidates
for initiation," unquote. Note: No reference is made as to physical qualifications, therefore no change is necessary.
LANDMARK 24. States that Masonry is: Quote, "The foundation of
a speculative science upon an operative art, and the symbolic use and explanation of the terms of that art, for the purpose of religious or moral teaching."
Unquote. This is self-explanatory and tends to refute the opinion that symbolism has no place in our ritual. See C.M.C. Sec. 511} for reference to symbolism. We must remember that we will now confer the second or third degree
of Masonry upon a candidate who may have suffered an accident after he has
received his first degree, thus employing symbolism or exemplification to do
so. It seems rather ambiguous that we could do this in one case and not in
another.
LANDMARK 25. Quote, "The last and crowning landmark of all is,
that these landmarks can never be changed." Unquote.

Remarks:
It is our contention that a landmark must have some basis or meaning to
substantiate it so as to be a landmark. No. 25 does not fit this category and
is therefore not a landmark but rather an opinion. Change is change within
itself, which is inevitable, and must be recognized as such. Anything that can
be, or has been, established by man may also be altered by man.
The written laws, together with the landmarks, constitute the foundations
of Masonic law. The landmarks where applicable should not be changed, but
where they no longer exist due to our own change, i.e. from operative Masonry to speculative Masonry, they are then not applicable to the art. And
further that there is nothing in the landmarks that prohibit us from accepting anyone who is physically disqualified. It is only the old rules and regulations, practiced in the early history of operative Masonry, that mention anything of not accepting a perfect youth, or a man who is not of sound body,
or a person that may have a maim in his body. By reviewing all the written
laws and regulations prior to 1721, we find that they are totally inconsistent
with our present way of living and it would be impossible to comply with
them or even find a place for them in todays society. It is mentioned in the
C.M.C. on page 364, under Grand Lodge Powers In General, that the Constitutions and Regulations of 1721 thereto may be altered or amended by a
Grand Lodge; they, however, remain in force until so amended or changed
by positive enactment of the Grand Lodge. We therefore, repeat, that it is
the old written laws and regulations (and which it is stated, can be repealed
or changed) that is causing some of the minds to cling to the belief that a man
must be of sound limb and body to be accepted into speculative Masonry.

GRAND LODGE OP' CALIFORNIA

We also feel that by making a true analysis of this report, which is backed
up with documented evidence to support it and other evidence gained by men
in their travels and the fact that only seven out of the 49 Grand Jurisdictions
in the United States, including California, still adhere to the strict rule of the
perfect youth, that we will find it difficult to bring forth logical evidence that
we should not consider a change in California procedures for the acceptance
of physically-handicapped persons if otherwise qualified.
It is therefore, our strong desire and recommendation that further consideration be given to this matter based upon the information submitted in
this report. Ever remembering that physical sufficiency of the applicant shall
be left to the sound discretion of the Lodge, and that the degrees would be
conferred by "Blue Ribbon" ritualists.

At a meeting of this Committee, a vote was taken as to those favoring a
change ln the physical requirements necessitating a change in ritual; the
results were five in favor and five against. Those favoring a change in the
requirements have determined to present a separate report. This report is
made by the Chairman and those recommending no change in the physical
requirements.
The present regulations governing. physical qualifications in California
are contained in sections 511 and 512 of the California Masonic Code.
Sec. 511. Moral and Physical Qualifications. An applicant for the
degrees of Masonry must be a man; no woman nor eunuch; free born,
being neither a slave nor the son of a bond woman; a believer in God and a
future existence; of moral conduct;; capable of reading and writing;
having no maim or defect in his body that may render him incapable
of learning the art, and physically able to conform substantially to what
the several degrees respectively require of him.
Sec. 512. Sound Discretion Required. The question as to the
physical sufficiency of the applicant shall be left to the sound discretion
of the Lodge. When the applicant is unable to comply literally with the
physical requirements, the Master shall state the nature and extent of
his disabilities to the Lodge before ballot is taken.
There has never been any method of making Masons in this jurisdiction
except by the candidate individually receiving the degrees in strict accordance
with the ritual adopted by ·Grand. Lodge. According to section 554 of the
C.M.C., "each degree conferred •.. in this jurisdiction must be in conformity
with the ritual now taught by the Grand Lecturer and recognized by the
Grand Lodge, and such must be adhered to by all Lodges and Masons in
this jurisdiction".
Obviously, to accommodate disabled or deformed candi~U:S· it ~ould
require a complete change of ritual, indeed many different varieties of ntual,
depending upon the nature and extent of the disability or deformity. There
could be no uniformity of ritual.
Let us review the history of the rule in California.
The matter of physical qualifications was first discussed in this jurisdiction by Grand Master William H. Howard in May, 1855, when he stated
to Grand Lodge that it was not within the province of the Grand Master or
of the Grand Lodge to remove this ancient landmark. This was before Dr.
Albert Mackey formulated his statement of 25 Landmarks.
The position of the Grand Lodge itself was first declared in 1864, when it
adopted the report of its Committee on Jurisprudence, in answer to the
question, "Do the ancient charges require the applicant for the m~steries
of Masonry to be physically perfect, and if not, what degree of dismemberment or deformity shall exclude him?" (Proceedings of 1864, pp. 363-4)
That report, in its own words went for the answer to the "foundation the landmarks and andent charges". After referring to the 18th Landmark
as given by Dr. Mackey, the report quoted the ancient charges approved by

(B) POSITION - AGAINST CHANGE
At the 1970 Annual Communication of Grand Lodge, the Committee on
Policy and General Purposes moved "that this Grand Lodge instruct the
incoming Grand Master to appoint a special commission on Physical Qualifications for the purpose of conducting an in-depth study on the entire matter
of physical requirements for admission to Masonry in this Jurisdiction and
with the instruction to report in detail to this Grand Lodge when its work
is completed, and, if possible, to do so at the 1971 Annual Communication''.
The motion was carried and the Grand Master, Most Worshipful Herbert A.
Huebner, appointed your Committee, stating "I desire this Committee to
make a thorough study, and to submit a report containing its observations,
conclusions and recommendations. It shall be full and fair, so that the Grand
Lodge may intelligently act upon the question".
Your Committee has reviewed a wealth of material, including our own
proceedings, a copy of the Masonic Service Association booklet entitled
"Doctrine of the Perfect Youth", and reviewed many of the physical requirements of other Grand Jurisdictions, including the Grand Lodge of
Minnesota as published in the Proceedings of Educational Lodge No. 1002
of Minneapolis; the report of Indiana by its Grand Secretary; and reports
from the Grand Lodges of Louisiana and North Carolina; and the publication
of the Philalethes Society, which contains reports o( discussions taking place
on the subject of Physical Qualifications at the annual meeting of the Society
in Washington, D. C. February 19, 1971.

the Grand Lodge of England in 172 2: "No Master should take an apprentice
... unless he be a perfect youth, having no maim or defect in his body that
may render him incapable of learning the art. . . ." They concluded that
these, "taken together, form a part of the body of Masonry, in which we
are agreed that no man or body of men can make innovations". (Please note
that in 1722 Masonry was speculative, not operative.)
The question to be determined, the 1864 report stated, is as to the
proper interpretatio n of the language used in the landmark and the charge
quoted. To explain the landmark and charge, they referred to the 5th article
of the Old York Constitutions of 926: "A candidate must be without blemish
and have the full and proper use of his limbs, for a maimed man can do the
Craft no good"; to the Regulations of 1663: "No person shall hereafter be
accepted as a Freemason but such as are of able body; and to the Ancient
Charges at Makings, at about the year 1686: "That he be made able in all
degrees ... and that he have his right limbs as a man ought to have." The
report then stated that "one who has lost any of those members, or any of those
senses which are brought into use and required by the necessities of the work
of the lodge, would have such 'maim or defect in his body as to render him
incapable of learning the art', and he could not be said to 'have his right
limbs as a man ought to have'."
The Committee disagreed with Dr. Mackey's view that absolute perfection was required, but concluded "that it is a violation of Masonic usage
to admit any man who is incapable of complying literally with what is required of him in passing through the ceremonies of each degree."
The Grand Lodge thereupon adopted the express rule that
"The person who desires to be made a Mason must be a man . • .
not deformed or dismembered, but hale and sound in his physical eonformation, having his right limbs as a man ought to have; and be able to
conform literally to what the several degrees respectively require of him".
This rule was reaffirmed in 1872 (1872:556) and at various other times,
whenever the question was raised. (1894:767; 1897:234)
In 1900 the rule as to physical qualifications was again reviewed by the
Committee on Jurisprudence, which explained that in 1864 the Jurisprudence
Committee had endorsed the view that the perfection required by the Ancient
Charges approved in 1722 was simply that the candidate should have no
maim or defect that might render him incaPable of learning the art, and that
if he had no such maim or defect, then he was a "perfect youth" for all the
purposes of Masonry and therefore eligible. They then recommended, and
Grand Lodge adopted, an amendment of the rule to read as follows:
"The person who desires to be made a Mason must be a man . . •
having no maim or defect in his body that may render him incapable
of learntng the art, and physically able to conform literally to what the
several degrees respectively require of him".

The Committee was of the opinion that this did not violate the Ancient
Landmarks. (1900:865,868)
In 1914, the above rule, then contained in section 94 of the Constitution
of Grand Lodge, was modified by substituting the word "sub~tantially~' for
the word "literally" ( 1914: 173); but it was held that substantial compliance
could not be obtained by use of artificial aids (1919:615), and further, that
no dispensation could be issued to avoid the rule. (1922:260)
In 1928, a Special Committee on Physical Qualifications, ~ppointe? to
conduct an in-depth study, reported to the Grand Lodge. This conumttee
proposed that the Lodges themselves should determine whether or not a
candidate could substantially comply, and Grand Lodge then adopted an
amendment to the law by adding the following language:
"And the question as to the physical sufficiency of the candidate shall
be left to the sound discretion of the lodge. Where the candidate is unable
to comply literally with the physical requirements, the Master shall
state the nature and extent of his disabilities to the lodge before the
ballot is taken".
This is the present rule contained in section 512 of the C.M.C.
In 1931, Grand Master John Stewart Ross, author of the Ross Digest
and an eminent authority on Masonic law, decided that the Lodge must
determine whether or not the applicant is physically able to conform substantially q, what the several degrees require of him without the aid of an
artificially substituted hand or leg; that the ritual detem;unes the ~uesti~n;
and that Section 94 of the Constitution must be read ID connection with
the ritual and as a construction thereof; and that the amendment in 1928
in no way changed our law as to physical requirements. He further stated
that the results hoped for by the amendment of 1928 had not been attained
and recommended striking from Section 94 the word "substantiall y" and
also striking the provision leaving it to the discretion of the lodge to determine
whether a candidate could conform to the ritual.
After reports from the Committee on Policy and General Purposes and
majority and minority reports from the Cotnmittee on Juris~rudence, the
Grand Lodge sustained the decision of the Grand Master, but did not amend
the law in any respect. (1931:451,725-731)
The next major attack on the rule was contained in resolutions in 1946.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes, of which P.G.M. William
Rhodes Hervey was the Chairman, reported that from time immemorial the
course of the fraternity has been guided by certain unalterable landmarks,
and among the matters controlled by the landmarks was the matter of
qualification of candidates; that as far back as our written record g~, ~e
qualification of candidates has been a part of our landmarks, and had m its
inception, or in its later history, no connection with the occupation of the
operative Mason.
The report expressly stated that "this Grand I..o<!ge has r~gnized a!ld
is committed to twenty-five landmarks, of which the eighteenth is the qualifi-

cation of candidates for admission'; and that under our Constitution the
power of the Grand Lodge is limited 'by a strict adherence to the Ancient
Landmarks of the Order'· and that among the Ancient Charges and Regulations to which a Master ~ust submit before installation is the following: 'You
admit that it is not in the power of any man or body of men to make innovations in the body of Masonry'. The landmarks being unrepealable must

Subsequent resolutions having for their purpose the modification of the
rule on physical qualifications have been voted down. In 1962, Grand Master
Guy B. Mize, on recommendation of the Committee on Jurisprudence,. concurred in by the Committees on Policy and General Purposes and on Ritual,
declared a resolution purporting to rescind the physical requirements to be
contrary to the landmarks of Masonry and declared it rejected. (1962:263)
In 1963 ( 1963 :pp.298-300), the Committee on Policy and General Purposes summarized in its report the reasons for rejection of physical qualification changes which had been presented virtually every year for more than a
decade. It is worth reproducing here:
"Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes ... (has considered
the proposals to eliminate the requi~ements of physical qualification) .•.
without emotion and only from the standpoint of what, in our opinion, would
be good for Masonry.
"Masonry selects its candidate5 and admits them only after careful
investigation and a unanimous ballot. No one has a right to become a Mason.
It is a privilege granted to a comparatively small number.
"To begin with, we exclude half of the human race. No woman can
become a Mason. (It might be noted parenthetically that a 14,000 member
men's club in California, formed solely for the purpose of "getting the facts",
having been threatened with suit for failure to admit women, while receiving
a tax-exempt status, has now permitted women to become members). Half
of the remainder of the population is likewise excluded, namely any one under
the required age of 21 years. (Again we insert the question of this age
restriction against the background of the recently granted vote to 18-yearolds.)
"In California, for more than one hundred years, we have adhered to
the regulation that no one having a maim or defect in his body that may
render him incapable of learning the art and physically unable to conform
to what the several degrees respectively require of him, can become a Mason.
"The physical requirements of qualification of candidates for the degrees
of Masonry are probably as old as Masonry itself. They are a survival of
Operative Masonry and are peculiar to the Masonic institution, just as are
the regulations excluding women and minors. One of the Ancient Landmarks

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

261

stated by Dr. Mackey, and which for several decades has been printed in
the Ross Digest and our Masonic Code, is the 'qualification of candidates for
initiation' as the 18th Landmark.
"A natural sympathy for those unfortunate men who have suffered severe
physical injuries has caused numerous proposals to change the old requirements, and these have been presented throughout the history of our Grand
Lodge. They have been rejected except for the compromise which resulted
in the adoption of our present regulations many years ago, now contained
in sections 511 and 512 of the C.M.C.: 'having no maim or defect in his
body that may render him incapable of learning the art, and physically able
to conform substantially to what the several degrees respectively require of
him'. The question as to physical sufficiency of the applicant is left to the
sound discretion of the Lodge, and it is determined by the ritual.
"Since the rule as to physical qualification has existed for so long that it
is at least regarded as one of the Ancient Landmarks, it should not be changed
without some change in the condition of the Craft which would compel it.
We may properly inquire what change has occurred in the condition of the
Craft which would now require a change in our ancient regulation. We
know of none. Masonry does not go out and seek candidates; we select
those who apply, and they must apply of their own free will and accord.
"If these proposals were adopted, it would require a different ritual for
each case of physical defect, depending upon the nature and severity of the
particular deformity. This would completely destroy any uniformity in the
ritual. Under our law, the conferring of a degree must be in conformity with
the established ritual taught by the Grand Lecturer, and the conferring of
a degree in a merely symbolic manner is out of the question ... Unless we
are prepared to do away with uniformity of the ritual, carefully built up for
a century .•. we cannot change the rule as to physical qualifications . . .
"The most appalling thing about the elimination of the physical requirements would be that it would subject a man who may have suffered a
repulsive physical injury to the required unanimous ballot, with the great
probability that some one or more of the members would reject him. The
resulting damage to an already damaged personality would be both incalculable and irreparable. It would be far kinder to reject such candidates on a
purely legal ground, which they can understand.
"In our opinion, this Grand Lodge has already gone as far in meeting
physical insufficiency as it can reasonably go, making it depend upon the
applicant's ability to conform substantially to what the ritual may require
of him.
"The argument will be made that the requirement of physical sufficiency
is not one of the Ancient Landmarks, because it has not been expressly
adopted by this Grand Lodge. The same may be said for all the other
Landmarks, including belief in God and a future existence, and the Holy
Bible as an indispensable part of the furniture of a Lodge. If a landmark
exists, it needs no adoption, because it has existed from time immemorial and

will continue to exist, and Section 16 of our Constitution states that the
powers of the Grand Lodge are limited by a strict adherence to the Ancient
Landmarks of the Order.
"We recommend that the resolution be not adopted ..•"
The Committee on Jurisprudence presented an even stronger report concerning the Ancient Landmarks and the limitation on the power of Grand
Lodge to alter them. (1963:300-302)
Setting aside, for a moment, the discussion of Ancient Landmarks and
uniformity of ritual, the question remains: Are physical requirements essential to Freemasonry? To answer that question requires some thought as
to what is Freemasonry. Why and how did it become spectrlative or philosophical from an operative origin, and what has enabled it to survive? Bear
in mind that the Craft has been wholly speculative for more than 250 years.
The ethical philosophy of Freemasonry has been the same as the ethical
teachings of small groups in every civilization, but with this difference - in
Freemasonry it is imparted in a matchless symbolism whith is available to
each and every one of us, which teaches more and more as we reflect upon
it more and more.
We have been advised by 6ne Masonic historians that the transition
from operative to speculative Freemasonry took place for social and economic
reasons. Your Chairman disagrees. In the summer of 1970 he had the
privilege of spending two months at Oxford University, lecturlng and doing
some work in 17th Century English history. With the assistance of material
from the Bodleian Library, one of the finest in the world, and manuscripts
from some of the College libraries, and many visits to the Ashmolean Museum,
the Chairman became convinced that the earliest speculatives were attracted
to Masonry out of curiosity. On the 16th of October, 1646, Elias Ashmole,
antiquarian, was received into a Masonic lodge at Warrington Lancashire
tog~ther with ~ Roundhead friend and cousin, Henry Manwaring of
Carmcham, Chesire, and several others. Ashmole's motives for joining were
undoubtedly similar to those of the antiquary Stukeley (1687-1765) who
states in his autobiography that in 1720 "his curiosity led him to be
initiated into the mysterys of Masonry, suspecting it to be the remains of the
mystery of the ancients". Research has shown that neither Ashmole Manwaring, or any of the seven other Freemasons whose names are give:i were
in any way connected with operative Freemasonry.
'
We cannot help but believe that their most important reason for seeking
admission was the very manner in which the great lessons were taught. What
magnificient symbolism imparts the spirit of brotherhood in a certain handclasp. What better way to present the means of achieving and the importance
of peace and harmony in a Lodge, than to have the candidate so prepared
that these lessons are indelibly inscribed on his mind. At the same time he
learns a magnificient lesson in charity. There are a great many other l~ns
imparted in symbolism, the duty of man to man, man to neighbor, man to

God, to family and so on and on. None of these lessons can be taught as

they are described in the ritual without physical qualifications. We have a
practical, realistic means of imparting the greatest of lessons, but to ~press
them upon the mind requires some physical application and necessitates
certain physical qualifications that these lessons may be imparted in an
unforgettable manner.
According to no less authorities than Albert Pike and Dr. Albert Mackey,
Freemasonry is the spiritual successor of the Ancient Mysteries and was
designed to teach and perpetuate the same great moral and spiritual teachings.
No man could receive the Greater Mysteries unless he himself went through
and participated in all the ceremonies of initiation, which required physical
ability and stamina to undergo the pains and perils of those ceremonies.
And, Pike said, "Masonry, successor to the Mysteries, still follows the anc;ienedt
manner of teaching". "Thus, through the succession of ages, are tranSJDltt
unimpaired the most excellent tenets of our Institution". The. manner of
teaching is equally important as the teachings themselves, and is therefore
essential to Freemasonry, which was the very reason for establishment
of the Ancient Landmark.
The members of this Committee who favor a change in physical qualifications contend that such change can be made without violating the Ancient
Landmarks, and that the 18th Landmark does not apply to physical qualifications.
As we have shown from the history of the subject in this jurisdiction, our
Grand Lodge has declared from its very inception that the physic~ qualifi~­
tion of candidates is one of the landmarks. In the report adopted m 1946, it
was declared that this Grand Lodge is committed to the twenty-five Landmarks, and that the requirement of physical qualification is one of them, and
that under our Constitution the power of Grand Lodge itself is limited by a
strict adherence to the Ancient Landmarks, and that these Landmarks are
unrepealable. The claim that we violate the rule by conferring degrees upon
one who is injured after the first degree has no merit. The Landmark applies
only to "candidates for initiation". After initiation, the candidate is a
Mason and is no longer a candidate for initiation.
The suggestion that initiation of disqualified candidates in special lodges
would prevent destruction of uniformity of our ritual is also specious..The
very establishment of such lodges, to manufacture and perform a . ntual
appropriate to the physical deformity of each candidate, would be evidence
of lack of uniformity. It would also deprive the electing lodge of its right
to confer degrees on its own candidate.
We recommend that the question to be put to Grand Lodge should be
simply this: "Do you desire change in the present r~lations conc~rning
physical requirements of candidates which would necessitate change ID the
ritual, or do you oppose such change?

264

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

It must be remembered that a five-sixths' vote would be required, since
it would be a change in our Constitution and Ordinances. It must also be
borne in mind that this Grand Lodge has repeatedly declared the existing
rule to be one of the Ancient Landmarks to which this Grand Lodge is committed, and that to make a change in our regulations would be to change
that landmark and to alter the provision that the power of Grand Lodge is
limited by a strict adherence to the Ancient Landmarks. If landmarks at all,
they are by the very definition, unrepealable.

Respectfully submitted,
EUGENE S. HoPP, Chairman

REPORT OF INVESTMENT COMMITTEE
FOR FISCAL YEAR ENDING JUNE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

30, 1971

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:

The year ended June 30, 1971 was a good one from the standpoint of
securities under the control of the Investment Committee. Total investible
funds increased from $28,947,850 at June 30, 1970 to $37,446,790 at
year-end. The increase of $8,498,940 is accounted for by contributions and
other funds received of $2,392,481, plus realized and unrealized gains in
the portfolio totaling $6,106,459.
There are three major categories (or groups) of securities available for
investment. These are set forth in the Masonic Code and may be summarized
as follows:
( 1) Group I - Consists of cash, savings accounts, obligations of the
United States, obligations of the State of California and its political subdivisions, and such other securities as are legal for savings banks in California and Hawaii. In general, Group I may be said to consist of the highest
grade and most conservative securities. At least 20% of the funds available for investment must be maintained in such securities.
( 2) Group II - Consists generally of bonds, debentures, and other
evidences of indebtedness which do not meet the qualifications of Group I.
It also consists of preferred stocks which are listed on a National Securities
Exchange and the preferred stocks of corporations whose common stocks are
eligible for investment in Group III.

(3) Group III-Consists of common stocks, which must be fully listed and
registered on a national exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange
Commission, bank and insurance company stocks, shares of investment trusts,
and savings accounts with savings and loan associations. Total investm~nts in
Group III securities are generally limited to 60% of the total portfolio.
There follows a recapitulation of the consolidated portfolio as of June
30, 1971, at market values, compared with the portfolio as of a year earlier:
