corporate issues, which has increased the yield from this portion of our
portfolio. Increased attention has been given to convertible securities, both
debentures and preferred stocks - our total investment in these classes has
nearly doubled over a year ago. We believe that convertible securities
offer a unique opportunity to combine a satisfactory yield with a possible
appreciation in market value. In the area of equities, our total investment

income was $1,751,122, as compared with $1,555,890 a year earlier. This
increase has been particularly important in providing the major financial
support for our two Masonic Homes.
It has been the policy of this Committee to consider the safety and
preservation of capital as its primary goal. Nevertheless, recognition has
been given to the necessity for increasing income and at the same time
judiciously providing a measure of protection against the erosive effects of
inflation.

Corporation. Such recommendations are subject to the analysis and study
of the Committee prior to any action relating to purchase or sale of securities.

The Board of Control has carefully studied both Resolutions 32 and 33
and hereby submits our report on them simultaneously.
During the past two years this Board of Control has studied the problems
of the Boards of Relief.
T?ey are many, varied and further complicated by the wide divergence
of op1ruon of the persons connected with them.
Last year a special committee appointed by the Grand Master recommended that the Boards of Relief be discontinued as a June 30, 1970.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes however believed
~t some of the function of the Boards of Relief, pa:ticularly ilie operation of blood banks, to be vital to Masonry. Even though by the strict letter
of the law they were not legally the responsibility of the Boards of Relief
~should be.continued until an alternate method could be found for handl~
mg these functions.
In this, ~he Board of Control concurred although in our report we stated
that w~ ?elieved that the Boards of Relief, in the concept in which they
were ongmally formed had outlived their usefulness.
We believe that our Board has delved further into the problems of the

Boards of Relief system than any other board or committee and yet we have
no ready solution to the problem.
We are aware of an intense campaign by individuals who reportedly are
in favor of not only retaining the Boards of Relief but of expanding their
duties. We believe these people have a right to be heard. How much weight is
to be given this small but vociferous minority is for Grand Lodge to decide.

However, numerous persons have expressed opinions to us regarding our
statement that the Boards of Relief have outlived their usefulness. Some have
agreed. A few have recommended not only the continuance, but the expansion of their duties.
We have been impressed by one significant fact - not one Mason has
expressed to us this latter opinion who was not on the payroll of the Boards
of Relief system or in a position to be strongly influenced by it!
We believe that the Brothers who presented Resolutions 32 and 33 are
sincere in trying to solve the deep set and long standing problems of the
Boards of Relief. However, the problems are too complex to be solved by
either or a combination of these. At least another year of intense study will
be required before a practical approach to legislation can be made correcting
this problem.
This study should include, but not be limited to, a tabulated questionnaire, worded so as to elicit basic information, circulated to every active
Mason in the Jurisdiction. It should also give heavy weight to a searching
Qttestionnaire to the entire Inspectoral Corps who are probably closer to
individual problems of the Craft than any other single group, as well as being
the best informed.
In order that this Grand Lodge may have the opportunity to study
this problem in depth, your Board of Control recommends a "No" vote on
both Resolutions 32 and 33.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

Resolution No. 32 delineates the proper duties and responsibilities of
Boards of Relief based upon the careful and thorough study of the Special
Chmmittee on Boards of Relief.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes the proposal of
the Special Study Committee retains all the vital and timetested services of
Boards of Relief and provides a very satisfactory arrangement for their
9rganization and governance. We believe the present day functions assigned
to the Boards of Relief require they be more correctly designated as Masonic
Service Bureaus.
I therefore move the adoption of Resolution No. 32 with the proviso
that where the words "Board of Relief" appear there be substituted
"Masonic Service Bureau" and that all necessary changes be made in our
law to accomplish the change of name. The Committee on Policy and General
Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote on the revised resolution.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON CODE REVISION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Code Commission has the responsibility of preparing corrections,
deletions and additions to the yearly Pocket Supplement of the California
Masonic Code.
This work reflects the work done by Grand Lodge during the Annual
Communication including the passage of Resolutions which affect the California Masonic Code.
After the 1970 Communication the necessary Code section changes and
indexing were incorporated and submitted to the printer in record time, and
printed and disseminated.as promptly as possible.
The work of the Special Committee on Code Revision during 1970-1971
has been somewhat curtailed over previous years. This has primarily been
occasioned because during this year your Committee has completed a full
draft of the proposed amended Code but with the necessity of review by
certain designated Grand Lodge Officers and Committees, complete accord
has been slow in materializing. Additionally, the Committee suffered the loss
of Bill Davis, Past Grand Lecturer and consultant on the Committee who had
been extremely active in working with your Committee in the preparation of
the new Code.
It is anticipated that shortly after this Annual Communication the necessary Committees and the members of this Committee can meet to finally
prepare the draft for submission to the printer.
Your Code Commission requests a budget of $500.00 and the Special
Committee on Code Revision requests a budget of $2,250.00 for the coming
years.
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF COMM ITTEE ON RITUAL
CEREMONY FOR REMOVAL OF CORNERSTONE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Grand Master MacPhee's recommendation to prepare a ceremony for
removal of cornerstone (Recommendation No. 4).
Recommendation No. 4 made by Grand Master MacPhee at the Annual
Communication of 19 70 required that the Ritual Committee give consideration
to preparing a public ceremony for opening the copper containers removed
from cornerstones of buildings where the cornerstone was previously laid by
the Grand Lodge, and for replacing of such cornerstones by a plaque wherever
possible.
Your Ritual Committee has given careful consideration to this recommendation and herewith begs leave to report as follows:
A detailed study of this recommendation has disclosed the following
facts:
1. The incidence of simply removing the contents of a cornerstone container are so rare as to obviate the necessity for a ceremony strictly
for that purpose.
2. Should the Grand Master at this Annual Communication appoint a
Committee to adapt our present Cornerstone ceremony to the situation
of placing a plaque on a completed building, this ceremony would
then lend itself very readily to placing plaques on Public Buildings.
3. As to the actual removal of Cornerstones, Grand Master MacPhee
did correctly assess the situation: more and more frequently, Masonic
Temples, Public School Buildings and other Public Buildings are
being torn down or replaced with new construction, thereby making
necessary the romoval of the cornerstone of these buildings.
Item three above carries the import of this study: because of the increased
incidence of cornerstone removal, we conclude that a need does exist for
an additional Grand Lodge Ceremony.
Accordingly we have authored a new ceremony for the purpose of removing
the Cornerstone of Lodge Halls or other Public Buildings.
Even though the ceremony is in its finished form it has not as yet been
performed. We therefore move that this cornerstone removal ceremony be
adopted in principal, with the provision that after it has been performed
a sufficient number of times to as.sure that all modifications and corrections
have been made, that it then be printed and made available as an official
Ceremony of this Grand Lodge.
Respectfully submitted,
H. DOUGLAS LEMONS, Chairman

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO PREPARE
GRAND LODGE HISTO RY PUBLICATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
At the last Grand Lodge Communication in 1970, Grand Master Chester
R. MacPhee recommended and Grand Lodge approved the preparation of "a
concise history of our Grand Lodge to be available in a small booklet for
~hers visitors and other interested persons".
Her~rt A. Huebner Grand Master of Masons in 1971, acted upon that
recommendation and the pamphlet, "A Perfect Ashlar in the Making", is
the result.
The Grand Master appointed a Special Committee to Prepare a Grand
Lodge History Publication in February 1971, and the committee held its
first meeting in March.
On August 11, 1971, the final draft of the history was placed in the hands
of the Grand Master.
The committee of three accomplished a monumental task in the space
of less than five months - pressing the history of the Grand Lodge, covering
a period of more than 120 years, into a concise history in pamphlet form.
The chairman is very grateful to Brother Max L. Heyman, Jr. ~811) for
serving as editor and to Brother Edwin N. Stansel (421) who contnb~t~ so
much to the committee's task. We also are grateful to Brother Philip L.
Goldstein (42) and Raymond A. Jackson (2), who acted as consultants on
this project, and to the Grand Master, the Grand Secretary, Edward H.
Siems PGM DeWald Baum, Grand Marshal, and Brother Henry D.
Olip~t (360). Past Grand Master and committee chairmen were most
helpful to the committee.
We hope that the Grand Lodge and members of the Craft in our jurisdiction will find "A Perfect Ashlar in the Making" lives up to words of our
Grand Master, "a little giant of a volume worthy of your attention".
Respectfully submitted,
CHARLES C. HusHAW , Chairman

HAWAII

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes :
No action should be taken at this time in view of possible impending
establishment of a Grand Lodge of Hawaii.
The Cr>mmittee on Ritual:
Pursuant to the recommendation that the Ritual Committee study the
advisability of appointing an Assistant Grand Lecturer in Hawaii, such a
study has been made and we wish to report as follows:

276

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

We are completely sympathetic to Grand Master MacPhee's wish that
more adequate contact be maintained with the Hawaiian Lodges, and that
those Lodges be provided with more adequate representation in the California
Grand Lodge.
We do not feel that the appointment of another Assistant Grand Lecturer
is the proper method to apply, and our reasons for arriving at this conclusion
are as follows:
The great distance which separates the mainland from Hawaii would
make extremely difficult the transportation of the Hawaiian Assistant Grand
Lecturer to and from Ritual Committee meetings which are held in various
parts of California.
The relatively small number of Brethren who would directly benefit from
this appointment (Hawaii has only three Districts and Ten Lodges) does not
justify such a change being made.
The cost of maintaining an Assistant Grand Lecturer in Hawaii would
be prohibitive: an estimate of this cost runs to approximately $10,000.00 per
year, almost one quarter of the present total budget for the Committee on
Ritual. This, based on six division conferences in California, two Ritual Committee meetings in California, attendance at Grand Lodge Annual Communications for the additional Assistant Grand Lecturer, as well as possible ceremonial attendance on the mainland; cost of transporting the entire Committee
on Ritual and the Elective Line Officers to Hawaii for a division conference;
normal yearly expense of an additional Assistant Grand Lecturer, plus cost
of regalia, etc. etc.
The purpose which Brother MacPhee hopes to accomplish with this
recommendation can be achieved by requiring the Assistant Grand Lecturer
of Division Three pay multiple annual visits to Hawaii for the purpose of
instruction in the Ritual and better representation. The cost of this would
be relatively small in that travel for only one person is involved.
Based upon the foregoing, your Committee on Ritual feels that the
advantages of such an appointment are far outweighed by the disadvantages.
We recommend a "NO" vote on Recommendation No. 1.
Not adopted.

mendations contained therein, were reviewed carefully by this committee.
We specifically mention these reports and recommendations as they appear
to have created groundless rumors and baseless speculations throughout segments of this Grand Lodge. Your committee met with a representative of
the public accounting firm and was assured that their memorandum reports
were of a routine nature and followed a policy of submitting recommendations
to all clients after each examination or audit.
Paragraph No. 7

Subsequently, the public accounting firm advised the Grand Master by
letter (Exhibit A) of the conference with this committee and emphasized
that their recommendations were not designed to be critical of the officers
and employees of the various Masonic entities. On March 10, 1970, Grand
Master MacPhee issued a comprehensive twenty-one page commentary,
accompanied by several exhibits, designed to lay unsupported rumors to
rest, his report going to those brethren engaged in the management of the
several Grand Lodge entities mentioned in the so-called memorandum reports
prepared by the public auditors.
Paragraph No. 8

This report is divided into four sections: organization, accounting, internal
control and mechanization.
ORGANIZATION

Paragraph No. 9

The organizational structure of Grand Lodge is complex. It is comprised of the Grand Lodge governed by the officers elected by the Grand
Lodge. The Grand Master in turn appoints trustees to govern the Masonic
Homes, the California Masonic Memorial Temple and the California Masonic Foundation, which become semi-autonomous bodies. The Grand Master
also appoints members of various boards and committees such as the Masonic
Homes Endowment Board, which adds to the complexity of the organization.
Paragraph No. 10

There is no question but that the Grand Master, acting for the Grand
Lodge, as prescribed by the California Masonic Code, determines the general
policy of the entire organization. The trustees of the several constitutional
boards in turn determine the operating policies of their several entities. For
example, the implementation of operating policies of the Memorial Temple
is carried out by its manager who is appointed by the trustees of the Memorial
Temple. Likewise, the operating policies of the Masonic Homes at Decoto
and Covina are carried out by superintendents appointed by the trustees of
the Masonic Homes.
Paragraph No. 11

It also appears clear that it is the intention of Grand Lodge that the
administration of these policies is to be carried out through designated
officers of the Grand Lodge. It was not by accident that the Code provides

281

that the Grand Secretary and the Grand Treasurer also act as the Secretary
and as the Treasurer of constitutional boards.

Your committee recommends that all clerical-administrative personnel
in the Grand Lodge offices be considered to be employees of the Grand Lodge
and under supervision of the Grand Secretary. Their duties should be defined
by the Grand Secretary and all of said personnel should perform such work
as is administratively necessary for each of the entities of Grand Lodge.
The cost of all clerical-administrative personnel would then be under
review of the Grand Lodge Finance Committee. The entities other than Grand
Lodge would reimburse Grand Lodge pro rata for administrative costs as
determined by the Grand Secretary and approved by the Finance Committee
in consultation with the Grand Secretary and the entities involved.
An amendment was offered by a member of the Policy
and General Purposes Committee making the two Homes
Investigators and a private secretary for the Grand
Master exceptions to the recommendation that all clerical
and administrative personnel in the Grand Lodge offices
be considered to be employees of the Grand Lodge and
under the supervision of the Grand Secretary.

subject to administration of the Grand Secretary as

ACCOUNTING

Paragraph No. 17

Directly or indirectly most of the functions of the Grand Lodge office
are involved with accounting. They include maintaining records of nearly
a quarter of a million members, custodianship of over fifty million dollars
of assets, and annual receipts of approximately two and a half million dollars.
Four separate corporations are involved and five general ledgers are required.
Ten employees are engaged in the accounting and membership records six
secretaries are employed, three employees work in the supply room: all
administered through the office of the Grand Secretary. It is truly a large and
complex operation.
Paragraph No. 18

Your committee has reviewed the operations and the functions of the
various employees. We are satisfied that the work is performed economically

Paragraph No. 19

The end result of most accounting work is in reports. We have reviewed
the various statements prepared in the Grand Lodge office and believe most
of them are desirable and necessary. It is recognized that there is danger of
the officers and trustees, or other officials, of Grand Lodge and its entities
making ever increasing requests for reports and statements. It is also well
recognized that, once established, reports and statements are seldom discontinued and tend to proliferate.
Paragraph No. 20

Your committee did not believe that it was essential for it to attempt
to evaluate the present reports and statements. We do recommend that
the necessity of each report be examined by the officers or trustees of the
or~a:nzation that requires it and that outdated or unnecessary reports be
ebnunated. We would suggest also that the frequency of reports be considered
and that semi-annual or quarterly reports, rather than monthly reports be
employed wherever possible.
'
An amendment relating to paragraphs 19 and 20 that
"responsibility rests with the entity involved" was
adopted by Grand Lodge.
Paragraphs as amended adopted 5/6 vote.
Paragraph No. 21

Accounting is performed on a cash basis modified only slightly by recognition of some prepaid items. Under this method of accounting, revenues and
expenses generally are recorded at the time of receipt or payment of cash.
Paragraph No. 22

From time to time recommendations have been made that an accrual
method of accounting be adopted. It has been claimed that satisfactory
measurement of operating results can be achieved only in this manner.
Such a system would require that income be recorded when earned and
that expenses be recorded when incurred. This would, for example, require
recordings of dividend income when declared instead of when received. It
would require amortization and accumulation of bond premium and discount.
Paragraph No. 23

Your committee has considered carefully these suggestions. We point out
that Grand Lodge and its entities are not a business in a normal sense. In
addition, your committee is aware that most non-profit organizations in the
nature of fraternal groups find cash basis accounting adequate and that it is
not considered to be an improper method for such organizations.

284

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Paragraph No. 24

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

285

Par&ifllph No. 29

The principal interest in accounting data for a non-profit organization,
such as ours, is in the flow of cash which is well provided for by our present
method. Accrual accounting necessarily would lead to estimates which may
provide less accuracy and information than the present method. Financial
statements that show income that is not immediately available for use, or
expenses that have not been paid could make unduly difficult the understanding of the financial statements. Your committee has considered the
increased costs of clerical work that accrual accounting would require and
cannot justify the cost.

A recommendation was made that responsibility accounting be adopted.
This involves control of costs by identifying the costs with the person or
department responsible for the incurring of the cost. It is usually considered
as the relationship between the budget and the accounting systems. Your
committee consid.ered the suggestion and believes that adequate responsibility
accounting already exists in the Grand Lodge and the Masonic Homes
through the use of budgets and comparisons of actual with budgeted expenses
by those charged with administrative responsibility.

Paragraph No. 25

Paragraph No. 30

Some recommendations for accrual accounting have been made on the
basis that it would demonstrate a more accurate financial statement for the
Masonic Homes, for example, by considering depreciation, future care commitments and other items primarily of interest to governmental agencies.
Your committee believes that if such information becomes essential, adequate
supplemental reports may be prepared without changing the basic present
methods.
Paragraph No. 26
.. We r~ommend that the accounting method of Grand Lodge and its en-

tities continue to be the present cash basis modified only by certain pre-paid
expenses.
By separate action of Grand Lodge this specific paragraph was adopted by 5/6 vote.
Paragraph No. 27

From time to time recommendations are made and occasionally adopted
that depreciation expense be charged on long term assets and that allowances
for depreciation be shown in the balance sheets. This is desirable in commercial ~terprises but i~ generally understood to t>e meaningless in non-profit
orgamzation accounting. Such a practice would only make sense if funds
were. set aside to an amount equivalent to the depreciation provided. The
~unding of re~rves for depreciation is unnecessary and undesirable and injects
m the financial statements an expense that does not involve the flow of
cash. It should be pointed out that any replacement of depreciable assets
would come from contributions and from reserves derived from other sources.

An employee was recently hired and assigned the responsibility of
maintaining securities investment records and determining the proper receipt
of dividends and other income. We believe that this is a necessary position
required to watch over the records of almost thirty-three million dollars in
securities and we further believe that an adequate substitute job cannot be
done by the custodian bank or the public auditors.
Paragraph No. 31

Prior to 1965, detailed property records were not maintained in the
accounting records though details of acquisitions and retirements since 1965
are being kept. Your committee believes that such records are desirable as a
control over some thirteen million dollars of property. Such records are
particularly desirable to determine insurable values and to support fire and
other losses.
Paragraph No. 32

We recommend that the Grand Lodge obtain a current re-appraisal of
land, buildings, furniture and equipment of Grand Lodge and its entities, and
that, using the appraisal as a base, detailed records be maintained of such
property including acquisitions and retirements.
An amendment relating to paragraphs 31 and 32 that
"in view of the proposed redevelopment at Union City
and the redevelopment being concluded at Covina the
Masonic Homes Incorporation should be excluded" was
not adopted by Grand Lodge.
Thereafter by action of Grand Lodge the recommendation in paragraph 32
was not adopted.

Paragraph No. 28

Your committee recommends that depreciation not be charged on the
books of any of the entities of Grand Lodge.
By separate action of Grand Lodge this specific paragraph was not adopted. Thus the choice of action on this
matter is left to the "entities involved".

Paragraph No. 33

A recommendation was made concerning allocating of income directly
to expenses in some instances and the allocating of expenses from one unit
to another. We believe that expenses should not be reduced by the netting
of amounts thereby obscuring the actual total expenses; total expenses
should be available whether reported in detail or not.

Paragraph No. 35

In our study of Grand Lodge and its entities, we observed that the
Grand Lodge Committee on Taxation has concerned itself primarily in the

Paragraph No. 36
Y~u: committee recognizes that those charged with operating policies
of entities of the Grand Lodge are, perhaps, more familiar than others with
problems affecting their operations and the need for adequate accounting
and other records to enable them to function to the best degree. However,
when changes are contemplated the effect on and any balance or imbalance
with the general Grand Lodge accounting system must be considered.

Paragraph No. 37

In concluding this section of the report dealing with accounting, your
committee strongly endorses the implication in our law that the Grand
Secretary, as the chief administrative officer, is, and should be, responsible
for the accounting of Grand Lodge and all of its entities. We believe further
that centralized accounting is a necessity for comparable information and
particularly for economy. Additionally, we believe that uniformity of accounting methods between all entities is all important and must be maintained.
INTERNAL CONTROL

Paragraph No. 38

In an organization the size of Grand Lodge and its entities, with the
substantial assets it owns, sound internal control is essential. Internal control
involves the methods and procedures adopted to safeguard the assets, produce
accurate accounting data, contribute to efficient operation, and encourage
adherence to managerial policies.

Paragraph No. 40

Your committee finds that the administration is alert to the important
principles of internal control that responsibility for a sequence of related
transactions should be divided among different persons. We believe that
a practical and realistic observance of internal control exists in the three
main systems and your committee observed a constant review with change
and improvement taking place as circumstances have changed.
Paragraph No. 41

Your committee made a careful review of our Code which sets forth
responsibilities for the custody of funds and securities. We find that in most
respects an excellent system of internal control is already provided. The
code provides:
( 1) It shall be the duty of the Grand Secretary to collect all
moneys due the Grand Lodge, keep a correct account thereof
in proper banks, and pay the said money, within ten days
after its receipt to the Grand Treasurer.
( 2) It shall be the duty of the Grand Secretary to establish in
some bank an operating fund in such amount as the Grand
Master may approve, from which he shall pay such bills,
claims and demands upon the Grand Lodge.
( 3) It shall be the duty of the Grand Secretary to draw warrants
upon the Grand Treasurer for all appropriations by the Grand
Lodge, for all orders of the Grand Master to meet cases of emergency that may arise in a recess of the Grand Lodge, and for
reimbursement of the operating fund for such amounts as have
been disbursed in payment of bills, claims and demands upon
the Grand Lodge, but in the presentations of claims for reimbursement of personal expenses, approval of such claims must be
given by the Audit Committee prior to payment thereof.
(4) It shall be the duty of the Grand Treasurer to receive all moneys
belonging to the Grand Lodge from the Grand Secretary, receipt
therefor, keep proper books of account thereof, and immediately
upon receipt of said moneys, to deposit same to the credit of
Grand Lodge, in a bank or banks selected by the Grand Treasurer with the approval of the Grand Master. Funds on deposit
shall be withdrawn by the Grand Treasurer, or in case of his
inability or unavailability, by . the Grand Master or Deputy
Grand Master and the Grand Secretary.

Paragraph No. 44

Your committee does not suggest that major deviations from the Code
exist but has observed various minor alternatives which have developed
which could weaken the internal controls provided. As an example, the
auditors made an observation on the control of the facsimile signature plate
used in the check signing machine. Actually, according to the Code, there
is no reason for the Grand Treasurer to have a facsimile plate in the Grand
Lodge office. The Grand Secretary has the duty of paying all bills from
the operating fund. The Grand Treasurer or the Assistant Grand Treasure
would periodically sign checks to reimburse the operating funds.
Paragraph No. 45

Auditors have made observations concerning one weakness in internal
control concerning membership of the Grand Treasurer on the Investment
Committee. They were concerned about too much authority being centered
in one individual. They pointed out in their memorandum report that the
Grand Treasurer, as a member of the Investment Committee, can implement authorized security transactions, can sign checks in payment for same,
and is associated with an investment firm through which some of the security
transactions have been carried out.
Paragraph No. 46

Over the many years of its existence, the Grand Lodge of California has
been singularly blessed with a continuing succession of great Masons, leaders
in the business and financial worlds, who have lent their talents to our Grand
Lodge in the office of Grand Treasurer and as investment counsellors. None
of our leaders of the past stand higher than our present Grand Treasurer
who has given so much and so freely of himself to Masonry and to this
Grand Lodge.

Paragraph No. 42

Your committee is convinced that the Code provides excellent internal
control with responsibilities soundly divided between the Grand Treasurer
and the Grand Secretary, subject always to review by auditors. Further,
we recommend that the procedures set forth in the Code be strictly adhered
to and not be deviated from for convenience or otherwise and, if for any
reason the Code is not operable it should be changed.
Paragraph 42 deals with adherence to procedures set
out in California Masonic Code. No formal vote taken
as no action was required.

MECHAN IZATION

SUMMARY

Paragraph No. 59

Paragraph No. 65

The volume of accounting transactions and the requirements for membership information suggests that modern data processing methods may be used
to advanta ge by the Grand Lodge. Such suggestions have been made and
there may have been implied criticism that a mechanization program has
not been further advanced.

This committee was charged by this Grand Lodge to make a study toward
effecting any possible economy or increased efficiency.

Paragraph No. 60

Your committee is well aware that data processing by modem electronic
equipment is a difficult and very expensive program. It would be relativel
y
easy to rush such a program into being; however, the risk of failure is real
and the waste of large development costs is possible. Successful data processing installations are the result of excruciating planning. It should also
be apprecia ted that such installations do not generally result in savings of
personnel or money, but they may contribu te operating advantages.

Paragraph No. 66

Your committee believes that this report conclusively illustrates that
economy and efficiency can only derive from a cohesive organization of
Grand Lodge and its entities. Under the Code, there can be but one Grand
Master and he with ultimate power over Grand Lodge and all entities. There
can be but one financial officer, the treasurer, responsible for all the cash
and other designated property of Grand Lodge and all entities. There can be
~ut one administrative officer, the secretary, responsible for the administratio~ ?f the Grand Lodge office including accounting for Grand Lodge
and all
e!ltities. The functions and responsibilities of these elected officers cannot be
by.passed or nullified by non-observance of the Code requirements.

294

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Paragraph No. 67

Anything other than this cohesive organization is difficult to contemplate
and could only result in waste, inefficiency and probably chaos.
Paragraph No. 68

Fortunately this concept of our organization has been recognized and
observed by the brethren working together In harmony even when it has
not been required by the regulations written into our Code.
Paragraph No. 69

This, your committee believes to be of the utmost importance. It is
entirely inconceivable to think in terms of a separate accounting method
for each entity of Grand Lodge. It would make mechanization infeasible
if our records wete not maintained on a uniform basis. Our costs would
swell if each of the entities employed its own administrative-clerical personnel.
We would elll.barrass ourselves if we had conflicting investment policies.
There are lhnumerable other examples, some of which are discussed in our
report.
P8'dgraph No. 70

And so, in summary, we recommend that to make all things possible
it be the policy of this Grand Lodge to recognize that all of the entities are
integral parts of the whole with common management represented by the
Grand Master under the authority granted him by the Code and a maximum
of common administration represented by the elected Grand Treasurer and
the Grand Secretary together with other common functions such as investment
control and retirement plans.
Paragraph No. 71

We also recommend that all officers, trustees, and boards and committees,
elected or appointed by the Grand Master, be made cognizant that their
activities are a part only of a greater whole and that harmony must always
be preserved in the interrelationships that exist.
Paragraphs 70 and 71 were considered jointly by
Grand Lodge. The Committee on Policy and General
Purposes offered the amendment to insert the word "office" between the words "common" and "administration"
in paragraph 70. It expressed its concurrence with the
principles set out in the paragraphs.
The amendment was adopted 5/6 vote.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes thereafter submitted the
following supplement for action by Grand Lodge.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes, in its discussions concerning the In-Depth Study Committee Report, found that it was frequently
directing its attention to what it regards as a fundamental policy for the
Grand Lodge organizational pattern. This policy is that the responsibility

295

of the Grand Treasurer and of the Grand Secretary, in their individual relationship to the governing boards of the various entities of Grand Lodge, is to
provide the facilities of their office for service to the boards.
It is not contemplated that the Grand Treasurer or the Grand Secretary
are to be members of the various Boards which they serve in their respective
capacities as Grand Treasurer and Grand Secretary.
We believe that full understanding of this fundamental principal is essential for assurance of thorough, conscientious and efficient execution of all
of the duties and responsibilities of the members of the various governing
boards and of the elected Grand Lodge officers involved.
The supplement was adopted.
Paragraphs 70 and 71 adopted as amended and supplemented 5/6 vote.

Paragraph No. 72

In concluding this report, your committee would be remiss if it did not
report the utmost cooperation of all the officers and employees of Grand
Lodge.
Paragraph No. 73

Your committee found the administration and operation of Grand Lodge
and its entities to be in the hands of loyal and devoted people, sincerely
attempting to do a good job, willing and anxious to do a better job whenever

and the Trust Agreement.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PAY OF MEMBERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Pay of Members submits the following report covering the 122nd Annual Communication of Grand Lodge.
Those entitled to mileage compensation are the Master, or in his absence,
the ranking Warden, or in the absence of the Master and Wardens, the duly
Elected Representative and Past Grand Masters, if they attend Grand Lodge
in such capacity only.
Mileage from the various points within the State of California to San
Francisco has been taken from the published records of the California State
Automobile Association. Mileage from points in the State of Hawaii to San
Francisco has been taken from the published records of air lines, in accordance with Sections 174 and 176, California Masonic Code. No compensation is allowed to members from San Francisco or the immediate vicinity.
Compensation of members from the State of California has been computed
on the basis of ten ( 10) cents per mile, the rate fixed by the Committee on
Finance. Compensation of members from the State of Hawaii has been
figured on the basis of published first class round trip air rates of regularly
scheduled major airlines, from Honolulu to San Francisco, plus inter-island
air fare to Honolulu when necessary.

To reply to sub-paragraph 2 pertaining to Quitman Lodge No. 88
and
its restoration.
North Bloomfield is in the Mother Lode country which is rich in Masoni
c
Lore. This town (North Bloomfield, California) and lodge site
is in the
Malakoff Diggins State Historical Park. During the gold rush days
this
was the site of a large placer mining operation.
The community of North Bloomfield was the adjacent town that
at its
peak had a population of about 1,000. Quitman Lodge No. 88
received
dispensation under the name of Unity Lodge on July 27, 1855.
It was
chartered as Quitman Lodge on May 8, 1856. It took its new name
from
John A. Quitman, P.G.M. of Mississippi. It first met in Orleans
Flat in
Nevada County. When the Diggings paid out there, it moved to
Moore's
Flat where it met until 1887. As the gold again ran out, the Lodge
moved
to North Bloomfield, which was about five miles to the southwest.
It stayed
at North Bloomfield until the gold of the Malakoff ran out. In 1910,
because
of small membership, Quitman Lodge consolidated with Nevada Lodge
No. 13.
The State of California, in making this site a state park, has marked
up the
site of many of the early buildings in North Bloomfield. The site of
Quitman
Lodge has been duly marked. There is nothing left of the building
, except
two or three foundation poles.
At the present time the State Depart ment of Parks and Recreation
has
authorized the restoration of the town of North Bloomfield to
its "Gold
Rush" eloquence. An old church is in the process of being built. The
general
store is being restored. There is a museum depicting scenes and display
ing
artifacts of that era. This has been done mostly with private or institut
ional
funds. It is the understanding of this committee that little or no state
funds
are to be available in the near future for any of these projects.
Many Masons are petitioning that Quitman Lodge be rebuilt and
restored on its original site in North Bloomfield. Research has develop
ed that
the original building was a two-story wood frame building. The first
floor
contained the commercial enterprise, a drugstore, with all the
lodge facilities being on the second floor. The estimated cost of reconstruction
is
between $60,000-$75,000, which includes facilities and displays.
Brother Charlie Gaus, now a member of Nevada Lodge No. 13,
was
the last man raised in Quitman Lodge No. 88 in 1909 and 1910.
He is 92
Years of age and still living in North Bloomfield.
The major problem in considering a recommendation to restore
this
lodge hall, regardless of our personal desires or wishes, is that
the park
does not own the land or site upon which the building would be constru
cted.
Rather it is owned by a private individual. While current negotia
tions are

305

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

in progress for obtaining this land or site, this has not been accomplished
to date. Until such time as the Park obtains ownership of the building site,
your committee cannot recommend any action from Grand Lodge.
Access to the Malakoff Diggins State Park is through Nevada City,
California by two routes.
The shortest is 14 miles, accessible by automobile. About one half the
distance is by paved road, the balance by dirt road. The turns can be
difficult to negotiate. The alternate route is 27 miles which would be necessary for bus travel or those who prefer a paved road.

REPORT OF CALIFORNIA MASONIC FOUNDATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The California Masonic Foundation, a non-profit, charitable corporation,
has been organized since March 5, 1969, and has now completed approximately two and one-half (2~) years of operations.
The Articles of Incorporation provide that there shall be fifteen ( 15)
members of the Board of Trustees, but during the past year, one member
resigned and has not been replaced; therefore, we have been functioning with
only fourteen (14) members. We also regret to report that one member,
Brother Fred B. Hack, of Piedmont, passed away. His place was filled by
Brother Paul F. Balck of San Francisco. Brother Hack was an able and
dedicated man and we express our heartfelt sympathy to his family.
Eight (8) of the trustees are from Southern California, four (4) from
Northern or Central California, one (1) from Santa Barbara, and one from
Hawaii. The names of the officers and trustees are hereinafter set forth.
During the past fiscal year, ending June 30, 1971, we have had many
collateral matters arise which have required much time and attention and
have, to some extent, interfered with the awarding of scholarships to worthy

RECLASSIFICATION OF THE FOUNDATION
During the month of November, 1970, we received notice from Internal
Revenue that we had been classified as a private foundation under the newly
enacted Internal Revenue Code, which has become commonly known as "The
Tax Reform Act of 1969." This classification was appealed, but no different
ruling was made - at least no notice thereof was received from Internal
Revenue, and we have proceeded upon the assumption that the classification
will stand.
This has necessitated numerous consultations with tax counsel, as well as
with the accounting firm of Touche Ross & Company to determine, first, just
what the chances were of reversing the private foundation classification and
second, just what restrictions are imposed upon a private foundation if the
classification remains.
As to the first item, it has now been pretty well determined that because
all of our assets came from one source, namely, Grand Lodge, we do not
qualify as a public foundation. As to the second matter, the restrictions on a
private foundation, while onerous in some respects, are not fatal, and will
not prevent us from accomplishing our charitable purposes.
Among other things, a private foundation must pay a tax of 4% (four
percent) on its net investment income, cannot engage in an unrelated business
without being taxed to the full extent, and there can be no "self dealing" by
a major contributor. These restrictions sound simple, but definitions, as in all
tax situations, are complicated and would require more space than is available
here to discuss in further detail.
THE UCLA CLUBHOUSE
We regret to report that the UCLA Clubhouse has not as yet been sold,
and title remains vested in the Foundation. This results in considerable annual
expense, including taxes, maintenance, and up-keep with no appreciable income therefrom to off-set such expense.
The property is now listed with Coldwell Banker Company under an
exclusive listing agreement for a period of six ( 6) months beginning August
17, 1971. Considerable interest has been shown in the property, both by
prospective purchasers and lessees, but thus far, there has been nothing of a
sufficiently definite nature to report at this time.
SCHOLARSHIPS
During the fiscal year ending June 30, 1971, we awarded approximately
eighteen (18) scholarships to various deserving and worthy students through-

306

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

out the State. The average award to each student was $400.00, although, in a
few instances, $500.00 was granted, and in others, $100.00. The total amount
of these grants was $8,600.00, but $4,000.00 was withheld, and either have
been, or will be, awarded during the current fiscal year.
We also have pending new applications which have been approved totalling
approximately fifty (50) at $400.00 each. It will be readily apparent from
this statistic, that a total of $20,000.00 will be needed to fund these applications alone, and that requests for assistance are increasing rapidly.

As will be seen from the section on scholarships, in order to fund the
scholarships already approved, some $20,000.00 will be needed. More and
more applications are being received, and it would appear to be most undesirable to curtail the program at this critical time, as its acceptance and
recognition by the Lodges is just beginning, and can become more and more
a factor for the advancement of Masonry throughout California and Hawaii.

BUDGET AND FINANCE

JoHN S. HUNT, Los Angeles, President

The report of Touche Ross & Company, Certified Public Accountants, as
at June 30, 1971, shows assets on hand of $345,337.00. At the same date a
year ago, they were $363,983.00.
Revenues for the year amounted to $25,055.00, derived almost entirely
from interest and dividends on investments. Actual expenses for the year
were $22,990.00, consisting of: Scholarship grants - $4,600.00; Clubhouse
expense - $15,966.00; Travel expense - $1,897.00; Miscellaneous $205.00; and reserve for excise tax (federal) - $322.00.
Added to these expenses, however, was a loss on sale of securities amounting to 20,822.00; so that there was a net excess of expenses over income
amounting to $18,757.00.
Investme nt policy is controlled entirely by the Investme nt Committee of
Grand Lodge. Said Committee recommended conversion of certain maturing
securities to tax-free municipal bonds, but later, upon advice of tax counsel,
the Investme nt Committee determined that it would be best to sell these
bonds, even at a substanti al loss, and re-invest in higher-yield securities so
that ultimately, the loss would be recovered.
Present investments consist primarily of security transactions in transit $183,020.00; bonds - $110,240.00; common stocks - $26,883.00. The
UCLA Clubhouse is carried at $1.00. Cash on hand as at June 30, 1971, was
$21,764.00.

MORNING SESSION-Thurs day, October 14, 1971
Grand Lodge was called on at 9:30 A.M., the Grand Master presiding.
Brother Safa Cicin, Master of Monterey Lodge No. 217, raised Grand Lodge.
The Grand Chaplain delivered the invocation. The minutes of the morning
session of Wednesday, October 13, were read and approved.

RESOLUTIONS
The Grand Secretary presented the following resolutions which were
referred by the Grand Master to the committees noted. Committee reports
and action taken are printed below each.

MASTER MASON DISTINGUISHED SERVICE CERTIFICATE
(1)
To the Most W01'shipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of Calif01'nia:
WHEREAS, recognition of services rendered contributes to the successful functioning of the Masonic activities, and
WHEREAS, frequently those who work hardest are not Officers or even
members of Grand Lodge and therefore are overlooked when compliments
are passed out, and
WHEREAS, it will be of assistance to Inspectors Masters and others
in authority if they can recommend brethren for reco~ition by the Grand
Master,
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that a new section be added
to the California Masonic Code to read as follows:
"Section 134.1. To cause to be issued a certificate of appreciation to
any Master Mason who has rendered outstanding service, whether or
not a member of Grand Lodge."
Respectfully submitted,
RoY E. RosWURM, M., No. 504
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence and on Policy and General

Purposes.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This resolution proposes to authorize a certificate of appreciation for any
Master Mason rendering outstanding service.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes is in complete accord
with the intent of the resolution. We point out that Grand Masters in the
past have issued certificates of appreciation such as, for example, the certificate to fifty-year members, certificate to Committeemen and Consultants,
some of whom were not members of Grand Lodge.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

309

Your Committee also believes a personal letter of appreciation from the
Grand Master will frequently afford greater pleasure and reward than a
printed certificate. In fact, we suggest that Master Masons knowing of outstanding service by one of their Brethren, would do well to communicate the
facts, by letter, to the Grand Master.
Since our law presently permits the action requested and since the resolution would only be restrictive, the Committee moves the adoption of the
Resolution and your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends
a "No" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Resolution No. 1 was referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence. This
Resolution proposes to add a new section to the California Masonic Code to
be numbered 134.1. As there is already a section with the number 134.1, this
section will be 134.2.
The Jurisprudence Committee offers the following Resolution:
RESOLVED that a new section be added to the California Masonic
Code to read as follows:
Section 134.2 Powers Continued
To cause to be issued a certificate of appreciation to any Master
Mason who has rendered outstanding service, whether or not a member
of Grand Lodge.
A majority voted against the resolution.

LIMIT GRAND MASTER'S EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONS
(2)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the California Masonic Code now provides for no more than
the establishment of six general Divisions of the Grand Lodge jurisdiction
in the State of California, and
WHEREAS, The California Masonic Code makes no provisions for the
realignment of said general Divisions, and
WHEREAS, Such re-alignment must, of necessity, occur in order to
maintain a balance of responsibility placed upon the Assistant Grand Lecturers whose duty it is to supervise such Divisions, and
WHEREAS, Proper authority to establish such re-alignment must be set
forth, in order to place resporisibility for such action and to guarantee the
stability of said Divisions,
BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED, That Section 158 of the California
Masonic Code be amended to read, in addition to its present wording, as
follows: No re-alignment of the six general Divisions of the Grand Lodge
Jurisdiction in the State of California shall be permitted, except under the
following conditions; that such re-alignment be requested by the Grand
'.Master; that a plan for said re-alignment be devised by the Grand Lecturer

The Committee on Ritual:
This resolution proposes that no realignment of Division shall be permitted
except under the following conditions:
The G~and Maste.r must first make a request that the Grand Lecturer,
together with the AsSlstant Grand Lecturers, devise a plan for said realignment.
That before the Grand Lecturer may submit such a plan to the Grand
Mast_er for his approval and implementation, he must first obtain the
unanimous consent of the six Assistant Grand Lecturers.
It is made quite clear in Section 156, paragraph 1st of the California
Maso~c Code that. it shall be the duty of the Grand Lecturer "to supervise
and direct ~e ~IStant Grand I:ecturers and the Inspectors in the performance of their duties, and to reqwre conformity with the adopted Ritual and
work." Paragraph 6th of the same section establishes that the Grand Lecturer shall preside over the Ritual Committee.
These Code sections establish that it is the duty of the Grand Lecturer
to recommend any change or realignment of Divisions which might become
necessary to the proper performance of the Ritual and work.
T? obtain ~ous.conse~t of al! six Assistant Grand Lecturers on any
~uestion can be difficult if not 1m~1ble, and if the dissent of any one As,.
Slstant Grand Lecturer could overrule the recommendation of the Grand
Lecturer, it would be impossible for him to perform the duties required of
him as head of the Ritual Committee.
This resolution would on the one hand deny the power of the Grand
Lecturer to make recommendations as to change or realignment of Divisions
but! on the other, would permit anyone subordinate officer, in this case an
AsSstant Grand Lecturer, to reject such recommendation a situation equivalent to granting an appointive Lodge officer the pow~r to overrule the
Master.
We very strongly urge a "No" vote.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
. Resolution No. 2 proposes that no re-alignment of the six General Divisions ?f the G~~d Lodge jurisdiction shall be permitted except under the
following conditions: that such re-alignment be requested by the Grand

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

311

Master; that a plan for re-alignment be devised by the Grand Lecturer with
full consent of the six Assistant Grand Lecturers; that said plan be subject
to ratification by each and all of the six general Divisions, such ratification
being attained by five-sixths majority vote of the Inspectors of the respective
Division.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes feels that this resolution as submitted will seriously circumscribe and limit the authority of the
Grand Master and destroy the fundamental phUosophy of our Grand Lodge.
Under our present system, as defined in the California Masonic Code,
the Grand Master, during the interval between communications of Grand
Lodge may exercise all its executive, judicial, and legislative powers; except
that of granting charters. All of his decisions and recommendations are then
submitted to Grand Lodge, to which he is responsible.
The California Masonic Code also states that the Grand Master shall
divide the jurisdiction into six general divisions and appoint an AsSstant
Grand Lecturer to each division but cannot create new divisions without
consent of Grand Lodge. Also, the Grand Master shall divide the jurisdiction
into districts and appoint for each district an Inspector.
We feel that a decision of the Grand Master should never be subjected to
ratification by an appointive Grand Lodge officer before such a decision can
go into effect. As we have previously noted, the decisions of the Grand Master
and the Grand Master's actions are reviewed and, either ratified or rejected,
by Grand Lodge, and by Grand Lodge alone.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes is aware that the sponsor
of this resolution has asked to delete that section which relates to Inspectors
and their ratification - but still contains that portion which refers to the
Grand Lecturer and the Assistant Grand Lecturers.
We are still of the opinion that no legislation should ever be enacted, that
in the minutest way, shall tie the hands of the Grand Master in carrying out
his duties, as prescribed in our California Masonic Code.
We move the adoption of this resolution and recommend a "No" vote.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
The Committee on Jurisprudence, to which this Resolution was referred,
reports as follows:
This Resolution, as presented, is said to limit the Grand Master's executive function in the re-alignment of the general Divisions of the Grand Lodge.
It recognizes that re-alignment must occur. It provides that, upon the Grand
Master's request, the Grand Lecturer, with the cooperation and consent of
all of the Assistant Grand Lecturers, shall submit a plan for the re-alignment
of the Divisions to the Grand Master. It originally provided that when approved by the Grand Master it must then be ratified by a vote of the Inspectors in each and all of the Districts, but the proponent has asked that
this requirement be deleted and we submit legislation on the Resolution a.s
amended.
The proposed resolution requires the amendment of Section 158.

(3)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Section 192, Standing Committees, presently states that the
Public Schools Committee, to consist of not less than fifteen nor more than
twenty-five members;
WHEREAS, the Metropolitan areas of the State of California have grown
by rapid strides;
WHEREAS, the Public Schools of California have grown and expanded
in urban areas relative to the State's growth;
WHEREAS, that by increasing the number of members on the Public
Schools Committee from a maximum of twenty-five to a maximum of thirty
members, greater assistance could be given to each constituent Lodge in the
overall Public Schools effort;
WHEREAS, the Grand Lodge of California has a vast resource of members whose talents could be more fully utilized by assignments to Standing
Committees;
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED: That Section 192 of the
California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
The following Standing Committee shall be appointed by the Grand

Juru:pruden~e, on Policy and General Purposes, on Lodge Fin~cing, to
coDSist of rune members each; on Public Schools, to consist of not less
than fifteen n~r more than· thirty members; on Charters, to consist of

The Committee on Finance:
Resolution No. 3 has been referred to the Committee on Finance. While
we do not question the sincere and honest efforts of the Public Schools Committee, we do question the need of increasing its size.
In view of the present activities of all Lodges and their awareness of
Public Schools Programs, together with the assistance provided by the In!lpectors with their Officers Associations, it is the opinion of your Committee
on Finance that the present Public Schools Committee of twenty-five plus
two consultants might even be too large.
Increasing the size of the Committee would call for an increase in the
budget appropriation contributing to a possible increase in the per capita tax.
We, therefore, recommend a "No" vote.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This resolution proposes to increase the membership of the Standing
$rnnuttee on Public Schools from 25 to 30 members.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes is keenly aware that
Masons support the Public Schools because a free public education system
for all is essential to the survival of our system of government. We find,
llo.rever, that since 1920 when then Grand Master Charles A. Adams founded
Public Schools Week the problems of the schools have greatly increased and
today Public Education is threatened with extinction. Masons should be
iafonned on all aspects of the "voucher plan," should be knowledgeable on
lbatters of school financing in light of the recent California State Supreme

314

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

Court decision and should be aware of what curriculum changes are doing
to public education. We believe it is no longer prudent or indeed of any
great value to have a Public School Week once a year and visit a classroom
one day a year and be of any genuine assistance in supporting our Public
Schools. We believe the functions of the Public Schools Committee should
encompass those matters we have suggested and its efforts on behalf of the
schools should be on an all year basis.
In our opinion this does not require additional members on the Committee.
for assistance can be obtained in every Lodge in California and Hawaii among
non-members of Grand Lodge as well as members of Grand Lodge.
We feel certain the Grand Master would personally seek the services of
any of the Brethren the Committee might require to assist in its work.
Those who undertake such service on behalf of the Committee are truly
performing a Masonic duty.
Your Committee is also aware of the added expense to Grand Lodge of
five new members on a Standing Committee.
We hope the Public Schools Committee will carry out such internal reorgani:r.ation as will enable it to perform the additional functions we have
suggested and any others they may find necessary for support of our Public
Schools by utilizing the scores of our Brethren who recognize the need and
can serve Freemasonry.
The Committee on Jurisprudence has authorized me to inform you that
the legislation proposed will carry out the intention of the proponents.
I move the adoption of the Resolution and the Committee on Policy
and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.
A simple majority voted for the resolution. Failing a 5/6 vote, the matter
was held until the 1972 Annual Communication as a "Proposed Amendmenii
to the Ordinances."

RESTORE MASONIC TEMPLE AT
MALAKOFF DIGGINGS STATE HISTORIC PARK

(4)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of Ca/.ifornia:
WHEREAS, the California State Department of Parks and Recreation in
1966 established the Malakoff Diggings State Historic Park, which includes
the historical and spectacular Malakoff Diggings and the site of the pioneer
town of North Bloomfield; and
WHEREAS, the Department of Parks and Recreation has authorized the
authentic restoration of the historic town of North Bloomfield as a living
demonstration of a pioneer gold rush settlement for posterity to observel
study and enjoy; and
WHEREAS, the Masonic Fraternity played a leading role in the settle"'
ment and development of the great State of California; and

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

315

WHEREAS, a Masonic Temple was among the first buildings erected in

all of the Mother Lode pioneer towns, the Lodge building of Quittman Lodge
Number 88 being erec~ in 1863; and
WHEREAS, the thousands of visitors to Malakoff Historic State Park
should have the opportunity to observe the importance of the Masonic
Fraternity in the pioneer settlements of California; and
WHEREAS, the restoration of the Masonic Temple in North Bloomfield
will provide an historic and interesting Lodge room for all Lodges of this
jurisdiction to conduct visitations and degree work by reservation, and a
Masonic museum of interest to visiting Masons of all jurisdictions; and
WHEREAS, the Malakoff Historic State Park provides facilities for
picnicking, camping, swimming, panning gold, overnight cabins, scenic wonlers, a musuem and a trout stream, thereby providing entertainment for
the families of Lodge members conducting visitations; and
WHEREAS, the California Department of Parks and Recreation must
enlist the aid of many private groups and agencies in restoring the pioneer
town of North Bloomfield, since state funds are not available to reconstruct
buildings in the $30,000 to $60,000 price range; and
WHEREAS, nothing remains of the Lodge building of Quittman Lodge
Number 88 but traces of the foundation; and
WHEREAS, the old Catholic Church is already in the process of retf.oration; and
WHEREAS, Mr. William Penn Mott, Jr., Director of the Department
of Parks and Recreation, and Mr. Ray Hunter, Deputy Director, have
pledged full cooperation and support for the Grand Lodge Free & Accepted
Masons of California in a program to rebuild the North Bloomfield Masonic
Temple; and the project is likewise approved and supported by the Citizens
~visory Committee for Malakoff State Park, and the Park Superintendent
aas pledged the labors of his carpenters and maintenance personnel to reduce
the cost of construction; and
WHEREAS, this resolution was defeated in 1969 and 1970 because the
Committee on Policy and General Purposes felt Grand Lodge must establish
a firm policy governing the rebuilding or restoring of historic Masonic buildings, and entering into cooperative agreements with the California State
Department of Parks and recreation and other public agencies for such
projects; and
WHEREAS, such a policy is being adopted by means of a special comlllittee appointed by the Grand Master for this purpose during the current
Year, and under the provisions of an accompanying resolution; and
WHEREAS, the rebuilding of the old Masonic Temple at North Bloomield will constitute an important milestone in the history of our ancient and
labnorable fraternity by displaying the leading role played by our pioneer

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 4 is a renewed proposal for the rebuilding of the Temple
of Quittman Lodge No. 88 in the Malakoff Diggings State Historic Park at
North Bloomfield. The proposal calls for the appropriation of needed funds
up to a maximum of i6o,ooo, if required, prior to January 1, 1972. The
proposal to rebuild this historic temple is placed before this Grand Lodge for
the third successive year.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes again states its belief
that the proposal to rebuild the Masonic Temple at North Bloomfield is
worthy and that it should be accomplished, and again we commend the
Brethren who have worked so diligently and with so much enthusiasm toward
that end. We still believe that Grand Lodge must establish a ti.rm policy
respecting proposals of this kind. We believe that a satisfactory policy has
not yet been developed.
Your Committee, some of whose members have carefully studied the
details of the present status and situation of the Malakoff Diggings State
Historic Park, also believes that further delay in embarking upon this
project will not endanger the possibility of restoration of the Temple of
Quittman Lodge No. 88. As we reported to you at the 1970 Annual COID·
munication, we believe that the point of commitment for the project has
not been reached and we accordingly urge a "No" vote on Resolution No. 4.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 6 proposes the adoption of a policy concerning the restoration of historic Masonic buildings. At both the 1969 and 1970 Annual
Communications your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, in reporting on the proposals to rebuild the Temple of Quittman Lodge No. 88
at North Bloomfield in the Malakoff Diggings State Historic Park, recommended the appointment of a special committee to develop and propose
a policy for the Grand Lodge concerning the restoration of historic Masonic
buildings. Grand Master Huebner appointed such a committee and on
Tuesday, October 12th, of this Communication you heard the report of that
committee.
It is the opinion of your Committee on Policy and General Purposes
that Resolution No. 6, in limiting restorations to be financed by the Grand
Lodge to locations only within the boundaries of publicly owned parks and
Jnstitutions, does not propose a policy that adequately copes with the
problem of Grand Lodge responsibility and participation in the area of
historic site restoration and preservation.
Historically important Masonic buildings and sites are not limited to
those located within state or national parks, or similar publicly owned areas.
As time passes there will undoubtedly be many proposals for preservation
of places of importance to the history of Freemasonry in this jurisdiction.
It is the belief of your Committee that the policy proposed in Resolution
No. 6 is too limiting to be acceptable. In short, it is our opinion that this
Grand Lodge can and should develop a more adequate and embracing policy
than that which is proposed in this resolution.
I am authorized to state that the Committee on Finance concurs in this
report.
I move adoption of Resolution No. 6 and your Committee on Policy
and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.
The Committee on Historical Site Restoration and Preservation did not
report.
A majority voted against the resolution.

The Committee <>n Masonic History:
Resolution No. 6 clearly lays out the guide lines for the restoration
and maintenance of old Masonic Temples.
Your Committee on Masonic History appreciates all of the thought and
work that has gone into this resolution.
We feel that guide lines should be laid out for the restoration and
maintenance of Masonic Temples. But we believe that this resolution is
much too limiting in its scope.
1. There may be Masonic Temples not located on public lands that
Grand Lodge may wish to restore and could not when limited by the intent
of this resolution.
2. This resolution calls for Grand Lodge to expend its funds and then
deed the property over to a State agency.
3. This resolution also calls for the State to make certain concessions
to the Masonic Fraternity by making available the use of the buildings to
Masonic groups upon advance reservation - at any time. This would make
guided tours unavailable to the public at the time the Fraternity wishes to
use it. We do not know if the State can fulfill such a commitment.
In view of these facts your Committee on Masonic History recommends
a "No" vote on this resolution.

WEARING OF APRONS

(9)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS: This Grand Lodge has not previously adopted an apron
~ropriate to the Rank of Past Master, even though the Rank and Title
of Past Master is clearly established and defined in Section 490 of the
California Masonic Code; and
WHEREAS: Many of our Brethren have expressed a desire to wear an
apron appropriate to their Rank or Station at the "Public" or open Installation of Officers;
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED: That Section 328.1 be added
to the California Masonic Code, reading as follows:
328.1. Wearing of Aprons. The apron appropriate to ones Rank or
Station may be worn at any gathering of Masons at which Officers of Lodges
are authorized to wear the apron of their respective Stations, and further,
that those who hold the Title and Rank of Past Master as defined in Section
490 of the California Masonic Code, may wear a Past Masters Apron having
the Jewel of a Past Master upon it, except that a Past Master shall not
wear said Past Masters Apron while occupying any Officers Station in conferring the Degrees of Masonry, but shall wear the Apron of the Station
which he is occupying for said conferral.
Respectfully submitted,
H. DOUGLAS LEMONS, P.M.,

ADVERTISING- PUBLICATIONS-APPLICANTS
(11)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, under existing Masonic law, a Lodge alone has authority to
inform its own members of the names of its candidates and the dates of
conferral of the several degrees; and
WHEREAS, many Masonic associations exist for the primary purpose
of promoting Masonic fellowship and to encourage attendance at the Initiation, Passing and Raising of fellow employees or business associates; and
WHEREAS, there are good reasons for permitting Masonic associations,
under proper safeguards, to inform their members of the names of candidates
and dates of conferral of degrees on fellow employees or business associates;
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that there be added to
Section 334 of the California Masonic Code (or the revised section) the
following paragraph:
"On obtaining permission of the Master of a Lodge in which a degree
is to be conferred, a Masonic association, which shall be an organized group
of Masons with common employment or profession and with a membership
of not less than twenty-five Master Masons of this jurisdiction in good
standing, may inform its members by bulletin or letter enclosed in sealed
envelopes, by United States mail, of the name of an elected candidate and
the dates of conferral of the several degrees."
Respectfully submitted,
ROBT. IRONS, S.W., No. 545
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, and on Policy and General
Purposes.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Section 356 of the California Masonic Code; specifically, Article IX,
Section I of the Ordinances; provides for the payment of annual Lodge
dues quarterly in advance. Under the provisions of Section 356 of the Code
as it now stands if an increase in dues is legislated and approved. it becomes
effective at the increased rate on the first day of the quarter next following.
The effect of this resolution would be to defer the effective due date of the
increase to the following January 1st even though the increase was voted.
and approved in the preceding January or February.
It is the opinion of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes that
while a probable great majority of our Brethren are able and do meet the
annual dues for the support of the Lodge and its obligations in a single payment it is, nonetheless, a regrettable fact that some of our older Brethren
living on limited. and fixed. incomes are unable to do so and we believe that
the Code provision of the payment of dues on a quarterly basis is wise and
fraternally considerate. Certainly, if a Lodge has determined. that a need
exists for increased revenue from dues and a necessary amendment is legislated, for example, in February there seems to be no substantial reason why
eleven months must elapse before that need can be met. The Code presently
provides for effective relief on the first day of the subsequent quarter.
It is the opinion of the Committee that fraternal consideration for the
whole membership far outweighs a possible, but improbable, "complication
of records" as referred to in this resolution. The Committee moves the adoption of this resolution and unanimously recommends a "No" vote.

Sec. 512. The question as to the moral and physical sufficiency of the
applicant shall be left to the sound discretion of the Lodge. When the

the aid of a prosthesis or hearing device, the Master shall state the nature
and extent of his disabilities to the Lodge before the ballot is taken and

under directions from Grand Lodge so as to preserve the uniformity of

Resolutions Nos. 14 and 15 pertain to our law respecting physical qualification of Candidates for the degrees of Masonry in this jurisdiction. Your
Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends that action on these
two resolutions be deferred until the 1972 Annual Communication.
On Tuesday last you heard the full report of the Special Committee on
Physical Qualifications. It is a carefully prepared and thorough report,
presenting in a fine manner opposing views on this most difficult subject.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes proposes that mimeographed copies of this report be forthwith sent to every Lodge in this jurisdiction in order that the members of the Lodges may have the opportunity
of hearing or reading the report. In the judgment of this Committee two
important benefits would accrue:
1. The opportunity for thoughtful judgment of the issue by the members
of the Lodge and an instruction or indication to their Officers to guide
them as they may be called upon to vote on proposals being considered
by Grand Lodge.
2. The opportunity for Masonic education of the members of the Lodges
as many members may for the first time become aware of the history
and philosophy behind our law respecting physical qualifications.

Committees on Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes, and Ritual will

form for submission to the Grand Lodge at the next Annual Communication

Well-qualified men who through mis-fortune have suffered physical impairment requiring the need for prosthesis, and are currently restricted from
applying for the degrees of Masonry, and
. WHEREAS, Since we no longer work in operative Masonry but speculative only, this restriction is now obsolete, and
WHEREAS, In numerous Masonic jurisdictions around the world with
whom we are in fraternal accord, have eliminated this restriction without
detriment to the Craft and without incurring the displeasure of the rest of
the Masonic fraternity, and
WHEREAS, It is now one of our basic and universally accepted teachings
and precepts that it is the internal and not the external qualifications which
recommend a man to be made a Mason, and
WHEREAS, Section 511 and 512 of the C.M.C. regulations "having no
maim or defect in his body that may render him incapable of learning the
art, and physically able to conform substantially to what the several degrees
respectively require of him" would be conformed to if the candidate would
be permitted to use prosthesis while taking the degrees of Masonry.

THEREFO RE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the question as to the physical
sufficiency of the applicant shall be left to ·the sole discretion of the Lodge.
The Master shall state the nature and extent of the disabilities to the Lodge
before ballot is taken,
BE IT FURTHE R RESOLVED, that all references, rules and regulations
pertaining to physical restrictions of Masonic candidates be rescinded.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This resolution proposes to reduce the minimum age for applicants for
)fasonry among DeMolays who have reached the age of 19 years and details
certain other requirements. The Section cited therein incorrectly refers to
Article V, Section 208 as contained in the Ross Digest whereas the proper
citation is Article V, Section 511-a, of the California Masonic Code.
It is recognized that some Grand Jurisdictions accept applicants of 18
years of age and older. It is the opinion of the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes that if it is desirable to reduce the age limit for DeMolays
it should be desirable to similarly accept all applicants of the same age. To
limit the age reduction to DeMolays only would create two classes of applicants and we believe this to be contrary to Masonic principles.
I move the adoption of this Resolution. The Committee on Policy and
General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

(17)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, some Master Masons postpone becoming proficient in the
Third Degree; and
WHEREAS, those who are Master Masons should be fully aware of the
psponsibilities they assume at the conclusion of the Third Degree; and
WHEREAS, those who take the Third Degree proficiency examination
do become more fully informed of their Masonic responsibilities; and
WHEREAS, education and knowledge of such responsibilities are the
key to the fulfillment of Masonic effectiveness;

334

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, That each newly raised
Mason b~ required to become proficient in the Third Degree as well as the
First and Second before being acknowledged as a Master Mason.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the appropriate additions, deletions,
or adjustments be made in our Masonic Law and/or Ritual to accomplish the
intent of this resolution.
